What we know about Cornell University frat house rape investigation

BBC News Thu, 01 Oct 2026 18:26:26 GMT

New York state prosecutors have reopened an investigation into the alleged rape of a woman at Cornell University in 2024.

The woman filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university on 16 September alleging she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house at the university.

She also alleged that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved.

The men have been dubbed the "Cornell Seven" and the woman was identified as Jane Doe in court filings.

Cornell has said it supported presenting the case to a grand jury, while rejecting claims that it failed to punish those involved. It has also agreed to have the case examined by an independent investigator.

Here's what we know.

In a 101-page civil lawsuit, the woman alleged that on the night of 19 October 2024, seven men from Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity chapter assaulted her for hours in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine.

She was a 20-year-old Cornell undergraduate at the time.

Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and incapable of providing consent.

She said she left her sorority sisters after drinking that night and "stumbled alone" to the Chi Phi fraternity house in the city of Ithaca to see a male friend.

The lawsuit alleges sexual assault and battery, negligence, breach of contract and violations of New York's Human Rights Law.

It was filed against the university, fraternity sorority and men involved in the alleged attack.

The lawsuit contains an image purported to be from a fraternity group chat in which a participant alerted other members, in vulgar terms, to the potential for a sexual encounter with Doe.

Her lawyer has said she was "traumatised, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened" in the days after the assault, which she reported to Cornell University Police on 8 November 2024.

The outrage in recent weeks grew when Doe alleged in her lawsuit that the men were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays".

Doe's lawyer has said two of those involved were expelled. He has told CBS that the woman dropped out of university after the alleged assault.

Cornell newspaper's editorial board published the names of the defendants in the lawsuit on 21 September in a piece titled "Cornell Won't, We Will", fuelling outcry on social media.

The Cornell University Police Department provided an image of the Snapchat group, titled Chi Phi Actives, to prosecutors as evidence in November 2024, the university said.

The members are named in the chat and discuss a "free" sexual encounter with Jane Doe, using coarse language, just before 02:00 local time on 20 October 2024.

CBS News New York has also published excerpts of additional text messages reportedly exchanged between one of the defendants and a woman who appears to be the person who made the allegations.

The messages were reportedly sent two days after the alleged assault.

In one message, one of the men appeared to apologise for "how things went down".

He said his memory was "kinda fuzzy", and that he and another man felt bad for being too intoxicated to "shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand".

The woman in the text chain replied saying her memory was "super clouded too" and that they were all intoxicated.

She also wrote that "non(e) of the sexual stuff was illegal" and that she liked being with him and another man.

Doe suggested they smoke together again, but leave out "the extra five billion men and ketamine".

The woman said she reported the incident to Cornell University Police two weeks after it took place.

Shortly afterwards, Cornell University issued a public statement regarding the "serious and deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house".

It said the campus police department was investigating and that it had suspended the local chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity, as well as "a number of students".

Cornell also said it had opened an internal investigation as well as a civil rights inquiry under the Title IX law, which bars sex discrimination in schools that receive funding from the federal government, including most universities.

Following the new lawsuit, the university disputed Doe's allegation that it did not adequately investigate or punish the alleged perpetrators.

The university said in a statement that the matter was referred to a "panel of trained faculty and staff" that issued "a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell".

Cornell did not deny the punishment for some of those involved included writing an essay. It said: "None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement."

Cornell said in a statement on Tuesday that "temporary suspensions and other restrictive measures" were issued when the conduct was reported.

It also said the events that took place on its campus in 2024 "were appalling then and remain so now".

"We are doing all we can to foster a culture where sexual misconduct is never tolerated," it said.

On Wednesday, New York state Governor Kathy Hochul said that she had called the university president, who had agreed to allow "an independent outside investigation of what happened".

"They understand the importance of this," Hochul said in a post on X, adding that "this culture has to stop". Cornell confirmed the independent investigation to the BBC.

The Xi Chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.

Doe named Chi Phi fraternity as one of the defendants in her civil lawsuit, alleging she suffered physical and emotional damage as a result of their actions.

Trey Robb, interim executive director of the Chi Phi fraternity, said in a statement that the organisation had expelled the accused members of Cornell's chapter.

"Our records confirm that just three days after 'Jane Doe' filed a police report, the Xi chapter voted unanimously to remove the accused members from its rolls," Robb said.

"The chapter also recommended that our national fraternity permanently expel them, and our Grand Council did so at a subsequent meeting."

The fraternity "will not comment on matters before the courts or under investigation", Robb said.

The county's top prosecutor said on Monday that his office would reopen a criminal inquiry into the alleged rape.

Once appropriate charges were determined, the case would be prosecuted "in the most objective and impartial means possible" through a grand jury, said Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten.

In the US legal system, prosecutors convene grand juries to weigh evidence and testimony, and eventually vote on whether they merit criminal charges.

The prosecutor said that at the time of the assault two years ago, his office concluded that evidence from the woman's statement to authorities did not meet the legal bar to bring charges.

He said he contacted Doe and her lawyers for more information as he prepared to bring the case to a grand jury.

In his statement, Van Houten included a summary of what Doe told the Cornell University Police Department in 2024 after the alleged attack, noting it differed from the allegations laid out in the lawsuit.

"Jane Doe's sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped," Van Houten said in a statement on Monday.

"On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual."

A Cornell University spokesperson told the BBC that its police department shared a "lengthy police investigation report" with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office.

New reports have detailed what Doe reported to Cornell University's police following the incident.

CBS News New York obtained a transcript of Doe's interviews with campus police that began on 14 November - more than three weeks after the incident.

She tells police of the initial sexual encounter: "I was pretty OK with all of this."

But the outlet reports that she said of what happened later: "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."

ABC News also obtained a police report from 15 November, in which Doe said in a statement that during one of the later encounters that night, "I felt like I was unable to make any decision because of how intoxicated I was".

"To me, that felt like coercion," she said in her statement. "Also I felt like due to my intoxication, they should have known how intoxicated I was based on how I was slurring my words."

The BBC has contacted Van Houten's office and Doe's attorney.

Van Houten told CBS News he had never seen the transcript of the interview with campus police.

He also told the New York Times on Wednesday that he hoped to speak to Doe "to discuss new evidence that exists".

Van Houten told the Times he did not believe the allegations in the civil lawsuit meet the legal bar to bring charges.

He did note that "the significance of it means that she believes that crimes were committed, and we want to get to the bottom of that".

There has been a palpable tension on Cornell's campus since Doe filed her civil lawsuit in September.

The BBC spoke to students and a faculty member who said there was a "dark cloud" hanging over the school. Many chose to remain anonymous.

One senior who was on campus at the time of the alleged assault in 2024 told the BBC that it had been a hard time to be there, as rumours began circulating about Doe.

Now, two years later, the student described how she and her friends felt "overwhelmed" and "disappointed" because they believed Cornell greatly mishandled things, adding that it was hard to focus on their classes.

A faculty member also described the mood on campus as being "dismal".

Staff are not trained therapists, she said, so it was hard to know how to navigate these discussions with students.

"Incredible situation that was so... I just don't understand," she said.

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide.

A list of UK organisations that can help is available here.

HMRC urged to scrutinise tax implications of Man City case

BBC News Thu, 01 Oct 2026 18:21:22 GMT

Manchester City were found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges against them

Findings from the Premier League's case against Manchester City require scrutiny from His Majesty's Revenue and Customs, the chair of a cross-party group of MPs has told the tax authority.

It was confirmed on Tuesday that an independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

City have repeatedly denied guilt, and have signalled an intent to lodge an appeal by Friday.

The club were found to have artificially inflated revenue through "sham" sponsorship agreements with the help of their owners.

The independent commission which studied the case found City "utilised devices" to "disguise the true extent of certain club liabilities".

The Treasury Committee, which is responsible for overseeing policies and administration of HMRC, has therefore asked whether the government department has requested the redacted documents contained within the commission's report.

Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury Committee, said she would "welcome reassurance from HMRC that you are seized of the importance of these issues and the public interest in this case".

The letter follows a report from the Tax Policy Associates, external which claims City failed to pay as much as £12m in unpaid tax because of a "sham" contract with former manager Roberto Mancini.

In addition to unpaid income tax and National Insurance, the report claims City could face a penalty charge that would take their liabilities to £24m.

Manchester City vs The Premier League

Man City not 'above the rules', says No 10 after backlash to Burnham remarks

Manchester City will claim as part of their appeal that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners.

Owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy prime minister Sheikh Mansour - are said to have topped up the value of commercial deals as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of £830.69m.

This, it was argued, enabled the club to appear to comply with Premier League and Uefa financial rules.

However, as first reported by the Daily Mail and Times, sources have told BBC Sport that City are expected to tell an appeal board that they have evidence showing the money directed to state-owned sponsors came from the Abu Dhabi government, rather than from ADUG.

Premier League rules allow state-owned bodies to sponsor clubs.

In its 40-page decision, the independent commission detailed how City had "denied there had ever been any disguised funding scheme of the type alleged by the Premier League. Its case was that [it] had misunderstood how Abu Dhabi sponsorship agreements had been funded... The reality was [the club contested] that Abu Dhabi sponsors had always been liable for all recorded sponsorship fees and all had in fact been paid to the club by Abu Dhabi sponsors from their own funds/resources.

"No part of any recorded sponsorship fee had been paid by ADUG or from using ADUG funds. Abu Dhabi sponsors had from time to time applied for financial assistance from the Abu Dhabi government toward their liability to pay the recorded sponsorship fees - such applications had been granted…"

The independent commission rejected this submission as "untrue", saying: "We concluded that it was an 'explanation' that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the disguised funding scheme."

This video can not be played

How did Man City's 'disguised funding scheme' work?

City's argument is likely to lead to renewed debate over the extent to which City's ownership is separate from the Abu Dhabi state, and over the ramifications of club ownership with state connections.

Mansour is a member of the ruling family of Abu Dhabi, and the brother of UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

Since the takeover in 2008, City have insisted the club is a completely private enterprise, and not state-owned. However, some critics have questioned the distinction, with human rights campaigners claiming the ownership of City has been used to "sportswash" the UAE.

On Saturday, City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak referred to "irrefutable evidence" that he claimed supports the club's claims of innocence. City have claimed the commission's decision contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe".

It has emerged that Al Mubarak, who was appointed chairman of City following the takeover in 2008, is named as an Emirati diplomat on the UK government's current directory of all foreign representatives.

Representatives of foreign states and their diplomatic staff "enjoy privileges and immunities under the Diplomatic Privileges Act (1964)", giving diplomats immunity from prosecution under criminal, civil and administrative laws.

City's principal sponsor Etihad Airways has said it is considering legal action against the Premier League, claiming the release of the commission findings had "damaging implications… despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings".

The UAE's state-owned national airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".

Etihad is owned by sovereign wealth fund L'Imad which is chaired by the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, the son of the UAE president.

The Premier League declined to comment when contacted by BBC Sport.

Additional reporting from James Landale, diplomatic correspondent for BBC News.

Man City not 'above the rules', says No 10 after backlash to Burnham remarks

BBC News Thu, 01 Oct 2026 17:26:40 GMT

Downing Street has said Manchester City are not "above the rules" after Andy Burnham was criticised for his comments about the club's breaches of Premier League financial rules.

The prime minister said on Wednesday he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners decide to sell up after City were found guilty by an independent commission of most of the 115 charges they faced.

His remarks were branded "completely out of touch" and "extraordinary" by the Tories and took many in the football community by surprise.

In a statement following the backlash, Downing Street said the PM had made clear "the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules".

In an attempt to clarify the PM's position, a No 10 spokesperson added: "He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.

"Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."

Man City deny any wrongdoing and have until Friday to submit an appeal.

Sources told BBC Sport that City are expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

The Premier League said City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

In an interview on Wednesday with the BBC's political editor Chris Mason, Burnham - who was mayor of Greater Manchester until June - said he was "not getting directly involved in the process", saying it must be undertaken independently by the Premier League.

He said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and it would be "wrong" to "jump to a conclusion".

Asked if he was worried the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, a royal and the United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister - might sell up, Burnham said: "I would be really concerned to lose them.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

"I can't intervene more in the process, it would be wrong for me to do that."

In response, the Tories accused Burnham of "publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues" and questioned whether "political pressure" was being applied.

Shadow minister for sport Louie French called for the government to "keep politics out of football and ensure the Premier League's independent commission can do its job free of outside influence".

"The club face unprecedented allegations and fans are horrified by what they are reading in the papers," the Tory MP said.

"Yet Burnham is publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues. Fans will rightly ask whether political pressure is being applied here and how it relates to the owners' well-reported investments in Manchester.

"Football must be governed independently, with the rules applying equally to everyone. Fans deserve confidence that no club or owner is above those rules."

And Lib Dem MP Anna Sabine, the party's spokesperson on sport, said: "Fans of every club deserve to know the rules apply to everyone... Burnham needs to remember he's prime minister for everyone, not just Manchester."

It comes as the chairwoman of the Commons Treasury committee, Labour MP Dame Meg Hillier, wrote to HMRC on Thursday to ask for reassurance that it has "seized of the importance" of the case for any potential tax implications.

In his BBC interview, Burnham also said he was "of course" confident that his own interactions with City's owners as Greater Manchester mayor would stand up to scrutiny.

He compared City's situation to how the club he supports, Everton, had been charged with a more minor breach of Premier League financial rules in 2023, but said he "hold[s] the view very firmly that they weren't fairly treated in that process".

Burnham made his comments amid widespread shock in football about the scale of the independent commission's findings – and the strength of Premier League comments about City's actions.

The independent panel that found City guilty of rule breaches will hold a sanctions hearing – which could take months to convene – to decide the punishment, which could include a huge fine or points deduction.

City have maintained their innocence of all the accusations made.

The chairman of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) – set up by the government in 2025 – said the case had raised "serious issues".

In a statement, David Kogan said the IFR "has powers to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives and we will use these powers where appropriate", while "taking account of the findings made by the Leagues".

He added that proceedings remain ongoing and he hoped for a quick resolution.

Travelodge failed sex assault victim 'at every stage'

BBC News Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:40:03 GMT

A woman who was sexually assaulted by a man given a key to her hotel room was "fundamentally failed" by Travelodge "at every stage", an independent review has found.

Barrister Paul Greaney KC said the chain's security policies at the time of the attack at its Maidenhead hotel in December 2022 were "not fit for the purpose of keeping guests safe".

He found guests were still not as safe as they should be, with room intrusions reported at nearly one-in-10 Travelodge hotels this summer, and no policy in place on violence against women and girls.

Travelodge apologised "unreservedly" to the woman. The review did credit the company with making changes since March.

Kyran Smith, who obtained the key by falsely claiming to be the woman's boyfriend, was jailed for seven-and-a-half years in January.

The review found he was handed the key less than three minutes after approaching the reception desk, by a receptionist who had received no training in key security.

Greaney said blame rested with Travelodge, that has its HQ in Thame, Oxfordshire, as an organisation rather than with individual staff, and a culture had developed in which room intrusions were regarded as "one of those things".

The woman emailed a complaint to Travelodge in January 2023, addressed to chief executive Jo Boydell and others.

The review concluded the email was handled by her office without her knowledge, and did not come to Boydell's attention until March 2026.

The woman's complaint was instead investigated by a manager who was himself criticised in it, and the customer services team offered her a refund for her night's stay, which she understood to be £30.

Boydell stepped down as chief executive in August following criticism over the company's handling of safety complaints. The review said she deserved credit for driving improvements from March.

The attack became national news in March after the woman contacted the BBC, saying the case raised serious questions about room security at Travelodge hotels.

Since then, dozens of people have shared experiences of strangers entering their rooms, including a domestic abuse victim whose abuser was given a key to her room at a Travelodge in London.

Then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer wrote to Boydell in March urging her to "seriously engage" with the government over security. Greaney was appointed to lead the review the following month.

The review makes 38 recommendations, including moving towards a system that requires guests to show ID to get a room key, which Travelodge has been trialling at some hotels since May.

It also calls for body-worn cameras for reception staff, better checks that staff have understood their training, and for housekeepers to always send guests to reception.

Greaney said Travelodge must "urgently" create a policy on violence against women and girls, drawn up with the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, and train all staff in it.

The review said changes made this year had been done quickly "albeit years too late" and its new key security policy would prevent a repeat of the Maidenhead attack if applied correctly.

But it found the policy was "not being applied with anything like sufficient consistency on the ground".

Mystery shoppers were able to get into rooms through housekeeping staff at all five hotels tested, including Maidenhead, without being sent to reception or asked for proof they were entitled to enter.

At three of the hotels, staff confirmed a guest was staying there, and at two, room numbers were said out loud at check-in. The Maidenhead hotel scored worst of the five.

Other recommendations included networked CCTV across the chain and key card-controlled access to all residential corridors.

Greaney said room intrusions were a problem across the hotel sector.

He praised the woman's courage and determination, saying the problems would have remained "beneath the surface" had she not shared her experience.

Freddie van Mierlo, the Liberal Democrat MP for Henley and Thame, where Travelodge is based, said he was worried the company was "still trying to do safety on the cheap".

He said the review's recommendations would require "significant capital investment", and Travelodge needed to make clear it was prepared to deliver that.

In response, a Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are committed to implementing the recommendations and will make the necessary investments to do so.

"We cannot provide a specific figure but can assure people that all required investments in guest safety will be made and we have the resources required."

Ray Reidy, Travelodge's interim chief executive, said the review made clear there were failures in its policies and in the way customers had been treated.

"I apologise unreservedly on behalf of Travelodge to all guests where we have failed," he said.

"We have made significant progress in preventing and addressing these issues over the past six months, and we recognise we still have further to go."

Travelodge said a new board committee would oversee the changes, with independent assessments of its progress after six and 12 months.

England avoid Australia & India in World Cup draw

BBC News Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:31:47 GMT

Holders Australia beat India in the 2023 final

England have avoided defending champions Australia and world number one-ranked side India in the group-stage draw for the 2027 ICC Men's Cricket World Cup.

India and Pakistan are, once again, placed in the same group, alongside Australia, Afghanistan, Zimbabwe and a qualifier.

England, who won the trophy in 2019, are in the same group as co-hosts South Africa, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, New Zealand and a qualifier.

Harry Brook's side, who have enjoyed a resurgence in the 50-over format, begin their campaign against Bangladesh on 8 October, and Sri Lanka on 13 October in Windhoek, Namibia.

They will come up against South Africa in Gqeberha on 16 October before travelling to Harare to face a qualifier on 20 October. They round off the group stage when they face New Zealand, again in Gqeberha, on 23 October.

The visit to Zimbabwe is significant, with England having not played there since 2004.

Political unrest in Zimbabwe under the regime of former president Robert Mugabe caused problems for England's men's team throughout the 2000s.

England boycotted their fixture against Zimbabwe in Harare at the 2003 World Cup - a decision which ultimately derailed their campaign.

Relations have improved in recent years, however, and BBC Sport reported in 2025 that the two cricket boards were discussing a potential England tour of the country in the next cycle of international cricket between 2027 and 2031.

After three matches to decide the final two qualifiers, the tournament group stage will open with a repeat of the 2023 final when India and Australia face each other in Cape Town on 7 October.

Arch-rivals India and Pakistan, who do not play each other outside tournaments, will meet in Johannesburg on 10 October.

The top three, plus the best fourth-placed finisher, from the two groups progress to the Super 7 stage.

From there, the top four teams will qualify for the semi-finals, which are scheduled for 17 and 18 November, before the final on 21 November in Johannesburg.

Liberal Democrat MPs have criticised their party leader over his defence of the pension triple lock.

Senior Lib Dems, who are on the party's frontbench, have privately attacked Sir Ed Davey for his response to the prime minister's plans to adjust the policy, which guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% – whichever is highest.

They joined unsolicited criticism in public and private from others in the party, with one saying the majority of Lib Dem MPs disagree with their leader.

It comes after Sir Ed told the BBC removing the triple lock "would put more pensioners into poverty".

"This would mean people who are working hard now - the millennials - when they retire would have a very poor pension," he told the Today programme.

Under Andy Burnham's plan - which he hopes will raise £15bn a year by the end of the 2030s - the automatic annual link with average earnings would be removed from 2030 so the state pension rises with at least 2.5% or inflation, whichever is higher.

"His proposals are to deal with social care in the next decade when it needs to be done now," Sir Ed said.

"It's a little bit of a vibe. It's not a solution," he said.

But multiple Lib Dems at different levels have now criticised Sir Ed's response.

A Lib Dem MP contacted the BBC after Sir Ed's interview to say the majority of the parliamentary party would not support opposing Burnham's changes to the triple lock.

Another, Tom Gordon, who represents Harrogate & Knaresborough, said Sir Ed's criticism of Burnham's plan to adjust the triple lock was "nonsense" and "gaslights an entire generation into believing it's for our benefit".

He wrote on X: "The idea that we're keeping the triple lock to help millennials is at best for the birds, and at worst downright insulting. I say that as a millennial."

He added: "Telling millennials we're keeping the triple lock to help us in 30 years' time is nonsense.

"We're on course to be the first generation worse off than our parents. We're locked out of the housing market, paying higher taxes, repaying student loans that never seem to shrink, and putting off having children because of the cost of living."

Vikki Slade, the party's MP for Mid-Dorset and North Poole, said on Bluesky: "Most millennials don't think there will be a state pension when they retire so this isn't being done with them in mind."

She added that she was "proud" of the triple lock when it was introduced by the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government in 2010, "but we must plan for future not venerate the past".

A Lib Dem spokesperson said: "The triple lock has always been controversial.

"It's done a lot of good but its job isn't done yet, so Labour's plan would push too many of today's workers into poverty when they retire.

"We want Andy Burnham to get back around the table so that we can find a lasting consensus on social care with a sustainable funding model - not one pulled out of the pockets of a group of people who can least afford it."

The Lib Dems, and other opposition parties, are battling to respond to a new set of priorities from the Labour government under Burnham.

One frontbench Lib Dem MP told the BBC after Burnham's Labour conference speech: "Lots of us [are] struggling tonight with [a] Labour leader articulating Lib Dem values better than we do."

They pointed to Burnham's promises on electoral reform, social care, the water industry, and relations with Europe - all Lib Dem campaign points in recent years.

"I'm honestly utterly despondent with the state of things," another Lib Dem MP said.

Some senior Lib Dems believe Sir Ed's position as leader has been vulnerable for some time, even if they stressed no challenge is imminent.

"A plausible candidate could take him tomorrow in a bloodless coup," one prominent party figure said.

"But that person hasn't yet revealed themselves as far as I'm aware. Nobody is going to blow anything up without a clear plan to put something in its place."

Hundreds of criminals start leaving prison under new early release scheme

BBC News Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:18:22 GMT

Hundreds of criminals are being released early from prisons in England and Wales under new rules introduced to prevent facilities reaching capacity.

The first 700 of an expected 4,500 inmates eligible under the scheme were due to be let out on Thursday.

The government has stressed they will remain subject to strict monitoring arrangements, including the expanded use of electronic tagging, and has said action was needed to prevent prisons from becoming full.

But the plan has been strongly criticised by victims and questions have been raised over whether the Probation Service has sufficient resources to monitor thousands more criminals in the community.

Prisons in England and Wales are a matter of months away from reaching capacity, with Ministry of Justice data showing as of Monday 87,499 people were incarcerated, taking prison population levels up to 98.2%.

Thursday's release is the first of 10 scheduled to take place, with the final slated for June 2027.

Prisoners released initially were serving sentences of up to 19 months, with the most serious offenders - serving fixed sentences of more than 12 years - leaving in later waves.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Treasury minister James Murray said: "I know the level of concern and maybe anger will be intense, and it's worth me making clear that this is not a situation where there is any good solution - there's just a series of very difficult choices we've got to take."

He said the government "inherited a prison system on the brink" and without early releases the country would face a situation where "people who are arrested now can't go behind bars".

Murray said measures were in place to restrict criminals' movements in the community, adding: "I can't guarantee exactly what will happen, but I can tell people we have done everything we can to reduce the amount of people being released as far possible."

An early release programme introduced by the Conservatives saw more than 10,000 prisoners freed early between October 2023 and September 2024.

Sir Keir Starmer's government introduced the Sentencing Act to deal with the ongoing capacity crisis, which stipulated that offenders who were due to spend 40% or 50% of their sentences in prison would leave after a third - while prisoners who previously served two thirds would leave after half.

The number of people expected to be released under this scheme was cut from around 6,000 after Prime Minister Andy Burnham intervened to review its terms, removing eligibility for crimes including all forms of manslaughter, grooming offences and causing or allowing the death of a child.

The scheme does not apply to indeterminate sentences, which are handed out for the most serious offences like murder, and require a parole board to deem a prisoner safe to be released.

London Victims' Commissioner Andrea Simon said the exemptions "have not included some offenders whose imminent release is a genuinely terrifying prospect for their victims".

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "[There is] no real reason to believe that an even shorter spell in prison will have dealt with the risk that their offender poses."

Simon also questioned whether electronic tagging would be an effective safeguard, saying the equipment "will tell you where someone is but it can't stop them from doing something they shouldn't be doing".

Earlier this week, the Chief Inspector of Probation Martin Jones said the electronic monitoring regime had "not kept pace" and could create "a false sense of assurance" unless failing are addressed.

Some newly released prisoners spoke to the BBC as they were freed, including former bus driver Michael Bogle - who described the conditions inside London's Wandsworth Prison as "awful".

"Tagging is better than prison," he told reporters in support of the early release scheme. But others said they were concerned about a lack of support awaiting them on the outside, while one man told the BBC he did not know he was being released until Thursday morning.

Kirsty Pellant is among victims whose perpetrator was expected to be released in the coming months.

A man was convicted of several offences against her, including stalking, and jailed for five years in January 2025 after she discovered her photograph had been used to create a fake identity online and portray her as a sex worker.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she had received assurances he would not be let out in the first wave of releases but was not told when he would be.

The uncertainty "leaves us in such a dangerous position as victims because we need to be prepared, we need to know what we're dealing with," she added.

Prisoners released early can immediately be returned to prison if they breach the terms of their licence, including by committing another crime, contacting a victim or living at an address not approved by authorities.

However, charities have raised concerns that domestic abuse survivors may still be put at risk, despite such provisions.

"We know that license conditions are frequently breached by perpetrators", the charity Refuge warned, and cautioned that it was "deeply concerned that newly released perpetrators will be able to continue their campaign of abuse" without proper enforcement.

Women's Aid chief executive Farah Nazeer meanwhile said the scheme could further erode "incredibly low" trust in the criminal justice system, meaning "even greater numbers of women and children may be left without protection".

Ministers have also introduced restrictions zones, which will allow the Probation Service - which monitors offenders after they leave prison - to stipulate they can only move within a small geographic area, limiting their chance of a victim coming into contact with them.

But the National Association of Probation Officers (Napo) trade union has warned the service is "significantly under-staffed", adding: "You cannot solve the prisons crisis unless probation is fully functioning and provides a real alternative to custody."

The union's general secretary Ian Lawrence questioned government pledges to increase probation staff to deal with the influx of released prisoners, telling the BBC he had "heard it all before".

Government projections indicate the prison population will still rise to around 100,000 by the end of the decade despite early release schemes.

Minister have pledged to invest £7bn in a prison building programme which will expand capacity by 14,000 cells by 2031.

'My boss stabbed me then left prison early, but no one told me for months'

BBC News Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:17:13 GMT

Hannah Pritchett was 18 when she was stabbed in the lower back and hip by her boss Luisa Santos.

She was about an hour into her waitressing shift in May 2022 at the Three Horseshoes pub in Princethorpe, Warwickshire, when the blade went in. It was a fish knife, and with its cuts came Santos's false accusation the teen had had an affair with her husband.

That October, Santos was jailed for 10 years after being convicted of attempted murder. She was released in January 2026 under the Early Removal Scheme, which allows foreign national inmates in England and Wales, under certain criteria, to exit prison before they would have previously been allowed for the purpose of deportation.

Pritchett did not know of her attacker's departure from prison until five months after the fact. Sharing with the BBC the scheme's effect on her, she said she had been made to feel like an "afterthought", which was "just appalling".

A Ministry of Justice (MOJ) spokesperson said: "This was an awful crime, and our thoughts remain with Hannah Pritchett. Keeping victims informed is a vital part of our work and we are committed to always improving our service."

When asked by the BBC what the timeline should be for victims being informed of an offender's release under the removal scheme, the MOJ said the intention was for all victims to be contacted as soon as possible once information was available.

In the case of Pritchett, who was informed by the Victims Liaison Unit in June, there was an administrative error, the MOJ said, adding the matter had been escalated to management in both that unit and the prison in question.

Santos was deported having served three years and eight months in prison. The BBC has also sought clarification on her native country.

"Foreign nationals deported under the Early Removal Scheme are banned from ever returning to the UK," the MOJ spokesperson said.

According to Pritchett, however, the situation had made her "see that victims aren't at the forefront of these decisions".

Now 23, she said she had expected Santos to remain in prison until 2032 and thought she would have that time in which to come to terms with what had happened.

"When you get told on a random Tuesday in June that your attacker is now out and [is not serving] their sentence any longer it makes you feel that everything you have fought for was for nothing," said Pritchett, who lives in Coventry.

"Receiving that news was incredibly difficult and left me feeling let down by the justice system."

"It was a reminder that although a sentence may come to an end, the impact on victims continues long after."

"I went through a very difficult time when I was told my attacker was released early, especially as I found out five months after – it made things so much worse," she said.

Pritchett underwent surgery in hospital following the attack and said she had been "incredibly lucky to survive".

On Thursday, hundreds of prisoners will walk free from prison as part of the government's expanded early release scheme to free up capacity in overcrowded prisons across the country.

Pritchett questioned whether hundreds of victims were going to be made aware that their attackers would be released.

"In my case an administrative error led me to find out five months after," she said.

"If someone's attacker is released in the UK, what happens if they go out one day and see them in the street without being made aware?"

She said victims should be "at the forefront" of decisions on early release.

"My case was horrendous and I wouldn't wish that on anyone."

As part of her recovery and healing, Pritchett now raises money for knife crime prevention charities.

She plans to walk the Great Glen Way in Scotland next year and is hoping to raise £5,000 and finish the challenge on the fifth anniversary of the attack.

"Five years ago, I was incredibly fortunate to survive - five years on, I'm choosing to keep moving forward," she said.

The MOJ said that offenders leaving prison from 1 October would be monitored under the "toughest supervision" with the "biggest ever expansion of electronic monitoring rolled out".

Offenders would be electronically tagged and monitored when they left prison and £700m was being invested in probation and community punishment, the MOJ added.

It said victims would be offered "better practical and emotional support" through a newly launched helpline operated by Victim Support.

Russia targets busy bridge in central Kyiv

BBC News Thu, 01 Oct 2026 14:31:03 GMT

Two Russian drones have hit one of Kyiv's main bridges, bringing public transport in the Ukrainian capital to a halt and signalling a new stage in Moscow's attacks.

The Pivdennyi or Southern bridge came under fire as a metro train was travelling across. Passengers described how dust from a blast wave entered their carriage through the ventilation system.

The Pivdennyi bridge is one of the main arteries across the Dnipro river dividing western and eastern Kyiv.

Kyiv's bridges had not been hit before Thursday's strikes - and despite a dramatic explosion close to a main support section, city authorities said preliminary checks "did not find any critical damage to the structure".

For the people of Kyiv, the drone strikes were another powerful reminder that Russia has their city firmly in its sights and is doing everything it can to disrupt life in the capital.

Kyiv had just suffered its first co-ordinated attacks on the city's energy grid since the end of last winter, and commentators believe Russia has stepped up its campaign seeing that Ukraine is suffering from a shortage of air defences.

Strikes on Wednesday also heralded a return to power cuts in the capital. Although Kyiv authorities have spent months constructing smaller-scale power plants to counter Russia's anticipated winter campaign, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said a combined strike on such a scale had not taken place since the end of spring.

The first big attack on the capital on Thursday came when a Russian drone slammed into the third floor of a school at about 09:00 local time (10:00 GMT).

Although more than 100 students had been at the school at the time, they had all reached a shelter when the drone hit. One of the school's walls partially collapsed.

"[The shelter's] structure is strong, so none of the children were hurt, neither were any staff," said head teacher Valentyna Chorna. "They just kept on with their lessons."

Russia denies targeting civilians, but Chorna said that to destroy her nation "they need to destroy children". President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had to be held fully accountable.

Later in the morning, two drones hit the Pivdenny bridge, one hitting the base of a central stanchion.

Ukrainian 5 Kanal TV reporter Mariana Mykytenko described how one of the passengers on her metro train shouted the word "Shahed", referring to Russia's Iranian-designed drones, before the blast sent dust pouring into their carriage.

No-one in her compartment was hurt, she said, and "the train took people to Vydubychi station on the right bank, then it didn't go any further". The right bank is on the west side of the Dnipro river.

Metro trains were suspended but road traffic was eventually allowed to resume.

It is not yet clear what kind of drone was used in the Kyiv bridge attack, but Ukrainian officials say a new design of Russia's jet-powered drones came into operation for the first time on Wednesday.

The drone has a 40kg warhead and is especially designed to destroy high-voltage electricity pylons and iron bridge structures, according to Zelensky's technology adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov, also known as Flash.

In recent weeks, Russia has had considerable success with jet-powered drones and Ukrainian air force officials say that, during September, at least 3,177 were launched. Their high speed has caused problems for Ukraine's beleaguered air defences.

Kyiv's Institute of Nuclear Research came under drone attack on Wednesday night and, earlier in the week, one person was killed when a drone targeted the National Academy of Sciences.

Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names

BBC News Thu, 01 Oct 2026 11:37:46 GMT

Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official national registry.

The US president wants AI to be called "super intelligence" - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian websites.

Register. si spokeswoman Klara Herman said 44,000 web addresses with the . si suffix had been registered in September, compared to less than 2,000 in August - an increase of more than 2,100%.

She said the scale of activity in late September was "unprecedented" compared to the previous 12 months.

Trump called for the technology to be renamed during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 11 September.

"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said.

"It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful... welcome to the new world of super intelligence."

Internet domains are the unique human-readable addresses people type into their web browsers to access websites - like bbc. co. uk.

Herman said registrations for . si web addresses in September stood out "very clearly" against the other months in the year, although she was "cautious" about attributing the entire increase to just Trump's comments.

She said on 30 September alone, 11,000 new registrations were recorded.

One possible explanation for the purchases is a practice in which people speculatively register specific domain names in case they increase in value later on and can be sold for a profit.

For example, in 1997 Rick Schwartz, known as "The Domain King", bought the domain name men. com for $15,000 (£11,300). He sold it for $1.32 million seven years later.

Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the people "building America's Golden Age" on Tuesday.

He signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence", and to no longer acknowledge the use of the term AI.

SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.

Images of the signatures for the order were mocked online however - when it was discovered "United States" had been spelt incorrectly underneath Trump's signature.

Correction 1 October: An earlier version of this article referred to cyber-squatting, whereby people register domain names in bad faith with the intent to profit. We cited as an example the registration of men. com by Rick Schwartz. The article was amended to delete the reference to cyber-squatting and make clear simply registering domain names as an investment in the hope they will increase in value, as happened with men. com, is a legitimate business activity.

BBC News Thu, 01 Oct 2026 05:23:19 GMT

Almost 1,000 people have gathered in Shetland for the island's annual celebration of wool, knitting and textiles.

The week-long event is marking its 17th year and features classes, workshops, talks, tours and social activities.

Shetland Wool Week draws enthusiasts from around the world, including the US and Japan.

This year's patron, knitwear designer Helen Robertson, said: "I think wool week is just such a fantastic organisation and festival, and it's really brought Shetland textiles to life."

Nancy Woodhouse, a knitter from Arizona in the US, brought some of her creations, including a woolly hat inspired by the crime drama Shetland.

"I love the show," she said.

Describing the head wear, Woodhouse said: "We start on the hat with detective Jimmy Perez of course and Tosh who's taken over as the lead detective, then we have the ever helpful Sandy and Ruth Calder, and this is the chalk outline of the victim.

"The hat has muted colours so the detectives would shine - it's the crime scene I wear on my head."

Satoko Nagakubo has flown from Tokyo for the festival.

"I come from Japan many times to Shetland for wool week because I love the sheep and the local people. I love Shetland lace knitting and spinning," she said.

Mary Randles, visiting from Lancashire, said: "I think the fact that you can chill, you can knit, meet people, buy wool and sit on your suitcase until it forces all the wool in before you take it home."

She said the event allowed her to see the sheep the wool she uses for knitting come from.

Randles added: "Once you've knitted with it and washed it, it drapes beautifully whereas sometimes when you knitting with synthetic it doesn't drape but this stuff does."

From Fair Isle knitting to spinning, fleece preparation, weaving, lace knitting to wool skirting, there is a huge range for visitors to discover.

It is an event that stretches far beyond the classroom, with activities taking place from Unst to the south mainland.

Local communities are at the heart of the week, with community halls, crofts and businesses, makers and musicians all helping to create the unique experience for the wool enthusiasts.

Patron Helen Robertson designed the much-anticipated wool week hat - the Birsie Beanny.

"It's such a joyful and happy week," she said.

The star attraction are Shetland's native sheep and the earthy shades of cream, brown and black of their wool.

Ronnie Eunson runs Uradale Farm on the west side of the islands and breeds native sheep and cattle which graze on the nearby hills and coastline.

He said: "Shetland wool is a fairly unique commodity.

"It's the history and heritage that makes it really special. You're looking at a type of fibre that has clothed Shetlanders for thousands of years."

Eunson said the sheep had a double coat of wool which protected them against the islands' harsh winter weather. The finer wool is below the top layer.

The farmer added: "Tourists are fascinated to see the sheep and to hear about the way we look after the sheep and how the sheep look after themselves."

As the nights draw in and winter approaches the festival is a big boost too for the island's economy.

Donna Smith, who runs Langsoond Yarn in Burra, said: "It's really an amazing event that's the highlight of the year for me at the end of the tourist season.

The "sewing of the loose ends" of the festival is on Saturday. Then it will be time for the hundreds of visitors to cast off and head home with their Shetland Oo for another year.

Anglo-Saxons got special treatment in medieval Rome

New Scientist September 30, 2026

A rare collection of early-medieval coins found by archaeologists in Rome has provided a window into a time when English travellers and expats had special rights in the papal city and thrived in their own vibrant Anglo-Saxon quarter.

Historical records show that the English had their own area within the city, known as the Schola Saxonum. The newly uncovered hoard of coins, along with the remains of craft items such as leather, bone and metal, is the first material proof that the Anglo-Saxon quarter truly existed.

Digital map lets you explore the Roman Empire’s vast road network

It also suggests that the English, unlike other foreign nationals, had the right to use their own currency in parts of Rome.

Advertisement

“The English quarter in Rome really was an interesting and vibrant place,” says Rory Naismith at the University of Cambridge. “It might be compared with districts in modern major cities that house a specific community, like the Chinatown areas of London, Melbourne, San Francisco and other cities.”

Since 2020, researchers have been excavating the walled garden of the Palazzo della Rovere near the Vatican, where they discovered the ruins of Emperor Nero’s theatre in 2023.

Subscriber-only newsletter

The site has yielded a total of 30 coins, 23 of which were minted in the 10th century, including 20 Anglo-Saxon pennies and one half-penny of the early to mid-10th century, minted in the names of Edward the Elder (899–924), Æthelstan (924–39) and Eadred (946–55).

Along with the English currency, the archaeologists also found two Italian coins from the same era, along with six Roman or late antique bronze coins, as well as one unidentifiable bronze coin that may also be Roman.

Many of the coins have been fused together and are difficult to identify. Those that can still be read include specimens from several different parts of England: East Anglia, Kent, London and the West Midlands. Naismith and his colleagues have published their findings in a book, Rome and the Others (300-1000): Foreigners in the city between conflicts and integration.

Francesca Tinti at the University of the Basque Country, another member of the team, says the “shape, size and thickness” of the fused, unidentifiable coins are consistent with the clearly English ones. The non-English coins were found intermingled with the Anglo-Saxon currency, says Tinti.

“This seems to have been quite a busy, active area of the city, as the craft remains indicate,” she says.

The surprising origins of Britain’s Bronze Age immigrants revealed

Naismith says it is exceptional that most of these coins are English. Although many other English coins from the 10th century have been found in Rome, they have usually been regarded as religious donations, not as part of the regular currency of the city.

It was previously thought that the papacy banned the use of foreign currencies in Rome, but the new finds suggest that in this part of the city, English coins were used as a major part of the local currency, alongside local Italian coins.

“This is highly unusual for the 10th century – the norm was to use the local coin of whatever jurisdiction you were in,” Naismith says.

An account by the Welsh scholar Asser in 893 notes that Pope Marinus I had granted the English special rights in the 9th century in recognition of their demonstrations of piety.

Until now there has been no real archaeological evidence for what the Schola looked like, how it operated, or what privileges this community enjoyed, says Naismith.

He and Tinti had dreamed of finding piles of English coins and artefacts at the site in Rome, but never expected that their imagined finds would be more or less right, Naismith says.

Earth’s geographic poles wander more than we had thought

New Scientist October 01, 2026

The Earth’s geographic poles – the points where the imaginary axis of the planet’s rotation is located – may be far less immutable than previously known, with a new study finding that ancient sea-level changes provide a clue to their movement.

Earth has two main pairs of poles: its magnetic poles, resulting from its magnetic field, and its geographic poles based on its rotation. The magnetic poles are constantly in movement and are often hundreds of kilometres away from the geographic north and south poles. They can even flip altogether.

The geographic poles are much more stable. But they can move a little, through a phenomenon called true polar wander. This is driven by the way plate tectonics and mantle convection slowly redistribute mass in Earth’s mantle and affect the planet’s spin.

Huge hot blobs inside Earth may have made its magnetic field wonky

When the spin of the planet is thrown out of whack, the solid outer layers of the globe begin to move in order to help Earth find a new stable spin equilibrium. This has the effect of moving the geographic poles.

“The crust and the mantle effectively slip over the core during a true polar-wander event,” says Mathew Domeier at the University of Oslo in Norway.

However, until now much of the evidence for true polar-wandering events has come from ancient magnetic data locked inside rocks that formed millions of years ago, and this evidence has yielded confusing and conflicting results about the frequency and scale of the events.

So, Domeier and his team took a different approach. They analysed the geological record of sea-level change looking for distinctive signals that might be expected during a true polar-wander event.

Hear from three of the world’s leading climate scientists at New Scientist Live 2026

Because of the way ocean water can more quickly adjust to the centrifugal potential changes than the rocky sea floor, true polar-wander events are expected to leave a telltale pattern. Sea level will rise in one half of the northern hemisphere and fall in the other half, and it will also rise in one half of the southern hemisphere and fall in the other half.

The northern and southern hemisphere signals are reversed, however, so if it is the western side of the northern hemisphere that experiences sea-level rise, it will be the eastern side of the southern hemisphere that does so, too, creating a beach ball-like global pattern.

“This is a very strange pattern that is not caused by other Earth processes,” he says.

On the time scales we experience, the events would be unnoticeable. But over longer periods of geological time, a wandering pole changes the distribution of land and sea.

Why geologists can’t agree on when the Anthropocene Epoch began

For instance, from their analysis of ancient sea-level patterns, Domeier and his colleagues discovered that the geographic poles moved dramatically, over periods of around 10 million years, four times in the geological past: at 20, 90, 140 and 190 million years ago.

“By the timescales of human experience, the movement may not seem fast,” says Domeier. “We cannot estimate the exact speed, but we can recognise events where the rate of polar motion exceeded about 0.6 degrees per million years.”

He says this is faster than the rate at which most tectonic plates move – fast enough to potentially have an effect on climate systems.

What’s more, we know that true polar wandering continues today, although maybe not at the rate seen during the four fast bursts in the geological past.

Rock weathering has helped keep Earth’s climate relatively stable for millions of years, but the process isn’t fast enough to keep up with human carbon emissions

“[It] is measurable by satellites at a rate of about 10 cm per year, but most people are unaware of this. So these events are totally unrecognisable according to our everyday experience,” says Domeier.

Sabin Zahirovic at the University of Sydney says very few people are aware that Earth’s 2800-km-thick outer shell of the crust and mantle are in motion with respect to Earth’s spin axis.

The study demonstrates that clues in the coastline change provide an independent fingerprint of true polar wander.

“This is a very exciting development that helps us link very deep Earth processes to changes in long-term climate and sea level on the planet,” says Zahirovic.

Science DOI: 10.1126/science. aec8423

Ukraine rolls out drone-stopping razor fence to thwart attacks

New Scientist October 01, 2026

A new type of barrier developed in Ukraine defends against fibre-guided attack drones by literally cutting their communications.

Radio-frequency jamming stops most small drones. In response, drone designers have begun using fibre-optic cable instead of radio to communicate with the crafts. The fibre-optic cable unspools as the drone flies.

Russia produced very few of these drones in 2024, and each could only reach a few kilometres. But 20-kilometre-range versions are now common, with 50-km ones also appearing. The drones have become far more abundant, too, with some 60 per cent of Russian FPV attack drones now fibre guided. In places the landscape is draped with discarded fibre cables.

Advertisement

Jet-powered drones pose a new threat to Ukraine – can they be stopped?

The Ukrainian forces have been experimenting with technology to cut the strong fibre-optic cables. One video shared by a Ukrainian government-led platform has shown civilians how to break a line by hand by looping it and snapping the brittle fibre. But other methods for breaking the cables are needed.

“The most reliable defences against fibre-optic FPVs have been passive barrier systems such as the net tunnels installed over key roads,” says Roy Gardiner, Intel Director at the group Defense Tech for Ukraine. Hundreds of kilometres of roads in Ukraine are now covered with these tunnels, which are physical barriers that catch drones or cause them to explode prematurely.

The Chaharnyk (“Shrubbery”), developed by Logika Design Bureau in Kyiv, offers an alternative. An acoustic sensor picks up the sound of a drone passing overhead and activates the barrier. This is a motorised wire fence in which the wire moves like a conveyor belt with hooks to trap any fibre-optic cable laid over it. The hooks carry the fibre to a cutting block where it is severed.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Chaharnyk is supplied as two 50-metre sections, which two people can set up in less than an hour. It is battery-powered and weatherproof, and can be turned on or off remotely as needed – for example, while friendly drones are passing over.

Barriers can be placed across known lines of approach used by drones, or as a perimeter to protect a fighting position or a facility.

“Vulnerable installations in the rear, such as electrical substations that are too extensive to cover with netting, could be given significant protection against long-range fibre FPVs by the Chaharnyk system,” says Gardiner.

Breaking the fibre cable generally disables a fibre drone, and the makers claim that Chaharnyk has a 95 per cent success rate in cutting the cable of any drone flying over. But it only works if it detects the drone.

“The reliability of the acoustic detection system to distinguish threats in the cacophony of the battlefield needs to be proven,” says Gardiner.

Logika Design Bureau didn’t respond to a request for an interview about the Chaharnyk system.

Elephants imitate each other when they produce deep rumbling sounds

New Scientist October 01, 2026

Elephants appear to harmonise their vocal rumbles when they join together to form choruses, tuning their voices to sound more alike as the chorus unfolds.

The findings come from a machine learning study, which also reveals that this convergence is particularly likely to occur during specific kinds of choruses – such as when elephants reconnect with one another or organise group activities – and that the calls themselves may contain information about what the animals are doing.

The findings could offer new insights into how elephants communicate and navigate life within their complex societies, says Sara Keen at Earth Species Project, a US non-profit organisation that uses artificial intelligence and machine learning to attempt to decode non-human animal communication.

Advertisement

IUCN report finds more African forest elephants than we thought

“It’s sort of like what humans do in conversation, where you almost start to adopt the speaking patterns or accents of whoever you’re interacting with,” says Keen.

Elephants communicate using a rich repertoire of body language, but also a wide range of sounds. These include their iconic trumpet call, and also throatier roars. The most common call is the rumble – so low-pitched it is often undetectable by humans – which can travel up to 10 kilometres, transmitting long-distance information that can potentially include the identity of the caller and what’s happening at the time.

Joyce Poole at Elephant Voices, a non-profit organisation based in Washington DC, that promotes the study and protection of elephants, says scientists have long been intrigued by the way elephants will rumble together in choruses. Studying those complex sounds, however, has proved extremely difficult because it is hard to pick out any given rumbling elephant in the chorus – what researchers call “the cocktail party problem”.

See Chris Packham at New Scientist Live 2026

With significant developments in machine learning, however, Poole, Keen and their colleagues have found that computers are up to the task. They used a collection of 902 recordings of rumbles collected across four decades, emitted by wild female African savannah elephants (Loxodonta africana) from dozens of family groups in Kenya’s Amboseli National Park. The calls were grouped according to six distinct social situations: staying in contact while separated; preparing to move; coordinating what to do next; comforting or reassuring calves; greeting close family members; and participating in large family reunions.

Machine analyses revealed that elephant choruses carry multiple layers of information at once, and vary in a way that suggests they encode information about what a family is doing together and what happens next, says Keen. Tracking rumbles of individual elephants in the same chorus, the data showed that in some cases, the calls became more acoustically alike as the chorus progressed. Specifically, this convergence occurred when elephants were staying in contact while separated, coordinating what to do next, and greeting after a separation. This suggests that vocal convergence may play a role in helping elephant families build a plan of action, says Keen.

Earlier research that Poole and her colleagues published in 2005 showed that elephants can learn to imitate each other’s voices when they are calling more generally: the new work shows that this imitation involves the rumbles, too.

A weatherproof box and motion-trigger camera help photographer Will Burrard-Lucas capture images of rarely seen African elephants

Combined with other communication tools, including body language, the rumbling calls seem to help facilitate complex social interactions. “They appear able to negotiate, agree and disagree – and make a plan of action,” says Poole.

The findings not only shed light on elephant communication and cognition, but they could also eventually aid conservation by helping researchers track their behaviour and movements remotely, the team says.

Because rumbles allow for long-distance communication, elephants’ ability to unite through their voices is an exciting reflection of their advanced cognition and evolution in their environment, says Andrew McLean, a member of the International Union for the Conservation of Nature’s Asian Elephant Specialist Group. “Evolving and elaborating this for social cohesion, group survival and foraging efficiency is very adaptive,” he says. “This is a fascinating finding – although it’s not really surprising, given how intensely social elephants are.”

Scientific Reports DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-68525-3

Placenta wrap hastens erection recovery after prostate surgery

New Scientist October 01, 2026

Erectile dysfunction is common after prostate cancer surgery, but wrapping thin sheets of dried placenta around exposed nerves during the procedure may allow faster recovery. A review of thousands of surgeries suggests that this approach enables an erection within one week of surgery, compared with two weeks without the intervention.

“To help men get better erections, we’re using donations [of placentas] from women,” says Shirin Razdan at HCA Florida Kendall Hospital in Miami.

We are finally improving prostate cancer diagnoses – here’s how

Her colleague and father, Sanjay Razdan, also at HCA Florida Kendall Hospital, had the idea to try the technique more than a decade ago. This followed a discussion he had at the hospital cafeteria with some neurosurgeon colleagues, who were investigating whether amniotic membranes from donated placentas could improve nerve healing in their procedures.

Advertisement

The amniotic membrane is the innermost, fetus-facing layer of the placenta, and is known to be packed with growth factors and immune-modulating proteins that promote healing. Some companies peel the amniotic membrane off placentas that have been donated after Caesarean sections, then dry, sterilise and package it in standard-sized sheets.

Between 2014 and 2024, Sanjay Razdan used dried sheets of human amniotic membrane to wrap nerves near the prostate during 2560 radical prostatectomies, surgeries that remove the entire prostate gland to treat cancer.

He placed these thin sheets, each measuring 4 by 6 centimetres, on bundles of nerves called cavernous nerves that run along both sides of the prostate. He then wet them with saline to make them cling around the nerves. This is like how moistening dried seaweed sheets allows them to be wrapped around sushi rolls, says Shirin Razdan.

A long-overlooked area of the penis has been found to have the highest concentration of nerve endings and sensory structures in the organ, suggesting that it is the “male G-spot”

Surgeons try to preserve the cavernous nerves when they take out the prostate because they signal for muscles in the penis to relax, so blood can rush in and produce erections. Robotic equipment is commonly used to improve precision, but “even when you do the most beautiful nerve-sparing surgery, there is usually still some damage to the nerves”, says Shirin Razdan.

This is because the nerves get stretched and heated by the surgical tools, and general inflammation tends to arise in the area. As a result, it is often difficult to have erections after prostate removal.

But applying the amniotic membrane sheets appeared to help. In the 2560 men who received them, the average time to first erection post-surgery was seven days. By comparison, in 1495 men who didn’t receive them, the average time was 14 days. These men were also operated on by Sanjay Razdan, but before 2014.

Free newsletter

Three months after surgery, 75 per cent of the men who received the amniotic membranes were able to have erections “sufficient for penetration”, compared with 60 per cent for those who didn’t receive them.

One risk of applying amniotic membranes to an area that has been affected by cancer is that they might spur further cancer growth, since they are rich in growth factors. However, the study didn’t find any differences in cancer outcomes between the two groups after an average eight-year follow up.

A limitation of the study is that it is a retrospective review of procedures by a single surgeon, rather than a clinical trial. It is possible that the better erection outcomes since 2014 are due to refinements in individual surgical technique, but Shirin Razdan says she doesn’t believe this would be enough to explain the significant improvements in erectile recovery.

Ejaculating within 48 hours of providing a sperm sample for IVF seems to lead to greater success rates than abstaining from ejaculation for longer

Arthur Burnett at Johns Hopkins Medicine in Maryland says randomised clinical trials will be required to confirm that amniotic membrane nerve wraps do indeed assist erectile function. “I’m pleased to see that they’re trying to think outside the box here, but nobody else is doing this routinely yet. It still needs to be further investigated.”

Inspired by her father’s results, Shirin Razdan says she is now applying amniotic membrane nerve wraps when she performs prostate removals, and is trialling them in surgeries for Peyronie’s disease, a condition where scar tissue forms under the skin of the penis and causes painful, curved erections.

Outside of urology, dehydrated amniotic membranes are also becoming an increasingly popular option for applying to skin wounds and burns, and have been found to reduce scarring.

Research Square DOI: 10.21203/rs.3. rs-10852428/v1
