The best popular-science books of October 2026

New Scientist October 01, 2026

Big issues abound in this month’s books, as we batten down the hatches against El Niño and the known unknowns out there. Luckily, here in our snug bunker, we have plenty of other things to think about. There’s the source of the next big conflict (it’s probably not what you think), how to eat healthily (as close to definitive as you’re going to get), and fighting talk from inside the rush to develop AI. There’s also the real story of pregnancy loss, giving animals their rightful place, the nature of family, saving childhood, and why humans ask questions. Oh, and there are some silly sums and extraordinary fantasy botanicals for those who fancy a spot of fun. Lovely.

Just in case you’ve been living in an off-the-grid shack next to a beautiful lake for the past few years, The AGI Chronicles looks like an essential re-entry book before returning to, er, civilisation. The clue’s all over the subtitle, “The inside story of the race to create an artificial superintelligence”, and author Kevin Roose is tech columnist for The New York Times, so he ought to know – a lot. New Scientist will be reviewing it soon in depth, but meanwhile, this zeroes in on the past decade’s efforts by a few companies fighting to build the “most powerful technology in history… artificial general intelligence (AGI) – a computer system capable of outdoing humans at almost anything”. Expect a fat volume (an alarming 448 pages, says the book’s website), based on “more than 150 interviews with insiders at OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind, as well as unpublished company documents and research memos”. It will be fascinating to see what our reviewer makes of the book. Just don’t drop it on your foot, OK?

Free newsletter

There’s a small band of mathematicians (think Matt Parker, Alex Bellos, Hannah Fry and Eugenia Cheng) who somehow manage to make a tough subject engaging, exciting or, whisper it, even funny. Tom Crawford’s title is certainly enough to raise a guffaw in the hardest of hearts, let alone Pokémon fans. Now try asking, as the publisher does, how many daily calories you would need to feed a Charizard. Could the Death Star’s laser actually blow up a planet? What is the half-life of the Incredible Hulk? And is the meaning of life really “42”? OK, we know the answer to the last question, but it does sound like Crawford is pulling out all the stops to use his Oxford fellow smarts on the fantasy maths of fictional, often wild, universes. Parting shot: just how would you work out Frodo Baggins’s life insurance premium for the journey to Mordor?

Advertisement

Primatologist Frans de Waal, who died in 2024, left a huge legacy for other scholars and campaigners fighting ideas of human exceptionalism and arguing that animals have complex inner lives. Minds I’ve Met is one of two books by de Waal posthumously published this year; the other is My Family Album, a selection of photographs taken during his work over 30 years, showing, say the publishers, “the rich social life” of the primates he studied. Both books sport the provocative and sometimes moving titles de Waal used to challenge the status quo (think Are We Smart Enough to Know How Smart Animals Are?, Mama’s Last Hug, or The Bonobo and the Atheist). In Minds, the kicker is also in the subtitle: “From denying to embracing the inner lives of animals”. The publishers say his “pioneering work… contributed to a new image of animals as intentional agents with minds of their own, capable of remarkable cognitive feats, demonstrating empathy and self-awareness, showing emotions and conscious”. He often wrote for and talked to New Scientist. If he’s new to you, you could do worse than starting here.

Forget, for a moment, grappling with AI conceptually and think about it as an environmental issue. All over the world, the data centres already built and those planned are crucial to the current AI successes and to the ambitions of the companies involved. What’s more, say the publishers of a polemical book called Hyperscale, the centres use up resources such as water and power at “dangerously unsustainable levels”. This book’s author is Paris Marx, a tech critic, journalist and host of the Tech Won’t Save You podcast. It sounds like a wild ride, with the publishers saying the “tech overlords are waging a resource war as they trade our future for their profit”. It is nothing less than a “civilisational time bomb in the making”, where tough reporting shows that “the greatest threat is not the spectre of AI, but a global disaster that has already begun”. The book is already longlisted for this year’s Financial Times Business Book of the Year award.

The sheer amount of advice on what to eat to be healthy is unnerving, especially since a lot of it is quite probably junk. But before you reach for a doughnut out of sheer despair, there are books out there that offer sane ways through the morass, with excellent science and tasty-sounding recipes. Food Sense is by Christopher Gardner, who’s been researching nutrition and health for decades, and is now the director of nutrition studies and a professor of medicine at Stanford University in California. His publishers promise that he “shows you where there is genuine scientific consensus so you can discern fact from fads and ignore the health food marketing hype. From weight loss to protein, ultra-processed foods, seed oils, GMO’s and fermented foods, this definitive and myth-busting guide answers all your nutrition questions”. Now there’s a big claim or two. Luckily, former New Scientist staffer (and all-round nutrition, health and longevity specialist writer) Graham Lawton is on hand to review the book later this month so we’ll find out how well they all stack up – that, and how good the recipes are.

Why are the clouds white? What made that artwork so special? Where does the cat vanish to at night? Who am I? From the existential to the trivial, questioning – curiosity and the seemingly endless desire for answers – feels hardwired in us. So, is it? And does it connect evolutionarily to the human way of learning? Could it even be that elusive thing that makes humans, human? Certainly, the subtitle of Tania Lombrozo’s new book – “The science of explanation and the human drive to understand” – tells us where she thinks we are. She is a professor of psychology at Princeton University, and her research, say her publishers, is all about turning our explanation seeking back on itself by asking, ”What does explanation do for us? And, most important, how can we do it better?” The idea that some explanations are more satisfying than others also sounds intriguing.

Have childcare and education in the UK been turned into a business – and if so, who is profiting? Certainly not the children, argues Cherry Casey, a journalist specialising in children’s rights. Her book comes billed as an “exposé of how chasing profits and league tables has come at the cost of developing well rounded, happy people”. As ever, the book’s subtitle positions her quest: “How we turned children into data and why we need to stop”. It’s an interesting argument, given the rise of mental illness even in young children and the overall datafication of our world, and the use (or overuse) of testing and “zero-tolerance” behaviour policies many schools advertise as a desirable end. So, who is profiting, and how do we turn the ship round?

This looks to be a moving but probably also essential book, dealing with the realities of one of life’s most important but common events: the loss of a pregnancy. The author is Kate Clancy, a professor of anthropology at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, where she’s based in the Department of Gender and Women’s Studies and the Program in Ecology, Evolution, and Conservation Biology. This is likely to give her book the kind of heft it needs to challenge the myths surrounding pregnancy loss. According to its publisher, Clancy “makes an impassioned, fact-based case for truthfulness and care at a time when inaccurate images of fetuses abound, electronic impulses continue to pass for a heartbeat, and reproductive autonomy is criminalized”.

Where the next war will come from is a question that keeps many of us awake at night – not to mention political analysts and defence chiefs fully occupied. One place you would be unlikely to guess is the bottom of the sea. But that is where an extraordinary-sounding book is set. A quick peek confirms that the book looks to deliver on its publisher’s description as a “gripping account of the hidden battles beneath the world’s oceans, where cables and pipelines – the lifelines of the modern world – are under constant threat from states, corporations, and hackers”. And remember, the stakes could hardly be higher at a time when so much global traffic – internet, energy, telecoms – runs through cables that are out of sight. Braw is a force to reckon with: she’s a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, where she leads the Threats to the Global Maritime Order initiative. She was previously a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute and is also a member of the UK National Preparedness Commission.

Here’s some fun – a chance to join New Scientist’s own Alison Flood (sidenote: this is included here without any pressure or suggestion from her…) on a strange voyage into the fictional botanical worlds created by authors drawn from the ranks of science fiction and fantasy. Published in association with the Royal Botanic Gardens Kew, it comes with over 100 beautiful (if occasionally scary) illustrations by artist Emma Tudor-Bloch, vividly bringing to life all manner of unreal plants and fungi. And for those seeking a bit of heft, there’s expert text and historical images from Kew’s experts, exploring the real-life plants and fungi that inspired the fantasy. So, watch out for a host worlds including nightlock (The Hunger Games, Suzanne Collins), weirwood trees (A Song of Ice and Fire, George R. R. Martin), Ents (The Lord of the Rings, J. R. R. Tolkien), redweed (The War of the Worlds, H. G. Wells), wheel trees (The Amber Spyglass, Philip Pullman) and the Cordyceps fungus (The Last of Us).

The best new science-fiction books of October 2026

Mother. Father. Son. Daughter. Grandmother… Most of us grow up in a family of some sort, no matter how dysfunctional. But Family: How the human need for belonging shapes our lives by Meredith Small is no self-help book. Small is a well-known anthropologist at Cornell University in New York state, and the author of Our Babies, Ourselves. Here, say her publishers, she sets out to examine the roots of the family and why this type of connection is the bedrock of human interaction in all cultures – and how getting to grips with its nature might help us “navigate our rapidly changing world”. Given the sometimes overemphasis on the family and “family values” globally, some might argue we should join Small as she asks why we form families and place such importance on family relationships, and whether family life does deliver – throughout our different stages and ages. As you would expect from an anthropologist, Small’s time frame spans millions of years and her scope is global – all human life and setup is here, promises the publisher. From a peek, it looks like family is as varied as the human experience. Lots of room for manoeuvre, thankfully.

A lack of rockets is creating a crisis for space technology companies

New Scientist October 01, 2026

Satellite operators are facing a launch crisis as the number of available rockets diminishes, a situation that could last years and prevent new satellites reaching space.

Just last year, wait times for a rocket launch were only 12 months or so, says Anatolii Papulov, founder and CEO of UK space tech firm NewOrbit, but the situation has now changed dramatically. “The lead times to launch right now are basically 30 to 36 months,” he says. “This will definitely impact a lot of start-ups.”

There “absolutely is a launch crisis at the moment”, says Caleb Henry, a senior analyst for US company Quilty Space, which is being caused by a number of factors. The first is that Elon Musk’s firm SpaceX is said to be sunsetting one of the most widely used rockets in the world, the Falcon 9. This reusable rocket, which debuted in 2010, transformed the launch industry and ushered in a new age of commercial space flight.

Advertisement

Is China catching up to the US and SpaceX on reusable rockets?

There were 165 Falcon 9 launches in 2025, the most of any rocket in the world and five times more than every other US rocket combined. While two-thirds of these were Starlink launches for the company’s space internet constellation, the others were a mix of government and commercial projects, including ride-share missions where companies can hitch a ride to space with others at a cost as low as $3000 per kilogram.

SpaceX, however, is reportedly no longer taking bookings on Falcon 9 beyond 2028. That is because it is transitioning to its much larger rocket, Starship, which reached orbit for the first time on 28 September. But it is unclear how available Starship will be for commercial launches, with SpaceX potentially focusing on more profitable areas like its own Starlink constellation – which generated $11.4 billion in revenue in 2025, nearly two-thirds of the company’s total revenue – or its planned orbital AI data centre satellites.

Matt Hausman at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign in the US, a former engineer at SpaceX, says the launch capacity crunch is “a little bit of a result of SpaceX’s success”. The firm has lowered launch costs by 10 times or more, making it “a lot easier for smaller players to get involved in the space industry”, he says. Ending Falcon 9 leaves many of those players without a route to space, says Hausman.

See Helen Sharman at New Scientist Live 2026

Starship, which NASA is hoping will return humans to the moon, may still offer ride-share missions. But the rocket is designed with flat Starlink satellites in mind, deploying them through a slot in the side like a candy dispenser. This design might not support bulkier satellites from other companies, although some versions of Starship might have a more traditional satellite deployment mechanism.

The war in Ukraine is also having an impact. Prior to Russia’s invasion in 2022, about a fifth of global launch capacity, including many commercial launches, was handled by Russian rockets such as Soyuz, says Henry. Since the war began, that route to space has ended.

Another issue is the lack of commercial rivals to SpaceX. Its next closest competitor is US company Rocket Lab, which launched 18 of its smaller Electron rockets to orbit in 2025, but has yet to launch its new, larger Neutron rocket. Many other firms are developing new rockets, but these haven’t started flying regularly. Another competitor, the New Glenn rocket from Jeff Bezos’s company Blue Origin, is grounded after exploding in May. Other rockets, such as Europe’s Ariane rockets and India’s Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, meanwhile, launch only a few times a year.

Not much is known about Starfall, SpaceX’s new delivery system, but an assessment published in May revealed its intended purpose

Much of global launch capacity was already taken up by another of Bezos’s companies, Amazon, before SpaceX reportedly ended bookings on Falcon 9. In 2022, the firm ordered 83 launches for its own space internet constellation, Amazon Leo, of which only 14 have launched so far.

NewOrbit did manage to book a launch to space on an undisclosed rocket in 2028, but the process was “very hard”, says Papulov. “I think we got one of the few slots which were available.”

China has also begun operating more commercial rockets, but US and most European satellites are barred from launching on these rockets because of US regulations. “Even if you have a satellite built in Europe, if it has a component from America, it cannot fly on a Chinese rocket,” says Henry.

That leaves the global launch industry in very uncertain territory. SpaceX could still make Starship widely available and the crisis would dissipate, or other launch companies “could come in and fill the void left by Falcon 9”, says Henry.

At the moment, though, we “don’t know what 2029 or 2030 will look like yet”, he says. “The worst-case scenario is Starship is not available, Falcon 9 is gone and no one has replaced that pathway to space. In that scenario, a lot of businesses will struggle.”

Can mathematicians still refuse to use AI at this point?

New Scientist October 01, 2026

I have been writing about mathematics for almost 20 years, and in that period, I don’t think there has ever been a time quite like today. For the majority of my career, landing a big maths story was something that happened perhaps every few months at most – the Venn diagram of maths results that are both interesting and explainable to a general audience has a pretty narrow overlap. That all changed as artificial intelligence became shockingly capable at mathematics, a story we have been covering in detail for the past year or so.

What’s next for mathematics now that AI is upending the field?

According to one analysis, 25 per cent of mathematical papers published on the arXiv preprint server in August acknowledge some use of AI, up from just 1 per cent the year before. Mathematicians are still reeling from the changes we’re seeing, and it has left me – and them – wondering whether it will even be possible to do mathematics without AI in the near future.

One analogy that springs to mind is chess, for which we have had superhuman AI players for decades. But that doesn’t mean that people stopped playing chess – instead, chess AIs can inspire and train new players. Where the analogy falls down, of course, is that one game of chess doesn’t build on every other game of chess that comes before it. In a way, mathematics is more like one big multiplayer puzzle, and once AI has joined the game, it is impossible to ignore.

Advertisement

Mathematical proofs are, by definition, true forever, which makes it impossible to unknow a result proven by AI. That is even the case for a proof written in such a way that humans don’t understand it, because its veracity can be verified via the programming language Lean, which breaks a proof down into elemental logical statements that can be mechanically checked by a computer.

The potential for a gap to open up between truth and understanding is concerning. Mathematician Terence Tao at the University of California, Los Angeles, has warned that solving problems with AI is akin to using up a non-renewable resource, meaning the pool of open problems. He argues that, while there are theoretically an infinite number of problems for mathematicians to work on, identifying particular problems that will lead to the discovery of new mathematical techniques is a key part of mathematical research. If AI hoovers up these problems and solves them without producing new techniques, where does that leave mathematicians? “The indiscriminate use of powerful solution-extraction tools can achieve the immediate short-term goal of solving problems at hand, but at the cost of sustaining the ecosystem for the next wave of progress, or in understanding the progress already obtained,” said Tao in a recent social media post.

One solution he suggests is that classes of problems should be ringfenced as deserving full analysis and understanding, not merely solving. I think this is probably impossible, as Tao essentially admits himself. It just takes one person – and it doesn’t even have to be a professional mathematician – to solve a problem using AI, and then it has been solved by AI forever.

The suggestion also reminds me of the 2008 novel Anathem by Neal Stephenson, which imagines a world in which the infosphere has been so polluted by “artificial inanity” that truth becomes impossible to discern. Researchers now occupy monastery-like institutions that are intentionally cut off from the rest of the world in order to rely only on their own reasoning systems. Ironically, the problem mathematicians face today is almost the exact opposite – thanks to Lean verification, truth is almost too easy to come by.

Could a similar idea – AI-free mathematicians, rather than AI-free maths problems – work? “I don’t think it’s ideal if all mathematicians on the planet use the same technology as an inescapable interface between themselves and their discipline,” says Alessandro Della Corte at the University of Camerino, Italy. “I think it’s better if a small minority, say 5 to 10 per cent, remains AI-free, while the bulk of the community engages with the tools, hopefully critically and within academia.”

Della Corte has set up an online declaration for other mathematicians to sign and join him in eschewing AI in their own work, but he agrees that it won’t be possible to ignore the spectre of AI completely. He says that if he encounters a result that would be useful for his work that was obtained using AI, he wouldn’t pretend it doesn’t exist. “As long as it is presented in an understandable way, preferably in a paper where a human author takes responsibility. I care for my personal workflow and like it to be ‘AI-clean’, but for sure I don’t want to promote irrational forms of tech asceticism.”

I made a free AI chatbot solve a decade-long maths problem in 13 minutes

Some mathematicians are more positive about the impact of AI. Daniel Litt at the University of Toronto has written that the profession is entering a new era. “I think we are at the beginning of an incredible, wonderful explosion of mathematics, and if we value human understanding, there will be more need for human mathematicians than ever before,” he writes – but what mathematicians do will have to change, with less of a focus on creating mere proofs and more on understanding and communication.

This feels like the most realistic scenario to me. Putting aside the fact that AI is still pretty bad at generating text you want to read, you can simply ignore AI-generated novels if you wish. I don’t see how mathematicians can ignore AI-generated mathematics once it enters the literature. As Litt puts it, it is now “impossible to stop people, amateur or professional, from pushing a button to produce mathematics”. As an outside observer, it is fascinating to watch mathematicians as they try to adapt to this new reality. I’m also very glad that I don’t have to be the one to develop new rules for the great mathematical puzzle, now that AI looks set to dominate the game.

El Niño could raise wildfire and water-quality risks in Hawke’s Bay, council says

New Zealand Herald October 01, 2026

The risk of wildfires in Hawke's Bay could be magnified by El Niño conditions this summer. Photo / Paul Taylor

Hawke’s Bay is bracing for the possible environmental impacts of El Niño, including fish deaths, algal blooms, wildfires and poor water quality.

Regional councillors were briefed on Wednesday on the potential effects, with Integrated Catchment manager Richard Wakelin discussing HBRC’s role if the region went into “extreme dry” conditions.

El Niño is a natural climate pattern that causes surface water in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean to become much warmer than usual.

The October-November forecast released on Thursday by Earth Sciences New Zealand says “very strong El Niño conditions” are present in the tropical Pacific and are expected to strengthen further.

“El Niño’s influence on New Zealand’s weather patterns is becoming increasingly apparent and is expected to be a dominant driver of climate patterns during the outlook period.”

For Hawke’s Bay, the outlook predicts temperatures most likely to be above average (50% chance), with potential for notable short-duration warm spells associated with strong, gusty westerly winds.

“Rainfall totals are most likely to be below normal [55% chance] over the outlook period as a whole and soil moisture levels and river flows are about equally likely to be below normal [45% chance] or near normal [40% chance].”

Wakelin said HBRC was not the primary responder.

But he said the council’s role was to monitor environmental conditions and forecast information, river flows, groundwater levels, soil moisture and ecological conditions.

El Niño conditions can cause low river flows and high water temperatures, leading to increased algae and cyanobacteria growth and lower dissolved oxygen levels.

Wakelin said it was important to share clear scientific information and advice with the community and partner agencies and that they would implement restrictions, including water take restrictions, where required.

HBRC would work alongside agencies such as DoC, Fish and Game and Health NZ, and iwi, hapū and emergency partners.

Chair Sophie Siers said that while El Niño accounted for about 25% of the influences that shaped Hawke’s Bay’s weather, current forecasts suggested it could be a significant event for eastern New Zealand.

“One of HBRC’s key responsibilities is understanding the science behind these climate patterns and helping Hawke’s Bay prepare for the possible impacts.”

She said council teams were monitoring forecasts and environmental conditions while working alongside Hawke’s Bay Civil Defence Emergency Management and other partner agencies to share information and co-ordinate planning.

“Whether it’s water resources, fire risk, land management or the health of our rivers and ecosystems, our role is to ensure decisions are informed by the best available science and that communities have the information they need as conditions evolve.”

Hawke’s Bay has felt the effects of El Niño before.

In 1972-73, 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16, El Niño conditions resulted in drought or very dry conditions in Hawke’s Bay.

HBRC’s agenda says forecasts indicate the current event will be stronger than those events and likely to extend into next autumn.

Deputy chair Jerf van Beek said that if this year’s El Niño was as bad as it sounded, it would have a serious effect on our population “especially our farming community”.

“In 1972-1973 we didn’t have as much irrigation along the Heretaunga Plains, but we are now far better equipped at dealing with that and I believe there is plenty of water there.”

Midwife censured for continuing care after unwanted sexual encounter with client’s partner

New Zealand Herald October 01, 2026

A midwife has been censured after she failed to end the client relationship with a woman who was pregnant with twins.

A midwife has been censured for failing to stop providing services to a client after an alleged non-consensual sexual encounter with the woman’s partner.

The Health Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal found that the midwife, whose name is permanently suppressed, committed professional misconduct amounting to malpractice.

It heard that she provided pregnancy, birth and post-natal care to the client for six months about 10 years ago.

During this time, there was an alleged unwanted sexual encounter involving the client’s partner, who was the father of her unborn twins.

Jo Hughson, counsel for the Professional Conduct Committee (PCC), said the midwife “felt pressured and did not willingly engage” in the encounter.

While the incident precipitated the events, the misconduct charge related to the midwife’s decision to continue providing care to the client afterwards.

“There is an obligation professionally on a midwife to take steps to facilitate the termination of the relationship and not provide services to the client,” Hughson said.

The conduct went beyond “minor human error”, she said.

The midwife continued to provide pregnancy, birth and post-natal care and, in those circumstances, acted in breach of trust and unethically, Hughson said.

Contact the Open Justice team

The tribunal heard that the midwife accepted the misconduct and acknowledged that she should have passed the client’s care to another midwife.

She is no longer practising as a midwife.

Tribunal chairman Truc Tran said the allegation had been established and amounted to professional misconduct and malpractice.

The midwife was censured and ordered to pay 25% of the PCC’s costs and 25% of the tribunal’s costs.

Brianna McIlraith is a Queenstown-based reporter for Open Justice covering courts in the lower South Island. She has been a journalist since 2018 and has had a strong interest in business and financial journalism.

Two arrested as protesters target NZ Aerospace Summit in Christchurch

New Zealand Herald October 01, 2026

Protesters outside Te Pae Convention Centre during the New Zealand Aerospace Summit. Photo / Chris Keall

Two men have been arrested after vehicles blocked emergency entrances to Christchurch’s Te Pae Convention Centre as protesters gathered outside the New Zealand Aerospace Summit.

About 20 police officers were at the central city venue this morning, where dozens of protesters opposed to the aerospace industry’s links to defence gathered outside entrances and chanted across the road in Victoria Square.

One person was chained to a vehicle near an entrance.

Writing on the car included “NZ complicit in genocide” and “this car blocks war crimes”.

Christchurch Metro area commander Superintendent Lane Todd said two men, aged 56 and 23, had been charged with obstruction.

The arrests came after vehicles blocked emergency entrances to the building.

“While we respect the right to peaceful protest, Police will not tolerate actions that threaten public safety or intimidate others exercising their lawful rights.”

Police had earlier said officers would monitor the protest throughout the day.

Attendees were warned by summit organisers to allow extra time for security screening and not to engage with protesters outside the venue.

The action was organised by Peace Action Ōtautahi, which had promoted a “Swarm the Summit” mobilisation and called for protesters to march from Victoria Park to Te Pae.

Protester Jae Duguid said the group opposed the involvement of companies with military and defence contracts in the aerospace industry.

“We’re here today because there’s a lot of companies at this aerospace convention held at Te Pae that don’t want to use space for peaceful means,” Duguid said.

“They want to use it for profit, and they want to use it for war.”

Duguid claimed companies involved in the sector had links to the United States and Israeli militaries and said the protesters wanted those attending to know they were “not welcome in this city”.

“We’re here to make them uncomfortable and we’re here to show them that we mean business.”

Peace Action Ōtautahi protester Aurora Garner-Randolph said protesters wanted stronger restrictions around the military use of New Zealand’s aerospace technology.

“Aerospace has enormous potential to do good in climate mitigation technology, but there need to be clear legal and moral parameters,” she said.

Garner-Randolph said the group wanted exports of aerospace and military components, as well as intelligence-related launches for foreign militaries, halted until stronger legal safeguards were in place.

“Ōtautahi has a proud history of peace, of being a peace city,” she said.

“The time for discussion is over and the time for clear legal change is now.”

By about 10.30am, nearly all of the protesters had left the area.

The New Zealand Aerospace Summit brings together aerospace companies, researchers, investors, regulators and international representatives.

This year’s programme includes more than 50 domestic and international speakers and covers autonomous aircraft, aerospace manufacturing, Earth observation, climate monitoring and defence applications.

Kea Aerospace chief executive and summit organiser Mark Rocket said protesters had a right to demonstrate.

“We live in a free and democratic country, so we support protesters’ right to protest.”

Rocket said defence was one part of a much broader aerospace sector.

“The reality is we have an aerospace sector that is working on environmental monitoring, telecommunications, a wide range of aspects, and defence is part of that for some aerospace companies in New Zealand.”

Responding to protesters’ concerns about companies working on defence technology, Rocket said many aerospace technologies had civilian and military applications.

“But from what we’re seeing, New Zealand has very much an approach towards looking at environmental monitoring, telecommunications, and really aligned with New Zealand’s values and ethos on how we approach the defence industry.”

Rocket Lab founder Sir Peter Beck earlier essayed a similar dual-use argument that spanned GPS to Tinder.

The protest follows similar action at last year’s summit, when activists blockaded Te Pae entrances and police removed some protesters.

The summit began yesterday and ends today.

Wellington teen uses giant sign to stand out in tough job market

New Zealand Herald October 01, 2026

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

A teenager struggling to find work in a tough job market has come up with a novel way to cut through the recruitment process, and it’s already delivering results.

Valera Maximovich Bonyushkin recently used his savings to move to Wellington City from Ōtaki but quickly discovered finding a job wouldn’t be so easy.

With the introduction of AI interviews and scanners to the already tricky process, he realised he would have to think outside the box to get noticed.

So Bonyushkin went slightly old school, walking a giant sign down the capital’s Golden Mile.

The sign which reads “Enthusiastic Person looking for a job” – alongside his contact details – certainly captured the attention of Wellingtonians.

Hundreds of messages of support have flooded in on social media, and public encouragement has followed him through his journey in the busy streets of Wilis St and Lambton Quay.

“I think it sends a very clear message, it helps prove that you’re hard working, that you’re enthusiastic, especially for a young person.”

Bonyushkin said he has previously worked in multiple roles including as a barista, front of house, managing, rostering and admin.

He said he had tried all the common ways to get a job - Seek, Facebook, calls, emails, handing in his CV in person and giving a personal introduction.

“It’s much easier to stand out when you’re physically there, when you’re talking to the person, it’s much more memorable.”

He even jumped into the ocean for a promotional Facebook video in the middle of winter with his advertising sign.

“Because we’re in a digital age, it’s so easy to overlook the person behind the CV.

“What I’m just trying to do is give a proper impression rather than just a piece of paper, because anyone can say anything on a piece of paper.”

Bonyushkin started out with a standard piece of cardboard but after his father’s recommendation upgraded to a $70 professional corflute sign.

The inspiration came from an interview workshop he did the first time he was unemployed at 17 years old.

He’s brought the sign back into action two years later after leaving his position at an Ōtaki bakery for bigger opportunities in the capital city.

Bonyushkin was prepared to walk all day if he had to but so far had been travelling the streets for about six hours a day.

His parents were supportive but doubted his luck with the current job market in Wellington after the public service was hit with job cuts.

Youth unemployment for 15- to 24-year-olds in the year to June 2026 in Wellington City was 9.3%, slightly below the national average of 13.8% according to Infometrics.

The idea seems to be working for the now 19-year-old, with opportunities arriving only four days after beginning his new endeavour.

He’s already had a trial for an admin role and another introduction meeting with a hospitality business.

Bonyushkin said he won’t stop promoting himself until it’s set in stone.

“I’m a pessimistic person by heart.

“I do not trust things working out.”

He said it’s another strategy for those struggling with the usual routes but wouldn’t encourage everyone to do it as it could take away from the shock value.

Grace Symmans is a Wellington-based reporter who covers news in the capital. Grace joined NZME in 2025 as a producer for Wellington Mornings on Newstalk ZB. She can be emailed at grace. symmans@nzme. co. nz.

Gisborne council votes to close Titirangi Maunga roads to vehicles overnight

New Zealand Herald October 01, 2026

While a majority of public submissions favoured it, councillors were divided on a proposal to close Titirangi Maunga to vehicles overnight. The closure passed with a vote of 5-4. Photo / Gisborne Herald.

Pedestrians and bikers will be the only people able to see the sun rise from Titirangi Maunga after Gisborne District councillors voted to impose an overnight road closure.

Local hapū Ngāti Oneone put forward the proposal in June because of concerns about vandalism, antisocial behaviour and illegal dumping at the site.

Gates will restrict vehicle access to Titirangi Drive and Queens Drive over Titirangi Maunga from 10pm to 6am year-round.

Emergency services will be provided with keys to access during those hours.

Exceptions will be made for specific events, such as Fire in the Sky on New Year’s Day, to allow the community to use the hill as a vantage point.

Gate installation was estimated to cost between $6000 and $10,000. Management of the closure would be part of an existing park closure contract with landscaping service Green by Nature.

Gisborne District Council’s Environment and Communities Committee received public consultation results on Thursday, which informed the staff-recommended closure.

Consultation asked the public to choose between closures from 10pm to 6am or until 5am year-round, seasonally adjusted opening hours or unrestricted access.

There were more than 190 submissions, with 187 expressing a preferred option.

Of those, 74.5% supported closure, with the 10pm to 6am closure receiving the most support at 38%.

Principal community assets and partnerships adviser Chris Visser said walkers from the Titirangi challenge supported a later opening time so they could participate without vehicles on the road.

Some submitters asked why a closure aimed at addressing illegal dumping was proposed and whether council would consider closures at other hotspots.

“This proposal is a very definite proposal to deal with a specific set of issues in a specific place that is of high significance to Ngāti Oneone. So we are not proposing that this is a mechanism by which council would control and mitigate or attempt to eliminate illegal dumping across our district,” Visser said.

Councillor Sam Gibson objected to the recommended closure, stating that while the proposal supported mana whenua, he felt alternative options were not thoroughly explored.

“I don’t think it’s a great solution, and I don’t think that we consulted with our ratepayer base on really significant alternative solutions. I don’t feel like we’ve investigated additional solutions to this issue that allow our public the freedom to enjoy such a beautiful maunga, whether they be people that don’t have the ability to ride or walk.”

Councillor Rob Telfer was concerned the closure would not fix the dumping problem.

“I’m just wondering, should we be punishing everybody for the few that are causing the problem when we can put camera technology that is around now and actually catch these people.”

Reporting offenders to police would take action against the problem rather than indirectly relocating it, he said.

“They’ll go out here and dump rubbish, or they’ll go find somewhere else to go and do it. So unless you actually address the problem, I don’t see that this is actually fixing anything in the long term.”

Some submissions shared those concerns, but the majority supported closure to protect the recreational and cultural value of the maunga, Visser said.

“I suppose the question for you is: do you choose not to attempt to fix this problem in this place because of the values of this place or just leave it as it is because it’s just a much larger problem.”

Councillor Larry Foster said he supported the paper, having seen the damage firsthand.

“Hopefully this will help mitigate a lot of that, and people can still access it by bike or by walking any time of the night or day even if the gates are closed.”

He expressed concern about the impact of the closure on watching the sunrise, but appreciated its flexibility based on event activity.

Councillors Colin Alder, Teddy Thompson, Telfer and Gibson voted against the recommendation, but it passed with the other five councillors’ support.

The restriction will begin in early 2027 and will be reviewed for effectiveness in 2029.

Election 2026: National pivots cost-of-living focus to lines companies with energy policy

New Zealand Herald October 01, 2026

National's energy spokesman, Simeon Brown, says the changes will make it easier for households to connect rooftop solar and sell it into the grid. Photo / NZME

The National Party has shifted its gaze to lines companies and grid operator Transpower, promising changes in a nine-point energy policy released this morning.

Energy spokesman Simeon Brown said the changes would make it easier for households to connect rooftop solar and sell it into the grid. It also reiterated National’s promise to force data centre operators to bring their own generation.

The charges most lines companies include in power bills are capped by the Commerce Commission. Brown said that, when the Commerce Commission set the most recent cap in November 2024, interest rates were high, which allowed it to lock in a high cap for lines charges until March 2030. However, interest rates had since fallen.

“Over the past year, lines charges accounted for around two-thirds of the rise in the average power bill,” Brown’s policy document said.

National is promising to review Part 4 of the Commerce Act, which regulates how much revenue lines companies can recover, saying the current regime does not balance investment and affordability.

The party is also promising to open up transmission to more private investment.

National says it will “provide a clear regulatory pathway for privately owned transmission assets to connect to and operate alongside Transpower’s grid, subject to the same fundamental technical, reliability and system- operation requirements as comparable transmission infrastructure”.

National pledges to amend the Electricity Industry Act and work with the Electricity Authority to change transmission pricing methodology to allow more private transmission infrastructure to be built.

“New Zealand is experiencing its biggest renewables boom in a generation under National, with more new renewable generation built in the past three years than in the previous eight,” Brown said.

“That’s helped lower the price power companies pay for electricity, with significant reductions in wholesale prices in the past year. That supports businesses, and puts households on a path to more affordable power.

“But the price of electricity itself is only one part of a power bill. Lines charges, red tape, weak competition, and the cost of keeping the lights on in a dry year all add to what Kiwis pay. Our nine-point plan takes on each of them.

“Lines charges accounted for around two-thirds of the rise in the average power bill over the past year. They’re set under an outdated law, so we’ll review it and make necessary changes ahead of the next price reset. We’ll also let Kiwis choose who does the connection work they’re paying for.”

The policy promises to force lines companies to approve residential and small-business solar connection applications within two working days, with automatic compensation for customers for every day a network goes over the deadline.

The party also promises to make “affordability” a core objective for the Electricity Authority by writing it into law, so the cost of power for households and businesses carries equal weight with competition, reliability and efficiency in every decision the regulator makes.

National would require the Electricity Authority to regularly publish an independent assessment of how much back-up generation New Zealand needs to get through dry periods, when hydro storage is low and wind and solar output is weak. It would also require greater disclosure of back-up contract volumes, durations and prices.

The party would create a standardised back-up power contract and require large generators to participate in regular auctions, so retailers, businesses and new investors can buy guaranteed cover on common terms. National’s policy document argues that the current back-up market is too concentrated, with the four major gentailers owning more than 95% of flexible generation.

The policy also notes the Government is “starting a procurement process” to deliver an LNG import terminal, which National says will reduce power prices by reducing dry-year risk. However, support for the terminal within the coalition Government is fragile.

Labour’s energy spokeswoman Megan Woods responded to the policy saying the policy was an “absolute fizzer’.

“Kiwis are sick of being told cheaper power is just around the corner. National has had three years to deliver, and power bills are still hurting households,” Woods said.

“After three years in Government, Simeon Brown should be delivering cheaper electricity, not another grab-bag of ideas and excuses.

“This is not a plan to bring power bills down. It’s an admission National hasn’t got a clue how to do it.

“Families are cutting back, people are rationing power, and pensioners are struggling to keep warm. Meanwhile, National is offering more reviews and working groups instead of relief,” Woods said.

Woods said Labour’s policy, “SolarSaver” which would help boost rooftop solar uptake, will cut bills and said Labour would ban price gouging.

National has announced a policy similar to SolarSaver to boost rooftop solar uptake.

Ryan Fox has described the surreal experience of meeting Donald Trump at the Presidents Cup, where the United States President offered the Kiwi golfer a memorable compliment.

Fox was making his debut for the International team at Medinah Country Club in Chicago when he got to meet Trump, who was attending the event as honorary chairman, and later participated in the trophy presentation.

The 39-year-old said the experience of having the US President at the tournament was unlike anything he had encountered in golf, with heightened security surrounding his appearance.

Speaking to Katie Bradford on Ryan Bridge TODAY, Fox said he got to shake hands with Trump at the first tee, where he congratulated him on his recent Open Championship success.

“I get on the tee and he just said to me, ‘I really like your game and a huge congrats on the Open’,” Fox said.

“To hear that from the President of the United States was pretty cool.

“Regardless of where any of us golfers stand politically, he’s a huge golf fan. There’s a lot of events around the world at his golf courses, and he is mad keen on it.

“Having someone in his office be a fan of golf has been good for the game of golf for the most part.”

Not many Kiwis would have had the chance to be in Trump’s presence, but Fox said it was like something he had never experienced before.

“There’s Secret Service everywhere, there’s snipers, there’s Delta Force squads and everything else rolling around,” Fox said.

“Having him there certainly added to the atmosphere. It did make life a little more difficult for us, with all the extra stuff going on, but that’s all part of it.

“He’s been to quite a few golf events over the last couple of years and I think everyone just knows what’s coming when he’s going to turn up.”

Entering the final day with singles matches, Fox’s international team were ahead by three points, but Team USA rallied to win nine of the 12 matches to secure a 17-13 win.

Fox was solid with his form, winning both of his foursomes (alternate shot) matches, teaming up with Australian Min Woo Lee. His losses came in his one four-ball (best ball) assignment – with him and Australian Adam Scott beaten 3&2 by Wyndham Clark and Collin Morikawa – while he fell in his singles match against Xander Schauffele 2&1.

Despite being on the losing side, Fox said the opportunity to compete in the team event was one he would remember.

Another surreal experience Fox got to be part of recently was being out on the field with the All Blacks, holding the New Zealand flag as the team sang the national anthem before the fourth test against the Springboks in Baltimore.

The honour came as a surprise, with Fox only finding out a few days beforehand that he would be involved.

He told his parents before the event who misunderstood his text, and were shocked to see him on the field.

“I never dreamt that I would do it,” Fox said. “And yet, to only find out a few days beforehand and to get that call was pretty special.”

“I actually told Mum and Dad that I was going to be out there before the game and they misread my text and they absolutely lost their minds when they saw me out there with the flag before the game.

“To be out there with the guys, I know the result didn’t go the way we wanted to, but the atmosphere was amazing and to get to feel what they feel week in, week out.

“We don’t get much like that in golf. I would say maybe the first tee shot of the Presidents Cup or first tee shot of a major is kind of similar with that kind of atmosphere, but to have 70,000 people screaming in the stands is pretty special and it was great to be a part of it.”

Ben Francis is an Auckland-based reporter for the New Zealand Herald who covers breaking sports news.

Tennessee suspends executions as Christa Pike’s lawyer says failed lethal injection leaves her in critical condition

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 21:44:49 GMT

Independent inquiry ordered after failed execution of Pike, who was convicted of 1994 murder

Christa Pike: what we know so far about Tennessee woman’s failed execution

Tennessee’s governor on Thursday said it was “deeply disturbing” that his state botched the execution of a death row prisoner who remained alive and snoring 40 minutes after receiving a double dose of the lethal drug that should have quickly killed her.

Bill Lee, a Republican, has suspended all executions in the state until at least the end of the year and ordered an independent inquiry after Wednesday night’s failed attempt to put to death Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder, at the execution chamber in Nashville.

Meanwhile, Pike, 50, remained in the hospital on Thursday afternoon. “We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment, but we do know that she is alive right now and receiving life-saving medical care,” Randy Spivey, one of her attorneys, said at an afternoon press conference.

“She is in critical condition receiving life-saving care. That is the extent of what we have at the moment.”

Spivey, of the office of the post-conviction defender, condemned Tennessee authorities for the manner in which the failed attempt unfolded. He said officials used seven needles, one of which became bent as it was removed from Pike’s arm.

“Last night was not just inefficient, it was cruel and it was torturous. It was also predictable,” he said, adding that he saw no life-saving care given after the execution attempt was abandoned at about 8.25pm.

Speaking to reporters on Thursday morning, Lee said he had spoken with Frank Strada, secretary of the Tennessee department of correction, but did not have an update on the condition of Pike, who was taken to an off-site medical facility after surviving two doses of pentobarbital.

“This is a tragedy,” Lee said, adding that he had not yet spoken to the families of Pike or the teenager she killed in 1995. “There is no one that wanted what happened last night to happen. It shouldn’t have happened.

“It’s the most difficult of circumstances as it relates to the sentence that should have been carried out by the state. It’s a tragedy, and it’s deeply disturbing that that has happened in this state. The people deserve better than that.”

Lee added, in comments reported by the Tennessean, that he had not yet chosen an investigator to lead a “comprehensive, third party review” he announced in a statement late Wednesday.

“There are a lot of questions,” he said. “The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered. I’m highly disappointed, along with Tennesseans, about what happened.”

Cameron Sexton, the Republican speaker of Tennessee’s house of representatives, said on Thursday in a social media post that he and other lawmakers would also be investigating what went wrong with the attempted execution. He added that they would look at other ways to prevent executions from failing.

“We will look at all options – expanding the alternatives, and changing the current medications to include potassium chloride,” he said. “Thirty years is too long for justice.”

Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said her group was aware of seven other people that have survived medical problems due to an execution team’s failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but nobody had remained alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions.

“This failed attempt is the worst we’ve ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era,” she said in a statement.

“What happened to Christa Pike can be attributed to the extreme secrecy Tennessee officials have maintained about their execution procedures, their refusal to answer reasonable questions and their unwillingness to accept responsibility for their mistakes.”

In May, Tennessee officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, another convicted murderer, after failing for more than an hour to place an intravenous line into his arm.

Pike, who was sentenced to death for the brutal 1994 killing of a teenage classmate, was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

The execution attempt was allowed to proceed only after the US supreme court intervened late on Wednesday to lift a federal court stay issued earlier in the day, a delay it said was necessary to assess whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her 1996 sentencing.

Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion to the Tennessee supreme court after the second pentobarbital dose was administered asking to halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony”, and that the state was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.

A representative of the state corrections department defended its handling of the unsuccessful execution attempt.

“The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office,” the spokesperson, Dorinda Carter, said in a statement.

“The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility.”

According to the AP, Tennessee’s execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.

Seven journalists who were present at the Riverbend maximum security institution as witnesses described what they saw during a livestream hosted by WVLT television station soon after curtains in the execution chamber were lowered for the final time.

They said Pike was snoring as corrections officials escorted them out.

John North, of ABC News affiliate WBIR, said: “It appears this did not go how this was supposed to go. When we left the building, so far as we knew, she was probably still alive.”

Pike and her boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp were 18 and 17 when they and another female friend tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in January 1995, using boxcutters and a rock.

The case garnered nationwide headlines due to the ages of those involved and the brutality of the murder, in which Shipp carved a pentagram into their victim’s chest and Pike later showed a friend a fragment of her skull.

Pike never denied the killing, and was later diagnosed with mental health disorders.

“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” she said in a clemency petition that Lee and the US supreme court denied.

Lee’s suspension order affects the only other execution set in Tennessee this year. Gary Wayne Sutton has been on death row since 1996 for the murder of a friend, and was scheduled to be put to death on 3 December.

UK airlines to be banned from charging parents to sit with children

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 21:41:19 GMT

Planned rule change forms part of Burnham’s bid to crack down on the ‘little charges that add up’

Airlines will be blocked from charging parents extra to sit with their children on planes, according to government plans.

The new rule would require airlines to seat passengers aged under 14 next to their parents or an accompanying adult free of charge. Passengers will also no longer need to pay to tweak the name on their flight booking if they need to correct a mistake.

It is understood that ministers will try to introduce the changes before the start of next year’s summer holidays. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said the rule changes are part of a crackdown on the “little charges that add up” when families plan their holidays.

MPs are in the process of debating a new set of rules for travel companies, as the civil aviation (consumer protection and regulatory reform) bill makes its way through parliament. The proposed law will give ministers flexible power to set out passenger rights and the duties of airlines and airports.

Burnham said: “Charging parents just to sit with their children is a rip-off, plain and simple. And being hit with a hefty fee for a simple spelling mistake on a booking form isn’t right either.

“People are fed up with these little charges that add up, so I’m putting a stop to them. This is what our everyday fixes are all about – giving people room to breathe by tackling the small irritations that catch people out, waste their time and cost them money.”

An arrangement to sit together can currently cost a parent and child up to £104 on a return journey, according to the Department for Transport.

Rory Boland, editor of consumer magazine Which? Travel, said: “It’s clearly unfair to force parents and children as young as three to pay an extra fee just to sit together. Airlines that have separated families are putting profit ahead of passenger peace of mind.”

Earlier this year, Ryanair adjusted its family seating policy after an investigation was launched into the company charging parents to sit with their children on flights. The Irish operator previously required parents travelling with children aged between two and 11 to pay to reserve what was referred to as a mandatory family seat.

Children were then allocated seats next to or near parents free of charge. The fee for a mandatory family seat was typically about £8 each way, the UK Competition and Markets Authority watchdog found.

Farmers’ market shoppers might not usually pay much attention to the local resident devouring fresh bread and pastries at one of the stalls with extra gusto – but some certainly did last weekend when they realized it was a hungry bear.

Onlookers on Saturday reached for their phones to take photos and videos of the bear in downtown Aspen, Colorado, after it wandered through the stalls and got up on to its hind legs to dig into the baked goods.

At one point it jumped up on to the table to get better access to the pastries.

Bears are particularly active and hungry ahead of hibernation as record drought has reduced food sources, pushing up the numbers of contacts with the public.

Manchester City played out a high-quality draw with Real Madrid in the Women’s Champions League after an unprecedented week of off-field tension at the English club.

The match was played in a week when the wider football club has dominated the headlines for the wrong reasons and, while Andrée Jeglertz was at pains to insist that it has been “business as usual” for the women’s team despite the damning guilty verdict released by the Premier League towards the men’s side, there was a strange mood around this stadium in the buildup to kick-off with opinions mixed.

Speaking to supporters on the bridge that connects this venue with the neighbouring Etihad Stadium, some appeared relaxed about the situation and unsure what it had to do with the women’s team, while others were clearly troubled and looking forward to watching some football as a form of escapism.

An elderly City fan, who did not wish to be named, said pre-match: “We’ve been through rough times before, we’ll come through rough times again,” in a matter-of-fact manner. Another simply demonstrated what appears to be a growing dislike for reporters asking about the 115 charges when they said angrily “you’re from the media?” before using an expletive and promptly walking away.

The day after Paris FC played their first Women’s Champions League home game at Stade Jean-Bouin, across the road from Paris Saint-Germain’s Parc des Princes, PSG’s women’s team entertained Leuven 20km away at the club’s suburban training centre.

Rasheedat Ajibade put the hosts ahead from close range after nine minutes against the Belgian side. Naomie Feller (pictured) then scored a quick-fire double, before Sakina Karchaoui and Vitória Yaya completed PSG's 5-0 rout.

In the early games, Modesta Uka scored Austria Vienna’s first goal in the WCL but Inter's captain, Ivana Andrés, levelled in the fourth minute of added time to earn a 1-1 draw. Inter dropping points left Barcelona, who thrashed Roma on Wednesday, as the only WCL team with six points after two games.

In a match between two teams that had lost in the opening round, HB Køge crushed visiting Swiss team Servette 5-1 in Denmark. PA

A much politer, younger woman simply expressed her sadness and her hopes that it wouldn’t cause the players stress. Once the match started, there were occasional references to the news from the stands; midway through the first half one home fan sang ‘Sheikh Mansour, my lord, Sheikh Mansour, oh lord, Sheikh Mansour’, to the tune of Kumbaya, although nobody else appeared to join in. There was also a small group of men carrying an inflatable banana in one corner defiantly chanting about ‘City going down with a billion in the bank’. In general, though, the regular Women’s Super League match-going fans who are members of the supporters club seemed focused on their usual repertoire of fan chants to encourage the players, whether singing about the brilliance of Aoba Fujino and later chanting the name of Mary Fowler, who hit the crossbar with a header before the break.

It was a sign of the Spanish team’s intent and they looked sharp through the opening 45 minutes, albeit City were moving the ball nicely at times too.

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 20:58:07 GMT

On a night when Erling Haaland moped around the pitch, dragging his hulking frame across the Cardiff turf, Wales registered a welcome victory over 10-man Norway and their first this year. Daniel James cancelled out Oscar Bobb’s well-worked opener in the first half and 17 seconds into the restart Torbjørn Heggem was sent off for fouling James as the Leeds winger streamed through towards goal, resulting in a free-kick from which Neco Williams earned Craig Bellamy’s side the three points. “You’re just a shit Kieffer Moore,” was the chant at Haaland from the locals.

Bellamy was under no illusions about the task facing his side. He described Norway as one of the best teams in the world and one riding the crest of a wave after reaching the World Cup quarter-finals. Martin Ødegaard, the Arsenal and Norway captain, was the visitors’ creator in chief and it was no surprise he was the architect for a crisp opener, slotted in by Bobb, one of two Fulham players and one of five Premier League regulars in the Norway starting lineup.

Ødegaard took the ball off Sander Berge, another of those familiar faces, and rolled a soft, weighted pass behind Ben Davies. Bobb scurried behind the Wales captain and beat Danny Ward at the near post.

Wales welcomed back Lewis Koumas, one of five changes from Sunday’s defeat in Denmark, and it was another player promoted to the starting lineup who was the catalyst for the hosts’ equaliser. Liam Cullen, who in the summer joined Leicester from Swansea, pinched the ball from Berge after the Fulham midfielder was sluggish to claim Fredrik Aursnes’s pass and Wales raced away in possession. Cullen and Koumas burst forward and Sorba Thomas, who was a constant danger on the flank, sent a low cross into the box, where James beat David Møller Wolfe to the punch. Wales had their first goal of the campaign and Haaland clamped his hands on his hips.

Wales had responded well after going behind and Norway appeared a little complacent. Thomas elected to square the ball for James rather than shoot when in on goal, allowing Møller Wolfe to intervene, and then the Brentford defender Kristoffer Ajer diverted a Thomas cross wide for a corner.

Norway equally should have doubled their lead and Ben Cabango, the Swansea defender asked to mark Cristiano Ronaldo and Haaland over the past week, was grateful Berge’s cross cannoned off him and straight into the hands of Ward after he got his feet in a muddle in front of goal.

Haaland had one of those Haaland halves; he was on the periphery of things and recorded only 11 first-half touches, the fewest of any player, including the Dortmund full-back Julian Ryerson who was forced off through injury after 16 minutes. Ethan Ampadu easily won what, technically, will go down as a duel on halfway but in truth Haaland just stuck out a flailing leg in the hope of catching the ball. His only whiff of goal in the first half came a couple of minutes before the interval but Ryerson’s replacement, Marcus Pedersen, misread Haaland’s movement and the moment passed.

Norway were punished for being slow out of the blocks, 13 seconds after Ødegaard got the second half started. Bobb played draught excluder behind a white wall of Norway shirts and Nyland stepped to his left. He was out of position when he had to shuttle across his goalline as Williams thrashed the ball into the bottom corner.

Ståle Solbakken turned to Jørgen Strand Larsen and Antonio Nusa with 15 minutes of normal time remaining.

Up the other end, Haaland ambled across the box before Pedersen sent another cross in from the right. When Pedersen whipped the ball in, Haaland soared highest but, unmarked, headed straight at Ward. Then came a puff of the cheeks, a look to the turf. It has been that kind of week.

Supreme court to hear case challenging Trump’s immigration detention policy

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 20:20:49 GMT

Court will review practice of indefinite detention for undocumented immigrants living in the US

The US supreme court agreed on Thursday to take up a case challenging the Trump administration’s practice of indefinite detention for undocumented immigrants living in the US and awaiting deportation proceedings.

At the center of the immigration case is a dispute over Donald Trump’s reinterpretation of a longstanding policy that has led to a huge surge in the number of migrants held in detention centers.

For years, undocumented immigrants, who had been living in the US could be released back into their communities on bond, so long as they did not pose a threat to safety or were considered a flight risk.

But last year, administration officials reinterpreted the statute to mean any migrant who entered the US illegally should be held in detention while awaiting legal proceedings.

The case was the latest Trump-era immigration policy to be added to the high court’s docket this term.

This week, justices said they would hear arguments in a case challenging the administration’s “third-country” deportations, which allow immigrants to be sent to a country other than their own.

The challenger to the Trump administration’s reinterpreted policy denying bond hearings is Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a Brazilian citizen who has been living in the US for more than 20 years.

Authorities say Barbosa da Cunha entered the US illegally in or around 2005. He owns a home in Massachusetts, runs a small construction company, has a wife and two US-born children, and has never been charged with a crime.

He was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents last year while driving to work and moved to an immigration detention facility in Buffalo, New York.

Barbosa da Cunha had requested a bond hearing but was denied.

A district court sided with Barbosa da Cunha, ordering the government to give him a bond hearing. An appeals court affirmed that decision after the administration appealed.

But now lawyers for the government are asking the supreme court to intervene.

The dispute is not unique to Barbosa da Cunha; lower courts have been split on the Trump administration’s policy reinterpretation in other immigration cases as well.

More than 500 district court judges and nine of the 11 federal appeals courts who have heard similar cases have rejected the Trump administration’s new interpretation, according to the New York Times.

Judges have largely agreed that the statute the Trump administration is using to indefinitely detain undocumented immigrants only applies to those who have been apprehended at a port of entry, such as the US-Mexico border.

The Celebrity Traitors review – Ross Kemp really needs to get a grip

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 20:15:00 GMT

The most hotly anticipated TV show of the year is here! And a number of the stars – ahem Grant Mitchell – are struggling already …

Warning: this article contains spoilers for episode one of The Celebrity Traitors.

So – have they managed to capture lightning in a franchised bottle again? The new series of The Celebrity Traitors, more hotly anticipated than Nigella entering the Bake Off tent, is here. Twenty-one contestants of varying levels of fame, but never dipping below C-list, have signed up to endure Claudia Winkleman’s tyranny in Ardross Castle, in the hope of winning up to £100,000 for their chosen charity and a place in the nation’s consciousness and possible heart for between one week and a lifetime, depending how things work out.

We get our first glimpse of the gang as they file into a church replete with masked guards and floral tributes spelling out RIP and VIP at the altar. Actors, broadcasters, comedians, musicians and some miscellanea start to fill up the pews. Young Sebastian Croft pauses to genuflect before continuing down the aisle, and such is the power of the format that you immediately wonder if this is a tactic to make himself seem trustworthy. Will it work? Or is anyone with a religious belief marked as a weirdo for whom anything is possible these days?

If you think that’s sensitivity gone mad, may I introduce you to Ross Kemp? Before the episode is out, he is turning bewildered circles in the castle, convinced that anyone who touches him is trying to murder him in plain sight. Get it together, Kemp. We’ve a long way to go yet.

But this is what we came for, of course. To see behind famous faces to the reality beneath. The hard man who is actually a soft target will do nicely. If mathematician Hannah Fry proves incapable of putting stats to work in her service, it will be noted. If Julie Hesmondhalgh (“I get hungry for friendship with people I see on the telly!”) turns out to be a Machiavellian genius, we will be over the moon. How long can they last in a game that is all about personalities before they have to reveal the true nature of theirs?

It’s about 30 seconds for Richard E Grant. Most people – apart from Hannah Fry (“I am dripping with prefect energy”) – want to be chosen as traitors. But Reg publicly longs to be chosen as a traitor (“It would be the jackpot!”). He is chosen as a traitor. He is asked by Joe Lycett whether he is a traitor. “I am a traitor!” he gleefully replies. A drama queen without guile. An actor’s actor. “Already iconic,” says Claudia.

Some choose to ignore this revelation – unprecedented in the history of either Celebrity or peon Traitors. “He’s just acting out because he hasn’t been chosen,” says Jerry Hall, who has known him for 30 years – and you can well imagine him doing so. But in this case, he has just exuberantly shared the truth. Much of his time in the extended opening episode is spent trying to walk it back.

His partner in treacherous crime is Love Island presenter Maya Jama (“My villain era has begun!”). Together, in one of the twists that any iteration of the series must serve up to keep participants and audience engaged, they must choose the third traitor from two people they haul in to plead their cases. The loser will be murdered (or, if you are one of the three people who do not know how the game works yet, “murdered”). They agree that they must choose two contestants who have taken Reg at his word and believe him (“I’m a traitor!”) to be a traitor. It’s between journalist Amol Rajan and comedian James Acaster. They wait in coffins – I am not a huge fan of this recurring motif, to be honest – to hear their fates, and we hear one of the lids bang shut as the credits roll.

So, the lightning – is it bottled? Not quite as successfully as last time. The law of diminishing returns is brutal in television. The cast feels slightly more muted – the energy is not quite there yet. But Claudia and her clothes and attitude are, and the opening episode of any Traitors outing is always the weakest. It is relationships and alliances that make the show, and they of course take time to build. Seeds have been sown (is Jerry Hall bossy? Is former army captain James Blunt about to reinvent himself as a national hero? Will Romesh Ranganathan and Rob Beckett’s real-life friendship be an asset or a liability?) and will flourish in due course. But it feels as if they are at work in ever so slightly less fertile soil this time round.

Women’s tennis tour announces prize money parity with men’s events

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 19:54:48 GMT

WTA announces ‘major milestone’ in fight for equality

Combined WTA 1000 events to award equal prize money

All combined WTA 1000 tournaments will award women equal prize ⁠money to the men from 2027, the Women’s Tennis Association has announced, ⁠with the Italian ⁠Open ​and other major events joining the rest of the category in offering the ⁠same payouts.

Billie Jean King has often said that she was moved to form the women’s professional tennis circuit after earning $600 for her 1970 Italian Open title while Ilie Nastase took home $3,500 for winning the men’s tournament the same year.

In 2027 – nearly six decades after King’s title at the Foro Italico – the Rome clay-court event will finally award women the same amount of total prize money as men, as part a “major milestone” for the women’s tour.

The initiative means that all combined WTA 1000 events will award equal prize money for the first time. Besides the Italian Open, the holdouts had been the Canadian Open and the Cincinnati Open. The other combined 1000 events in Indian Wells, California; Miami; Madrid and Beijing; as well as all four Grand Slams, already offer equal prize money.

“Achieving equal prize money across all combined WTA 1000 tournaments is a major milestone for tennis,” WTA chair Valerie Camillo said. “It demonstrates the WTA’s continued commitment to leading the sports industry in delivering our athletes competitive and financial equality and is a testament to the enduring nature of the founding vision of the WTA.”

In 2023, Italian Open organisers pledged to have equal prize money starting in 2025 but didn’t carry through on the promise. The total men’s prize money this year in Rome was $9.6m while the women got $8.3m.

Also announced for next year was an expanded WTA 250-level tournament in Manila, Philippines, amid massive interest surrounding home player Alex Eala, who is ranked 18th.

Also, the number of annual WTA 500 level tournaments required for players ranked in the top 50 was reduced from six to four, resulting in a total base playing commitment of 14 WTA tournaments plus the four grand slams in 2027.
