Borthwick’s England reign remains full of contradictions with World Cup a year away

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 19:00:01 GMT

England’s identity under Steve Borthwick is not as clear as it should be this close to the tournament

It was not so long ago that the Rugby Football Union would host an annual Christmas bash. Executives, head coaches, assistants, members of staff and an invitation to the press pack. Mince pies and mulled wine, even a touch of merriment if we were lucky. Eddie Jones would sometimes make an appearance, but the mind goes back to one year when he did not.

To give him his due Steve Borthwick, his assistant at the time, did. He would probably rather have been anywhere else, but one of the more clear-eyed RFU employees, who had long-since figured out that the then forwards coach was destined for the top job, did their utmost to involve him. Alas, Borthwick soon had a long-distance train to catch and hours of in-depth analysis on a laptop ahead of him.

That anecdote feeds a narrative about England’s head coach. That he is astonishingly diligent when it comes to analysis, but struggles with the more human elements of the job. Speak to anyone who has shared a dressing room with him and there are countless more. Equally, however, there is the time he surprised the 2023 World Cup squad by inviting their families to a training session and the compassion shown to Jamie George and Maro Itoje when his two captains were dealing with bereavements.

The point here is that Borthwick is much more complex than the robotic stereotypes that persist. Data-obsessed, yet a far more bold selector than his supposedly maverick predecessor. Full of contradictions.

So, too, are his England side. The players queue up to defend him and his gameplan. Yet they have produced their best performances when taking matters into their own hands and slipping the straitjacket.

Even the RFU’s recent public pronouncements about Borthwick have vacillated. A vote of confidence after the historic Italy defeat was unprecedented and read like an ultimatum. Less than two months later, Borthwick’s position had been strengthened after one of the union’s cloak-and-dagger reviews. A few weeks ago, we learned his contract was being extended.

All of which makes it hard to assess where England stand, almost four years into his tenure and with one year to go until the 2027 World Cup. Are they contenders any more than they were in the final throes of Jones’s reign?

Borthwick leans heavily on statistics, but his record does not stand up to much scrutiny. He has overseen 28 victories from 48 matches, a 58% winning percentage, marginally worse than Stuart Lancaster.

It is a feature of Borthwick’s term that records achieved along the way have been unwanted.

Their heaviest home defeat at the hands of France, first losses to Fiji and Italy and the worst Six Nations performance in England’s history. At the same time, there was the 12-match winning run and glimpses of what this team are capable of, occasions when Twickenham has rocked the rafters, but, in perhaps the greatest indictment, the absence of a statement victory away from home.

Borthwick did not want to take over as England head coach in December 2022 – nine months before he was supposed to – but could not say no. It is to his credit that he guided England to third place in the World Cup, losing to South Africa in the semi-finals by a point, all the more so after a catastrophic warm-up campaign. That he held his nerve despite losing at home to Fiji is a testament to his resilience because there were times he looked as if he might crumble.

It is also true that England could not have wished for a more straightforward draw in France, but then Borthwick had insisted his side “were not good at anything” soon after taking over. In many ways, a short-term run-up to a World Cup campaign is perfect for someone whose coaching credentials, in the true sense of the word, cannot be questioned.

As the ever excitable Jonny May said after England’s third-place win over Argentina: “We’re starting to see what a genius Steve is. You won’t find a harder working man and his approach to the game is a little bit like Alan Turing. If anybody is going to crack the code to rugby, it will be Steve. He’s got an analytical brain, evidence-based, scientific, Spock-like approach.”

The trouble is that the manner in which England’s third-place finish was achieved has entrenched the prevailing narrative. Rassie Erasmus has hit upon a similar theme, if not as complimentary as May, the South Africa coach describing Borthwick as a coach who “thinks like a machine” and as one who “chases trends”. The obvious inference being that he is not one who sets them.

The second part of Borthwick’s tenure began at the 2024 Six Nations. He insisted English rugby had turned a corner, effectively signalling this was when he was initially expecting to take over. Two steps forward, two steps back would be a better way to describe the ensuing period. It is hard to argue that any corners have been turned.

The championship began well enough, Borthwick was quick to put out new faces and in Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, who made his debut against Italy in Rome, you could argue there is no more important player to England’s hopes in Australia than the Exeter winger.

In round three, England arrived in Edinburgh with two wins from two but the wheels came off spectacularly at Murrayfield. Borthwick said his team had “played small”, that the jersey had weighed heavy and Itoje bemoaned “tip-tap, hot-potato rugby”. A week’s soul-searching at a training camp in York, when Borthwick is understood to have been implored to give the players more time to learn attacking structures, followed.

It paid off with a thrilling win over Ireland and though the campaign ended with a narrow defeat in France, the performance suggested England were rounding the bend.

Two more narrow defeats in New Zealand were greeted with optimism, but then came the departures of Aled Walters and Felix Jones, key members of the backroom staff. Beginning the 2024 autumn with three defeats, each more demoralising than the next, turned the pressure dial up, but Borthwick survived his first crisis, helped because the RFU chief executive, Bill Sweeney, was busy trying, and failing, to quell a revolt over his seven-figure salary and bonus.

The 2025 Six Nations began with another narrow defeat, but England broke the dam at home to France and proceeded to embark on a 12-match winning run. It is the most prosperous period of Borthwick’s tenure and included a stunning 68-14 win in Wales and an autumn clean sweep.

Sign up to The Breakdown

The latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewed

after newsletter promotion

Pull back the curtain, however, and fundamental to England’s winning streak was that they had stolen a march on their rivals in adapting to law tweaks around the aerial contest. When the rest caught up, England could not cope, lost four straight Six Nations matches and Borthwick was suddenly clinging on again.

A heavy defeat by South Africa this summer before wins over Fiji and Argentina have done little to move the needle. Hitting out at the “negativity committee” when asked about England’s indiscipline suggests Borthwick is still feeling the heat.

When it comes to coaching, he clearly knows his onions. Well-placed sources often describe him as a “world-class forwards coach”, which is a compliment, but again infers he is not quite up to the top job. Listen to the players wax lyrical about his methods, witness the fight that they demonstrated in patches against the Springboks and they have not all given up on him yet, however.

It is said there is a generational divide in the camp and a split of opinions along those lines about how best to play. Perhaps that explains the crossed words between Itoje and Fin Smith during the loss to Italy in March. But there is no mutiny yet and George was unequivocal after this year’s Six Nations: “Steve is one of the best coaches I’ve ever worked under. Under Steve I think we will be right up there with the favourites to win the World Cup in 2027.”

It is said he treats his players like princes, but is considerably more strict with his staff. A close look at his staff certainly says a lot about Borthwick and his tenure. The most pivotal moment of this World Cup cycle could be the departures of Walters and Felix Jones in the summer of 2024.

Walters’ reasons for heading to Ireland are easier to understand. His wife is Irish and he had strong ties from his time with Munster. Those of Jones are far more opaque, but clearly Walters’ decision to leave influenced his own, so, too, a difference of opinion with Borthwick in New Zealand. That Jones was forced to work out his notice by the RFU underscored what an odd situation it was.

Equally strange is that Borthwick has steadfastly appointed assistants of a certain type. Nick Evans, Byron McGuigan, Tom Harrison, Lee Blackett, Kevin Sinfield and Joe El-Abd had no experience of international coaching. All of which adds fuel to the argument that when it comes to coaching Borthwick struggles to relinquish control.

At other times, however, he has impressed with a willingness to delegate. Walters was a clever appointment because he is a vibes man, which Borthwick clearly isn’t. George was a clever choice of captain because he can connect with supporters in a way Borthwick can’t. Sinfield serves as a pastoral figure to the squad in ways Borthwick does not. The problem is, when these people either move, or are moved on, from their roles, they leave a void.

The contradictions continue to mount as we enter World Cup year – even the performance in their last outing, against Argentina, was Jekyll and Hyde. Sensational for 40 minutes, substandard thereafter and it all leaves you with the feeling that England’s identity is not as clear as it should be this close to a World Cup.

That first half against Argentina, the sense of liberation in defeat in Paris – admittedly when they had little to lose – must be the blueprint if Borthwick is to win over the public in the next 12 months. “If we have a pretty ropey autumn, on the back of building some momentum over the summer, I think we will need to have a pretty hard look at ourselves,” said the fly-half Smith recently.

O’Shea has said it is “not even remotely” a possibility that Borthwick is sacked before next year’s World Cup, but he underestimates the power of the fanbase, whose disapproval did for Eddie Jones. Whether Sweeney has the appetite for change so close to another World Cup is another question.

It would be misguided to believe Borthwick’s contract extension through to the following Six Nations has raised the temperature any higher. It merely buys the union time when deciding whether or not to sack Borthwick and who to replace him with.

Make no mistake, his tenure hinges on the World Cup in Australia, assuming he makes it that far.

Key disability benefit for young people may be axed under major welfare changes

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 18:43:00 GMT

Exclusive: Plan under discussion involves intensive support to help young people into employment

Ministers are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping a key disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work, the Guardian has learned.

Whitehall sources said the package of changes under debate was much bigger than previously thought, as Andy Burnham’s government hopes to persuade more people on benefits back into work.

The move could be fraught with political danger after last year’s dramatic welfare rebellion by Labour MPs. But ministers have spent weeks trying to persuade them the plans are about reform, and feel confident opposition has waned.

The plans are still awaiting the conclusions of reviews by Alan Milburn, who is looking at young people’s employment, and the Timms panel, which is examining the personal independence payment (Pip), a non-means-tested benefit that helps sick and disabled people with support costs.

However, a central option under consideration for young people is removing the health element of universal credit for claimants under 25, which has already been almost halved to £217 a month, and offering intensive support for people to get into work. The possibility of removing it for existing claimants – not just new ones – is being looked at.

The extra support will include subsidised jobs for younger people, more targeted “back to work” schemes and support with mental health, as part of a drive to help more of the nation’s one million 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neets) back into the workplace.

As part of the same package, officials are looking at a new system to replace the Pip, which is claimed by four million people, after attempts to change existing eligibility criteria were rejected by MPs last year.

One possible plan is for a separate regime to apply to the under-25 agegroup, with reduced or withdrawn entitlements – although those with the most severe and debilitating disabilities would not lose any money.

More broadly, officials are working up plans under the replacement system for a new set of eligibility criteria and assessments for the extra costs of disability, and looking at whether this would apply to all claimants of working age, or those below a cut-off point such as 50 or 60. Again, those with the most severe conditions would not lose money or be reassessed.

Officials have also been returning to the idea of cuts to the Motability scheme at a future budget, after axing tax breaks worth £300m. The scheme allows disabled people to use their Pip benefit to lease new cars for three years.

One Whitehall source said removing or further cutting the health element of universal credit for those older than 25 had been considered, but government sources said this was not on the table.

Officials have looked at systems in other countries, such as Denmark, which restricts access to its “disability pension” for under-40s, who instead are given help with flexible jobs and training unless they have no ability permanently to work.

A government source said: “We will be bringing forward a comprehensive package of support and reform to tackle the scandal of a million young people not in education, employment or training. The details are yet to be decided, but we are committed to enabling work and opportunity, while always protecting those unable to work.”

The significant changes would need legislation, with ministers and officials looking at a bill encompassing the replacement for Pip and changes to the under-25 system to be presented in the next session of parliament next year.

Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, used his conference speech this week to describe changing the welfare system as a “moral crusade”, saying too many younger people were stuck claiming benefits for too long.

However, the scale of the plans could reignite concerns among Labour MPs about the impact on the cost of living for disabled people, particularly when Pip is a non-means-tested benefit that is unrelated to a person’s employment status.

Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, has gone further by saying she would ban young people from signing straight on to the benefits system if her party won the next election, as part of a plan to cut £23bn from the welfare bill. Under-25s with less than six months of continuous employment would no longer be able to claim universal credit and would instead have to undergo intensive job coaching.

Reform UK plans to cut the overall welfare bill by £50bn, with Pip replaced by another cash benefit that would be restricted to only the “gravely ill and severely challenged”, while “lower level conditions” would get support overseen by local authorities.

after newsletter promotion

Polling suggests that while the public favours cutting the welfare bill overall, they believe that tackling the root causes of joblessness instead of cutting benefits is the best way to do it. Burnham has said he wanted to avoid “crude cuts”, and used his party conference speech to signal an overhaul of the welfare system to pay for an expansion of youth jobs and training support.

UK welfare spending has reached £333bn this year, with pensioners receiving roughly 55% of the budget, and young people including Neets – but not children – about 2.5%. Milburn said it was “shameful” the government spent 25 times as much on benefits for them than it did on supporting them into work.

More than 40 of the UK’s leading charities warned ministers earlier this year against imposing tougher benefit sanctions or cuts on disabled young people.

In their joint letter to Milburn and McFadden, they said cutting support or bringing in sanctions risked pushing thousands of vulnerable youngsters deeper into poverty and further away from employment.

The disability charity Scope has estimated about half of households with an under-22 receiving the universal credit health element are already in poverty, which it said could rise to more than nine in 10 if support was removed.

Campaigners warned that any move to cut benefits or increase conditionality rules was likely to drive many youngsters further away from the jobs market.

Lucy Schonegevel, the director of impact at Action for Children, said: “We are deeply concerned by reports that disability benefits for under-25s could be cut. If confirmed, that would be at odds with the prime minister’s recent warning against ‘crude cuts’ … Serious investment in high quality, tailored employment support is vital, but employment support alone cannot overcome a lack of jobs.”

A DWP spokesperson said: “The Milburn and Timms reviews, due in the autumn, will lay the foundation for sustainable reform, and we will not pre-empt their findings. “We are already changing the system through the youth guarantee, narrowing the gap between universal credit standard and health rates, restoring face-to-face assessments, and investing a record £3.5bn in employment support for disabled people and those with long-term conditions. We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work.”

Milburn has said that too few young people who moved on to disability benefits received help into work. Many became “trapped” on benefits, with evidence showing half were not in work 15 years later, an outcome he called a “catastrophic failure”.

He appeared to hint at the potential political risks of cuts to benefits at a Labour party conference fringe meeting on youth employment on Monday, saying “when it comes to benefit cuts it will be tricky” – but added that not acting would be financially unsustainable and worse for young people.

About 184,000 young people in the UK aged 16-24 receive the universal credit health element. The government has already cut this benefit, having previously announced a 50% reduction to £217 a month for most new claimants from next April.

Welcome to the new Reform roadshow. Same as the last but more desperate

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 18:42:56 GMT

Nige is not rattled that the UK likes its new PM. Or that Reform is second in the polls. Oh no. Because Nige believes in Nige

Nearly 10 years ago, Nigel Farage told LBC he would leave the country if Brexit were not a stunning success. For reasons that no one can quite fathom, he is still here. Could it be that he is a man who can’t be trusted to keep his word? Surely not.

Nige wants you to know he’s very much still around. He might have been a bit quiet over the past few weeks, as Reform had to deal with one or two unfortunate investigations into their funding, but now he’s very much back. And he’s definitely not rattled that Labour has a prime minister the country likes. Nor is he at all rattled that Reform has tumbled into second place in the polls. Oh, no. Because Nige believes in Nige. Now more than ever. The last creepy-crawly after the apocalypse. Lying on its back, gasping for air. But still breathing. The dream still alive.

Welcome to the new Reform roadshow. Much the same as the last Reform roadshow, only with added desperation. You can almost sense the jeopardy. A dream receding into the distance. Supporters clinging just that bit tighter to each other in the echo chamber. The cheers just a bit too forced. The performance ever more contrived. Just a rehash of all the old lines with a flashing light show thrown in. We are promised one a week from now until the next general election. It’s going to be a long three years. Even Nige might be sick of Nige by then.

For the first outing of The Rolling Grievance Tour, Reform had taken over a room at Doncaster racecourse. But we were made to wait for Nige. The Reform leader goes nowhere these days without a couple of charisma-free fluffers as his warm-up acts. Men whose sole job is to make Nige look good. Men who are guaranteed to have the audience begging to be let out within minutes. First up was Matt Goodwin, the candidate who failed to get elected in Gorton and Denton. Someone who everyone seems to dislike on sight. Because it saves time that way. His sole function appears to be to make Nige look a little less unpleasant.

Then we had Richard Tice. Dicky would travel the length of the country if he was told there was going to be an audience of two. He is the very definition of needy. He is also spectacularly dim in the way that only posh boys can be. On the self-awareness scale he drops below zero. He has no idea people are laughing at him, not with him.

His attempts to be down with the little people were met with collective despair. “My first job was digging trenches,” he said, desperate to ingratiate himself with an audience he openly despises. Mate, you became director of that multimillion-pound property empire because your grandfather owned it. In a fairer world, you would still be a complete nobody. At best, you would be a low-achieving middle manager somewhere. Instead, Dicky thinks he is eyeing up a cabinet post in the next government. “If I fail to deliver in 100 days, I will resign,” he promised. Why not just call it quits now?

Then a video of Nige saying he couldn’t be bought. Except he can. With a £70 cameo video or what looked like a £5m inducement from a Thai crypto-billionaire to lure him out of retirement. Then the man himself. Looking tired. Struggling to find his usual energy as he went through his familiar numbers. All this hate must be exhausting. But it was worth it, when he was a novelty. No one asked too many questions. He could pretend to be an insurgent. The anti-establishment choice. Except he will never be anything but the establishment.

He began by insulting his audience. First by claiming the St Leger was the first classic of the season when it is the last – if you’re going to try to ingratiate yourself, you should at least get some basic facts right – then by rubbishing Doncaster itself. It was a shithole. He couldn’t imagine why anyone still lived there. If what the residents did could actually be called living. Still, he was doing them a favour by granting them an hour in his presence. So they did have that.

“Ed Miliband is never seen in Doncaster,” he declared. Yup. And you’re never seen in Clacton. So that evens things up. At least he’s in the cabinet. Time to talk about foreigners coming over in small boats. They were all a security risk. As the incident at Fairford proved (not). I’m sure the police will be thrilled to have Nige commenting on a live investigation. He had earlier even suggested that the men had deliberately got themselves arrested so they could time the police response. Even Matt the Twat isn’t that half-witted.

On and on Nige went. Same old lines. Same old grievances. Nothing positive to say other than that he would miraculously cure the entire country in 100 days. A task that may take other politicians decades. It goes without saying he didn’t say how. Just believe. A man of his brilliance can do anything. Moral decline, he said sadly. We are a Judeo-Christian country. Foreigners had been put on warning. Yawn.

Inevitably, we got to Andy Burnham’s promise to reset the country’s relationship with the EU. Nige was certain it would be a disaster. Because Brexit had been a tremendous success and Burnham was seeking division. The irony meter had ramped up several notches. No one does division quite like Nige. It’s his USP. Though weirdly he has achieved some consensus. Thanks to him, most of the country now thinks Brexit was an idiotic idea. Quite the achievement. He also went on to accuse Andy of smashing the pensioners by removing the triple lock. He may want to tell Thick Dick that. Dicky is on record as saying the triple lock had to go.

“I am different,” he said in conclusion. He wasn’t in politics for rank or status. He had enough money to do what he liked. He was getting on a bit. In fact, he wasn’t sure why he was doing this. Other than the fact he is a raging narcissist who craves constant attention and affirmation. As if to prove the point he insisted that people kept begging him to save them. In his mind, he is the Messiah. The second coming. He didn’t want to change the electoral system, he wanted to abolish it. After him, there would be no need for elections. The thousand year Reich. Nirvana.

All he wanted was just a normal far-right country. A place where England was for the English. Once we had deported all foreign criminals there would be no need for prisons because white people would stop breaking the law. Foreigners were dragging us down. Spiritually, financially, morally. We had lost our way like lost sheep. All we had to do was believe in Nige. An act of faith. Only not even Nige believes in Nige any more.

Criminal or saviour? Rui Pinto abandoned by Portuguese authorities after Manchester City leaks

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 18:40:17 GMT

Man whose leaks of private documents prompted the investigation into City has been advised not to return home, contact family members or visit crowded places

More than a decade after Rui Pinto set up the Football Leaks website in a crusade triggered by the Fifa scandal in 2015, he finds himself in the middle of a growing storm. The former history student with trademark spiky hair who used to make extra cash selling books about the second world war has not held back with his statements on social media since Manchester City’s guilty verdict from an independent Premier League commission.

The first targets for Pinto, whose leaks of private documents prompted first Uefa then the Premier League to investigate City’s financial affairs, were what he alleged were the club’s “cheating” executives for demonstrating “a complete lack of respect for the rules”. On Wednesday he turned his attention to the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino.

Less than two hours later, Portuguese authorities confirmed Pinto would no longer be protected as a witness. That is understood to have come as a surprise to the 37-year-old, who finds himself without a job, a home or an income. He has been living in a safe house under protection and has never disclosed his location, and it is understood he has received no visitors.

The Guardian understands talks had been initiated to begin the process of reintegrating Pinto back into social and professional life. That initiative will be halted, leaving Pinto to fend for himself. He has been advised not to return home, contact family members or visit crowded places socially or for work.

Pinto has been a protected witness since 2020 after he agreed to grant Portuguese authorities access to millions of files acquired before his arrest in Budapest, where he moved after a year in the Hungarian capital as an Erasmus student. He has since become a cause célèbre who divides opinion in his homeland and been compared to Edward Snowden and Julian Assange.

The Premier League’s case against City drew heavily on evidence provided by Football Leaks, including the chief executive, Ferran Soriano, writing in an internal memo: “We will need to fight this and do it in a way that is not visible, or we will be pointed out as the global enemies of football.” City continue to protest their innocence and Soriano said this week the club would appeal on the basis that the commission’s verdict “contains clear, material errors of law, principle and fact and that it is unsafe”.

The question of whether the evidence should be used provoked huge public debate in Portugal, but the Premier League’s regulations stipulate that any investigation “shall not be bound by judicial rules governing the admissibility of evidence. Instead, facts relating to a breach of these rules may be established by any reliable means.”

That tallies with Pinto’s assertion in 2019 that it is “nonsense” to claim the data he provided is tainted because it was obtained illegally. “The documents are authentic,” he said. “That is what matters. This and the content. I don’t consider myself as a hacker, but as a citizen who acted in the public interest. My sole intention was to reveal illicit practices that affect the world of football.”

Pinto wore a bulletproof vest during his first trial in 2020 and came in through a dedicated entrance guarded by special forces. People attending the proceedings were searched three times and not allowed to bring mobile phones or computers into the courtroom. At the start of the trial, snipers were positioned on buildings near the courthouse.

He was given a suspended four-year sentence in September 2023 after being found guilty on counts of attempted extortion, illegal access to data and breach of correspondence. Pinto has always insisted he never received money but has admitted regret over asking Doyen Sports Investments for money after he obtained thousands of the agency’s internal emails.

He said to Der Spiegel in 2019: “I told myself: ‘If I allow them to buy me out now, I am no better than this whole business.’ So, I wrote to Doyen and told them to keep their money. Not a single cent was paid. What I did was very naive. Looking back now, I regret it. But I repeat that I deny having committed any criminal offence.”

That defence was found to be “not credible” by the judge, who said Pinto and his co-defendant, the lawyer Aníbal Pinto, were “well aware of the illegality of their conduct”. Rui Pinto started living in a safe house after being sentenced. He lost his mother to cancer when he was 11 and is permitted to communicate with his father occasionally. Even when he was in a relationship with the actor Mikaela Lupu, who he said he had met over “a glass of wine and a book” when announcing they had split last year, the security of the property was never compromised.

For six years, Pinto has been seen in public only twice. On one of those occasions, at a supermarket in Lisbon, he was accompanied by police officers and wore a cap and sunglasses. On the other, he was assaulted in an altercation believed to have been sparked for football-related reasons. It is understood that Pinto was left with a bruised eyebrow and the police were informed, although no complaint was filed.

The decision to end his witness protection has raised concerns for his welfare. Pinto is understood to fear for his safety. A bounty was reportedly placed on his head after the revelations made by Football Leaks and Luanda Leaks, which exposed the inner workings of the business empire of Africa’s richest woman, Isabel dos Santos. She denied corruption allegations.

The Guardian attempted to obtain clarification from the commission for special security programmes (CPES), a Portuguese body under the ministry of justice responsible for managing special witness protection programmes, as to why Pinto is no longer a protected witness but received no response. There has been speculation it could be a response to Pinto being accused of hacking the computer systems of PLMJ, the Portuguese law firm founded by José Miguel Júdice.

Júdice testified against Pinto during the Football Leaks trial, describing the episode as a theft that had caused him significant moral and psychological distress. Júdice is the father of Rita Alarcão Júdice, Portugal’s minister of justice since June 2025.

In April, Pinto was acquitted in a second trial of 241 counts of illegally accessing email accounts belonging to several Portuguese sports bodies, including Benfica, and to law firms, magistrates and the tax authority. None of the evidence he provided to the Portuguese authorities has resulted in any charges.

Brazil attorney general says meddling ‘cannot be tolerated’ after Trump funding plans revealed

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 18:34:10 GMT

Jorge Messias calls Guardian report ‘an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty’ as nation prepares to go to polls

Brazil’s attorney general has said foreign meddling in his country’s institutions and democracy “cannot be tolerated” after a Guardian report revealed how the Trump administration was pushing to direct funds to a campaign against the Brazilian supreme court.

Writing on X, Jorge Messias called the report “an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty”. “The information is especially serious in light of Brazil’s electoral process and the recent episodes of external pressure on our institutions,” Messias added.

Brazil is three days away from its presidential election – the outcome of which Washington has been accused of trying to influence – where the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, will face off against his far-right rival, the Trump ally Flávio Bolsonaro. The pair are neck and neck in the polls.

According to the Brazilian television network GloboNews, the attorney general’s office on Thursday filed a criminal complaint to investigate potential wrongdoing, in response to the Guardian story.

Last year, the Trump administration used a campaign of sanctions and tariffs in a failed attempt to pressure Lula’s government and the supreme court over the coup trial of Bolsonaro’s father, the ex-president Jair Bolsonaro. Trump called Bolsonaro’s prosecution a “witch-hunt”, but he was convicted and handed a 27-year sentence for trying to seize power after losing the 2022 election to Lula.

In recent months, the Trump administration has again been accused of meddling in Brazilian affairs by using tariffs and the designation of two Brazilian organised crime groups as foreign terrorist organisations to boost Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign and weaken Lula.

Writing on Thursday, Messias said: “Disagreements between governments are inherent to international relations. What cannot be tolerated is for foreign political interests to seek to interfere in the functioning of Brazilian institutions or to influence, directly or indirectly, choices that belong exclusively to the Brazilian people.”

Messias added: “It is the right of each generation of Brazilians to freely decide their destiny, protect their institutions, and hand over to their children a country that does not accept decisions about Brazil being made outside of Brazil. Our democracy belongs to Brazilians. And so it must remain.”

The attorney general’s comments came in response to a report that the Trump administration was pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa and the campaign against Brazil’s supreme court.

A $1m award titled “Countering lawfare and censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court.

Bolsonaro’s far-right movement considers the supreme court – and in particular justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw Jair Bolsonaro’s trial – its greatest foe.

Moraes is widely seen to have played a key role in thwarting Jair Bolsonaro’s authoritarian plot, which culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília, despite concerns about the judge overstepping his constitutional authority in his crusade to protect democracy.

During the rightwing riots, hardcore Bolsonaro supporters trashed the presidential palace, congress and supreme court. The court sustained the most severe damage.

Bolsonaro supporters continue to claim their leader’s imprisonment is unjust and that he is the victim of a politically motivated sham driven by a corrupt “judicial dictatorship”.

Their criticism of Moraes and the supreme court has been bolstered by a recent scandal linking several judges, including him, to Daniel Vorcaro, the playboy banker at the centre of Brazil’s biggest banking scandal. Vorcaro has also been linked to the Bolsonaro family.

The banker reportedly gave the family more than £9m, supposedly to produce a biopic about Jair Bolsonaro starring Jim Caviezel, who played Jesus in Mel Gibson’s film The Passion of the Christ. The Guardian view on Grenfell prosecutions: at last, survivors have a date

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 18:16:07 GMT

Prosecutors will decide who to charge within eight months. But ministers should also re-examine the law

Police have at last asked prosecutors to consider charges relating to the Grenfell Tower fire in 2017. The suffering of those who survived or were bereaved by the blaze, which killed 72 people, has been exacerbated by the extraordinary length of time that the investigation has taken. But they can now look forward to a decision about who will face criminal charges. The Crown Prosecution Service has promised that this will be before the 10th anniversary next June.

The names of the 20 organisations and 54 individuals in the police files will not be released by prosecutors unless they are charged. But the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and Kensington and Chelsea council have both announced that they are on the list. Angela Rayner promised on Wednesday that the government would cooperate fully whatever decision is reached regarding a potential breach of the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. Kensington and Chelsea council revealed that a charge of corporate manslaughter against it is being considered alongside health and safety and fire regulation breaches.

The police’s decision to let the public inquiry run before concluding their own investigation has been criticised. Some of the bereaved and survivors would have preferred criminal justice to take precedent. But the thoroughness of the inquiry at least means that well-evidenced findings of wrongdoing have already been made. Arconic, Kingspan and Celotex – three suppliers of materials involved in the tower’s refurbishment – were judged to have behaved dishonestly, although this does not mean that the inquiry’s findings were made to a criminal “burden of proof” level. An architecture practice, Studio E, and two building contractors, Rydon and Harley Facades, were each said to bear responsibility for the fire.

Arconic was also criticised for its disgraceful refusal to send witnesses to the inquiry. The Metropolitan police have warned that trials are unlikely to take place before 2028, meaning that an end to this painful process remains years away. Corporate manslaughter cases are widely recognised as being very difficult due to the need to prove gross negligence with management playing a substantial role. The government and the judiciary must do all they can to expedite the next stages.

Beyond any trials, the Hillsborough law will at long last create an obligation on public officials to be truthful. There are other steps that ministers should take, regardless of what happens in court. Survivors are right to object to the public contracts awarded to Rydon and Saint-Gobain (owner of Celotex), given the inquiry’s findings about their conduct. The explanations given so far as to why the Procurement Act 2023 cannot be used to bar them on grounds of poor past performance are not good enough.

The government should also consider changing the law to enable punitive damages to be awarded against companies that harm people. Proposals for a new, independent body to monitor the implementation of recommendations from public inquiries and inquests also deserve serious consideration. The current position, in which multiple independent reviews have been accepted but not implemented, is harmful to those affected by tragedies such as Grenfell. It also undermines public trust in the system’s capacity to put things right.

The Guardian view on the death penalty: Christa Pike’s execution was botched, but cruelty is inherent

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 18:14:43 GMT

Three-quarters of nations have rightly abolished capital punishment in law or practice, but killing by the state has surged in the US

What is the kindest way to kill? That’s the question being asked once more following Tennessee’s failed attempts to execute Christa Pike for the brutal murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, when she was 18. The 50-year-old was taken to a medical facility, her condition unknown, with witnesses describing her snoring loudly around 40 minutes after receiving two injections of pentobarbital on Wednesday. It is the second botched killing in months, prompting Tennessee’s governor to order a halt to executions.

Lethal injection was supposed to be the humane alternative to firing squads and electric chairs. They in turn were seen as an improvement on hanging, which looked much like lynching in a system disproportionately handing the death penalty to black men. The age and ill health of those executed, and the ethical refusal of most medical staff to be involved, may contribute to botched injections. But analysis of autopsy results has provided compelling evidence that suffering is inherent; injections – especially those involving paralytic drugs – have merely disguised it. What is described as safeguarding the dignity of prisoners is really about reducing the discomfort of witnesses who would otherwise see their suffering.

Pressure from campaigners on pharmaceutical companies has curbed the supply of lethal drugs, but it has not stopped executions. Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for the death penalty has spurred on state officials, with the highest number of executions for 16 years in 2025. Some states have found alternative drugs, which may increase the suffering of those killed. Others are using different techniques. In June, the supreme court stopped Alabama from executing a prisoner with nitrogen gas, which it has used in other cases. The use of firing squads has resurged. Experts say such deaths can be “excruciating”, especially where marksmen miss the heart of the condemned, with allegations that some executions could even have been deliberately botched.

The US is in a shameful minority. Three-quarters of countries have got rid of capital punishment in law or practice – with Lebanon this year becoming the first Middle Eastern country to abolish it.

Only 17 countries executed prisoners last year, though the total number killed rose to more than 2,700 – the highest since 1984. (The figures do not include China, believed to carry out the most executions.) But while Mr Trump and others champion capital punishment, the American public are turning away from it. In 1994, 80% supported it; by last year that had fallen to 52%. A majority of younger people oppose it.

High-profile miscarriages of justice have contributed to growing disquiet. So have cases such as Pike’s. She endured sexual abuse and rape by three perpetrators in childhood, as well as beatings and neglect – yet her experiences and age were not adequately put forward by lawyers at her trial. Her bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder were diagnosed only afterwards. Sandra Babcock, an expert on the death penalty who has acted on Pike’s behalf, argued that her execution would confirm that it was reserved “not for the worst of the worst, but for the most damaged and vulnerable among us”.

The ultimate problem, however, is not that the wrong people are being executed, but that anyone is being executed. The search for a humane way to kill is inherently preposterous. It is not just lethal injection, the firing squad or electrocution that should be rejected – but the death penalty itself.

The spousal humanising of a party leader is a well-worn political tool, but van Heel is likely to be a very different prime ministerial partner. The former senior marketing executive is poised to play a more significant role in promoting Britain than any other spouse in the last two decades, stepping up her political engagements after stepping back from her own corporate career.

Van heel has chosen a political adviser to help her navigate the role at home and promote the UK’s interests overseas, the Guardian understands.

She has shifted her role at Be. EV, an electric vehicle-charging network based in Manchester, quitting her job as chief customer officer to give her schedule more flexibility, while remaining on the company’s board.

While it is standard for the partners of prime ministers to have taxpayer-funded office support, van Heel has taken on a former special adviser to a cabinet member and is expected to play a more significant role behind the scenes than the previous prime minister Keir Starmer’s wife, Victoria, who continued her work in occupational health for the NHS throughout her husband’s tenure.

Last week, she travelled with Burnham to the UN general assembly in New York, attending a lunch hosted by the US first lady, Melania Trump, as well as holding meetings with Ukraine’s first lady, Olena Zelenska, and the Canadian prime minister’s wife, Diana Fox Carney. One gushing corporate communicator later wrote that she had spent half an hour making apprentices “feel like the most important people in the room”, adding that she was “a total class act”.

Van heel and her team are now speaking to charities and leaders and weighing up how to make best use of her “impressive” personality and professional experience to champion causes. They will be lucky to have her, said Rose Caldwell, the chief executive of Plan International UK, where van Heel was a trustee until July. “She brought valuable insight and unwavering commitment to the role,” she said. “She really made a lasting contribution to our mission of advancing equality for girls.”

Born in Roslyn, Pennsylvania, to Dutch parents, van Heel grew up in the Netherlands and Belgium and met Burnham on her first day as a student at the University of Cambridge. In a campaign video for his mayoral campaign, she asked the future PM if he remembered his response to her question about what he wanted to do with his life. “You said you wanted to be an MP,” she said. “Yeah. And I left the room at that point.”

After almost a decade in Manchester, van Heel is something of an unknown quantity in Westminster, but insiders say she has already impressed staff behind the scenes. “She’s incredibly cool,” said one source. “She’s very nice, very smart … she just gets it.”

The clearest picture of the prime minister’s partner has come from Burnham himself. Speaking to Elizabeth Day for the How to Fail podcast, he said that his wife of 26 years was “forthright” when she thought he had got something wrong. “She’s Dutch, and they don’t hold back,” he said. “They’re pretty plain speaking, and yeah, I’ve been on the receiving end of a lot of that over the years.”

Burnham has recalled finishing an interview when he was an MP and seeing a text from his wife exhorting him to “ANSWER THE F***ING QUESTION”. When he told van Heel he was planning to run to be Labour leader earlier this year, after failed bids in 2010 and 2015, she did not hold back. “She was like, ‘Oh, not again! They’ve told you twice. They don’t want you. Why again?’” Burnham said. “She took some persuading, to be honest, because I guess she didn’t want to see me go through it all again […] But she gives me good advice.”

But there are earlier hints, too. Much has been written of van Heel’s appearance on the Cilla Black TV show Blind Date in 1992, when she punctured the private school hubris of “Will from Surrey” – otherwise known as Will Harris, who later became the marketing director for the Conservative party.

But a full viewing of the video – in which van Heel flicks Harris’s wandering hand off her knee, before smacking her unfortunate date with a cushion when he calls her a “fridge” – gives a sense of her blunt confidence and quick wit. When Harris says his “interests were honourable”, she retorts: “I didn’t have any interest at all.”

Officially, Downing Street will say only that van Heel, who has three adult children with Burnham, is supporting her husband and “advancing UK interests” as spouses have done before.

Where van Heel’s energy will be directed now that her husband has reached No 10 is still being mapped out, but it is likely that she will be the most active – and potentially influential – prime minister’s wife since Sarah Brown at the start of the century. Brown’s diaries from Downing Street note there is “no formal spouse job to step into […] no permanent office, no salary, no allowance, no pre-set duties or official role, not even an official title” for the prime minister’s wife. It is a job that van Heel did not ask for, and may not even want – but it looks likely she will make it her own.

The global bond sell-off intensified on Thursday, driving 10-year US government borrowing costs to their highest level in 24 years in a frantic day’s trading.

The threat of a renewed round of inflation from the persistently high cost of oil has spooked investors on both sides of the Atlantic, with central banks expected to raise interest rates in the coming months to prevent price increases from becoming embedded.

The sell-off drove the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year US Treasuries to 5.34% – the highest level since 2002.

In the UK, where surging borrowing costs are increasing the pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget later this month, the yield on 30-year bonds hit 6% for the first time since 1998, before easing slightly later in the day. Yields on five- and 10-year UK bonds were also up.

Stock market investors sold heavily too, knocking almost 1.7% off the FTSE 100 in London – its worst daily fall since May. Bourses in other parts of Europe were also hit, with Germany’s DAX falling 1% and France’s CAC 40 losing 1.6%.

“There is carnage in the bond market, which is hitting stocks hard,” said Neil Wilson, the investor strategist at Saxo UK. “It looks like the relentless rout in the bond market is sending investors running for cover.”

The bond sell-off around the world is being driven by fears of high inflation, as the Middle East conflict continues to restrict oil supplies from the region.

Japan’s 10-year yield rose towards the 30-year high set last month.

US bonds weakened despite inflation data on Wednesday coming in lower than forecast, which was expected to calm investors’ nerves about the prospect of further increases in the cost of borrowing by the US Federal Reserve.

Traders remain anxious that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates to fight inflation, mainly in response to the strength of the US economy and the prospect of workers bidding up their wages.

Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said there was growing concern at the amount of debt being issued to fund government deficits, as well as inflation concerns.

“Inflation, deficit and issuance concerns continue to weigh on the bond market,” he said.

“There is also a buyers’ strike as investors do not want to step in till we get some form of stability. Hedge funds have suffered in the latest round of sell-off and do not have the risk appetite to fade the move. Real money potentially has the risk appetite, but won’t step in till we get some stability.”

Flipping public opinion on the triple lock was Burnham magic – he’ll need more of it to see his social care plans through

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 17:29:14 GMT

Rebuilding a complex and broken system into one that’s fair for all, and in the face of steely opposition: that will be the PM’s real challenge

Here is rare clearcut proof of the power of political persuasion. Party conference speeches, the lifeblood of political obsessives, rarely reach the public beyond a brief news clip. But this time was different. Andy Burnham’s speech spun the dial on public opinion on several political hot potatoes, defining who he is.

The pensions triple lock, which guarantees that pensions rise faster than average incomes, has been a no-go electoral minefield despite a groundswell of economists (and even a Times leader) calling for reform to prevent pensions skyrocketing. Touching this live rail was an act of bravery – or recklessness.

Polls over the years strongly supported the lock: a Persuasion UK poll this week found 65% in favour of keeping it, more among over-65s. A Times YouGov poll this month went as high as 93% of pension-age people defending it. So the sudden change in public opinion after the speech has been astonishing. YouGov now reports that 48% support the Burnham plan, with just 28% against. Survation finds 64% backing it with only 15% against. The magic was linking reform of the lock with creating a national care service. Never mind that it barely begins to cover the cost, it makes an emotional link between the two policies.

I can’t think of any other conference speech that reversed public opinion on such a sensitive policy. Kemi Badenoch’s Tories protested that it was just “robbing Peter to pay Paul”, while Nigel Farage’s party vowed, “Reform UK will always protect our pensioners and maintain the triple lock.” Both are out of touch with the public (at least, for now).

But this is only week one on a long and winding journey to 2030, when plans for the triple lock and a national care service have appeared in the next Labour manifesto – and fickle voters have reelected a Labour government. When the world so often turns upside down in the blink of an eye (Burnham keeps reminding himself he is the seventh PM in a decade), 2030 can feel light years away.

We don’t yet know what a national care service is. But the most moving and easiest to implement promise in Burnham’s speech is to improve the lives and status of care workers like those he watched looking after his father: “Caring for other people’s parents on poverty pay, but doing it with huge skill, humour and humanity.” He pledged, “I promise you, I won’t leave this job without doing everything I can to change things for you.” Starmer’s fair-pay agreement for care workers is already on its way, to be agreed between trade unions and employers. Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, this week announced the first national pension scheme for care workers. Next, they need training, pay and career ladders the same as NHS healthcare assistants, merging the two together.

But the rest of Burnham’s “landmark policy as significant as the creation of the NHS itself” looks perplexingly difficult. He promised “care that is about people, not profit”, but Margaret Thatcher privatised care, breaking it into fragments by denying central funds to any council keeping its own service. There are now about 19,000 organisations providing adult care in England, some big, most small, some good, some pretty terrible, some voluntary, many understaffed. In theory, they are inspected by the regulator, but the Care Quality Commission, knowing the shortage of beds and services, sets a low bar in standards. Could that be in-sourced?

But here’s the biggest conundrum of all. Who pays for social care goes right to the heart of social justice and fair taxation. Currently, most people in England already have their care paid for by the state, because they have less than £23,250 in savings and no property that is not lived in by a partner. But 23% of people in England who get at-home care and 37% of those in residential care are self-funders. Between them, they pay £14bn a year. Burnham seemed to imply they would be relieved of that burden, NHS style – but if so, that would be a whopping £14bn given to better-off elderly people, paid for by taxpayers. That’s unthinkably expensive and unfair to younger working people, a generation with less income and less property. So it won’t and shouldn’t happen.

Instead, as hastily explained afterwards, self-payers will only get their care paid for, but they will still pay for their bed and board in care homes – as in Scotland, where standard weekly costs of about £1,000 are mitigated by the state contributing £260 for care. Burnham said that people should no longer lose their homes to pay care costs; they still do in Scotland.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

And rightly. Only 21% of people think the state should pay for it all, regardless of the recipient’s wealth, according to a King’s Fund survey. Keeping an empty home to pass on as inheritance is not something the state should subsidise, when every spare penny is needed to pay for better social care. More than 400,000 are on official care waiting lists in England, while Age UK says 2 million older people have unmet care needs, putting a huge burden on families. Burnham himself talked of the miserably inadequate 15-minute homecare visits. Meanwhile, the NHS desperately needs a better care service to save the 13,000 beds a day filled with those waiting for a care package.

At any one time, few people use social care, so few understand the system, according to the King’s Fund. Simon Bottery, who leads its work on adult social care, says, “Frailty and dementia in later life are issues that most people just don’t want to think about until they really need to.” But it’s about to become a hot political battleground, with its fiendish complexities and its difficult moral and political choices.

When problems look insoluble, the last five prime ministers have summoned the great troubleshooter Louise Casey. She reports next year on what should be done. With the political right preparing for war, her job is to find answers acceptable enough to most. But that’s unlikely to include a carbon copy of the free NHS, nor should that be on the table.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

“Some of the allegations circulating about Mr Mickelson are false, and others revisit mistakes he has already acknowledged, publicly or privately,” a spokesperson for Mickelson told People magazine in June, in response to an article on golf website Skratch about alleged misconduct.

“Recovery is not a straight line. Throughout their 35-year relationship, his wife, Amy Mickelson, has supported Mr Mickelson and their family with extraordinary grace, unwavering love, and the belief that people are measured not only by their failures, but by what they do to make them right. Mr Mickelson’s priority is to become the husband, father, and man his family deserves. Right now, that means giving his full attention to a private family health matter. He understands that parts of his life are public, but his family’s private matters are not,” the statement concluded.

Mickelson has played just one tournament with LIV Golf this season, in South Africa in March. When he withdrew from the Masters in April, he said he would be out for an “extended period of time”, and he later pulled out of May’s PGA Championship. His plans to return to the sport are unclear, given the uncertainty around the future of the Saudi-backed LIV circuit.

He spoke publicly of his struggles with gambling addiction in 2023 after renowned gambler Billy Walters claimed in his book that Mickelson had wagered more than $1bn over three decades. He said he was “in recovery” after betting had alienated him from loved ones.

“After many years of receiving professional help, not gambling, and being in recovery from my addictions, I’m now able to sit still, be present in the moment and live each day with an inner calm and peace,” Mickelson wrote on social media in September 2023. “I still have a lot of cleaning up to do with those I love the most but I’m doing it slowly and as best I can.”

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 17:02:01 GMT

Counter-terrorism police arrest 25-year-old in Westminster and search two properties in central London

Detectives have arrested a dual UK-Iranian national on suspicion of terrorism offences as part of an investigation into a suspected plot near RAF Fairford.

Counter-terrorism police said the 25-year-old man was arrested on Thursday in Westminster on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts under section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006.

Five men in their 20s were arrested in the village of Whelford, Gloucestershire, outside the RAF base in the early hours of Sunday after police were alerted to suspicious vans in the area. They were released on police bail.

Announcing the most recent arrest, Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism police, said: “As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.”

Counter-terrorism police said two properties had been searched in Westminster, London.

Evans added: “The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of inquiry.”

An Iranian link to the events in the Gloucestershire countryside over the weekend is considered increasingly likely, as the police and security services’ investigation continues. Senior US politicians, including the president, Donald Trump, have expressed surprise that the suspects were released on bail.

It was revealed on Sunday that a farmer driving home from a party at about 1am on Sunday had spotted the men and vans and called 999.

But on Tuesday it emerged that one of the five men arrested near the base called the police to report the incident.

The mounting view among investigators that Iran was likely involved was a key reason for Andy Burnham’s decision to call a meeting of Cobra, the government’s crisis committee, on Monday, which was attended by senior police and security officials.

Tensions have been high at RAF Fairford since Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in July that the base was a legitimate target. Iran’s embassy in London has denied any involvement in the events of the past few days.

Ministers have been briefed that Iran has various reasons for hiring proxies, who sometimes are unwitting, to carry out acts that aim to eat up resources and create chaos.

The suspects were first arrested on explosives charges and then later for preparing acts of terrorism. The decision on Monday to bail the men came after an examination of what was found in the vans, and searches of addresses linked to them across London, all of which found no evidence of a viable device.

Counter-terrorism police are leading the investigation, which is trying to establish why the five men, all British nationals from London, were in the Gloucestershire countryside, close to a sensitive site in the middle of the night.

The vans were marked with the logo of a legitimate fuel transit company that later denied ownership of the vehicles.

People detained for terrorism offences can be detained under two legal schedules that dictate how long they can be held without charge.

Under the terrorism schedule, a suspect can be held for up to 14 days but cannot be bailed.

The 25-year-old man arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts is being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (Pace), a spokesperson for CTP said.

That means he could be released on bail under investigation, but detectives have much less time to hold him.

The five men arrested early on Sunday in the Gloucestershire countryside were held under Pace before being bailed the next day.

The Iranian embassy in London has said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” of Iranian involvement.

Eighty-five households were forced to decamp to a leisure centre on Sunday as the bomb squad and counter-terror police descended on Whelford.

Some of the evacuated residents were able to stay with families, about 60 people received support from a Cotswold district council rest centre in Cirencester, and 28 people were accommodated overnight in hotels.

You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceit

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:51:21 GMT

No spoilers here – TV’s grand illusionist meets his match when he moves in with Theranos founder and her family

For anyone remotely near the worlds of documentary, comedy or medical fraud, there has been one thing on the mind for weeks now: a single-minute clip of Nathan Fielder, the absurdist comedian whose boundary-pushing HBO series The Rehearsal cemented his status as docu-reality’s premier auteur, staring into the deep blue eyes of Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of the blood-testing startup Theranos. Unblinking, faces inches apart, the famously dry purveyor of harebrained business schemes and the convicted fraudster appeared locked in a battle of wills. “Are you being real right now?” Fielder asked her, in a classically meta bit – could Fielder really have spent years filming a secret documentary with one of Silicon Valley’s most notorious pariahs?

The prospect of TV’s grand illusionist versus emblematic girl-boss scammer seemed potentially too good to be true; buzz for You Can See Everything, Fielder’s furtive documentary co-directed with wunderkind du jour Lance Oppenheim (whose narrative feature debut, the Robert Pattinson-starring Primetime, premiered last month) was such that access to the film’s New York film festival premiere on Wednesday became this fall’s hottest ticket.

Those who were there can confirm: the hype is deserved. You Can See Everything is, somehow, more shocking, twistier, thornier and revealing than billed – a stupefying and gloriously destabilizing hall of psychological mirrors, a thrilling once-in-a-lifetime collision of director and subject. You know from the minute Billy Evans, Holmes’s shifty husband-cum-business partner who entered the picture post-Theranos, claims that “the best way for people to see who she is … is to give as much access as possible into our daily lives”, while lying with Holmes on a playroom floor, that you’re in for a wild ride. My mouth was agape for, conservatively, one half of the film’s unusually deserved three-hour run time.

Let me say now, if you’ve made it this far: I will not spoil major shifts – and if you are at all familiar with the Fielder canon, you know they’re coming – for a singular movie whose enjoyment depends, in part, on an element of surprise, both for viewers and for film-makers who genuinely seem to not know what they signed up for when they walked into the Holmes-Evans household rental in 2023. Arguably the less you know about anything that is to come, the better.

What I can tell you is that You Can See Everything is a masterpiece of who’s playing who, the fragility and absurdities of trust, seemingly begotten by chance. Back in 2023, convicted of wire fraud and conspiracy and awaiting the start of her 11-year sentence in prison, Holmes, along with Evans – who appears to be her match made in heaven, as neither ever blink and are maybe always lying – sought out a film crew to document their life with their two young children, in an attempt to protest her innocence and, perhaps, rebrand for Theranos 2.0. For some reason, they chose Oppenheim, a documentarian whose distinctive style – hyper-saturation, tight frames, creeping zooms – exposes the eerie in the mundane, and Fielder, whose precise style of spectrum-y, extreme cringe means that no question will be off the table. As Fielder points out on camera, in one of several exquisitely blunt confrontations, it is an odd choice to allow a comedian famous for his business scams to make a documentary that will supposedly clear your name of arguably the most famous fraud scandal of the 2010s.

The result is a three-hour documentary filmed like a thriller and scored like a drama that plays like an unraveling of certainty in real time. Oppenheim’s house style, shots tightly hugging then boring into a face with laser-like curiosity, perfectly suits the material; scenes that could be an unlikely tableau instead become a fascinating parade of inscrutable motivations, isolated actors bristling against the others. There is something extremely satisfying in watching Fielder’s sharp angles – arched eyebrows, needling questions, dispensation of social buffers – tangle with Holmes’s disposition (or performance? or genuine personality?) of guileless warmth, a strange and compelling chemistry building within a reality distortion field. If Fielder’s earlier work felt at times like it was punching down, trading on the naivety of regular people, well, he has finally met his match.

I am, admittedly, writing around a film that must be seen to be discussed, and will surely engender much chatter as to what, exactly, we just witnessed. But trust that things devolve in a very Fielderian spiral, into a dissection of the form unlike anything I have ever seen or, as things get going and participants’ either lose their filters or sharpen their game, anything I have ever hoped to see when it comes to the figure known as Elizabeth Holmes. Trust, too, that if there was a question you were hoping to ask Holmes or, moreover, her husband – did he really have no reservations when he met the disgraced founder at a party in 2017, at the height of her scandal? – it gets asked, and then some (I did not need to know about conjugal visits, or lack thereof, in the Texas prison where Holmes continues to reside).

Trust, ultimately, that you can see more than you ever imagined you’d see about Elizabeth Holmes and maybe get no closer to discerning the truth – and yet it will all be worth it.

You Can See Everything screened at the New York film festival and will be released in the US on 16 October with UK and Australian release dates to be announced

Smashing glass ceilings, Strictly and a courageous final sign-off: Esther Rantzen’s 10 best TV moments

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:49:07 GMT

Rantzen was one of the most powerful women in British television. From making vegetable innuendos to changing lives and bestowing her own medals on brilliant people – here are her finest small-screen moments

Dame Esther Rantzen obituary Esther Rantzen: one of the UK’s boldest, bravest ever campaigners – right to the very end

Esther Rantzen, who has died aged 86, revolutionised three areas of TV: consumer journalism, the visibility of presenters and viewer participation. Hers was a remarkable career full of landmarks – and here are some of the highlights.

This early customer advice programme, fronted by Canadian émigré Bernard Braden, created Rantzen’s TV persona: bashfully ambitious and passionately championing public causes but also, as a very rare frontline female presenter at the time, making some male colleagues resentful. She was hired as a researcher but had a sliding office doors moment after a decision was made to put the off-screen team in the studio to make the scams and complaints more dramatic. In an acknowledgment of her break, Rantzen made backroom staff a feature of the show that soon made her career.

When Braden returned to Canada, Rantzen, in her early 30s, took the helm of the BBC’s prime-time replacement. As de facto editor, she became one of the most powerful women on British television then or since. Braden’s Week had made shopper support into light entertainment and Rantzen, in a paradox that always confused her critics, made it both lighter – puns, poems, ditties, vegetable-based innuendo – and heavier: exposing institutional and domestic child abuse, campaigning successfully for rear seatbelts and safer playgrounds and, after taking on the case of one viewer’s child, improving the NHS organ transplant system. The lurches in tone – signalled by Rantzen smoothing her toothy grin into a grave face – were controversial but, with the show reaching more than 20 million viewers at its peak, among the thousands of lives changed by the programme was Rantzen’s own.

Rantzen has been given insufficient credit (or, for some, blame) as a pioneer of the now engulfing genre of reality TV. Her consumer work was viewer-driven – often incorporating high-street vox pops – and, in The Big Time, she enabled citizens to live out their dreams: a keen home cook cheffing at the Dorchester, a gymnast performing as a circus trapeze artist or, most prophetically, becoming a TV star for a day.

The queen of TV went on to set up her own honours system, bestowing medals on members of the public secretly commended for feats of kindness, courage and caring. The show’s prank and ambush element – recipients were lured to the presentation by a ruse and surprised by Rantzen and team, often in disguise – confirmed Rantzen’s theory that viewers preferred their TV with a cheesy garnish.

Claudia Winkleman’s recent doomed attempt at the format illustrated the extent to which the celebrity chatshow is a male-dominated field. Some early coverage had even suggested that Winkleman may be breaking the glass ceiling. Characteristically, though, Rantzen had smashed it long ago with 532 episodes over eight years of her biggest show after That’s Life!. For some, its standing as the UK’s most successful solo female-fronted talkshow was reduced by it not airing at prime time, but Rantzen also flourished as one of the most able substitutes for fellow chatshow host Terry Wogan.

She started her career at the BBC and met her husband and mentor, Desmond Wilcox, at the corporation, so Rantzen was something of a Beeb loyalist. However, she participated in two ITV documentaries about Nicholas Winton, a British stockbroker who organised rescues of mainly Jewish refugee children from Nazi Germany. His story was first told by Rantzen on That’s Life! in 1988 and Rantzen’s six-decade connection with him culminated in the 2023 movie One Life, in which she is played by Samantha Spiro.

Having pioneered, in The Big Time, the type of reality TV that makes celebrities of ordinary citizens, Rantzen got in early on the genre that forces already famous facesout of their comfort zones when she took part in the second series of Strictly, in 2004. She was paired with Anton Du Beke and was the third contestant to be eliminated.

Whether doing a waltz or chewing marsupial genitalia, reality TV is a circular industry: participation in one show makes you more likely to be offered another. Rantzen completed the big two with the eighth series of I’m a Celeb in 2008. The audience’s relatively benevolent attitude to her was evidenced by her always ranking low in the public vote-off and being fifth to be eliminated, before Joe Swash eventually won.

Widowed young, Rantzen, in the last phase of her campaigning TV career, focused on bereavement and the potential loneliness of older age, issues she also tried to tackle through numerous charities and trusteeships. In this thoughtful documentary, she benefited from 5’s policy of forefronting former BBC presenters.

A commendable and courageous recent tradition on Good Morning Britain has been inviting terminally ill TV personalities – such as Bill Turnbulland Dermot Murnaghan – on as guests to promote research and encourage at-risk viewers to attend medical screenings and seek early diagnosis. In her final broadcast, Rantzen advocated for assisted dying, a topic that she had discussed in numerous TV appearances even as her health precipitously declined. Unusually for her, in what had been a career marked by successful campaigning, her aim was thwarted by parliament last month.
