Specialist services are vital to help people with ME/CFS

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:39:06 GMT

Readers respond to George Monbiot’s article about how those with myalgic encephalomyelitis, or chronic fatigue syndrome, have been failed by the health system

George Monbiot (Abandoned, dismissed and gaslighted: there is no excuse for the way ME sufferers have been betrayed, 24 September) is right about one important thing: people with severe ME/CFS (myalgic encephalomyelitis, or chronic fatigue syndrome) deserve much better care than many have received. But two different questions are being conflated: how patients have been treated, and what the evidence tells us about the causes and treatment of ME/CFS.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence no longer recommends the old form of graded exercise therapy, in which activity was increased according to a predetermined schedule regardless of symptoms.

That is an important change, particularly given the significance of post-exertional malaise. But it does not establish that exercise is inherently dangerous or that all forms of physical rehabilitation are useless. Clinical trials have found improvements in fatigue and physical functioning in some people following exercise-based interventions, albeit with important limitations.

Similarly, cognitive behavioural therapy should not be presented as a cure for ME/CFS or treatment for an assumed psychological cause. But helping someone manage anxiety, depression or the consequences of a disabling chronic illness does not imply that the illness itself is psychological.

The growing evidence of biological abnormalities is important, but does not establish whether individual abnormalities are causes, consequences, adaptations or part of a feedback loop. Monbiot’s patient testimonies deserve attention, but a self-selected group responding to a Bluesky appeal cannot establish how common particular experiences are.

As a GP, I believe that there is a much simpler failure to address: specialist ME/CFS provision remains remarkably limited. Many chronic conditions, including rheumatological and neurological illnesses, have no cure but still have specialist services for diagnosis, symptom management and support.

Patients deserve to be believed and treated with respect. They also deserve honesty about what is known, what is uncertain and what the evidence actually shows. Name and address supplied

I had a mild (undiagnosed) form of ME for 20 years, triggered by a virus, before another virus caused my illness to worsen. My otherwise excellent GP advised me to go for a walk every day, which left me so ill that I barely left the house for more than three years.

Twenty-four years later, not only are there no treatments for ME but in some places, such as where I live, there is no support at all. When I first claimed sickness benefits, I had to pay privately to see a consultant in infectious diseases with a special interest in ME as the Department for Work and Pensions would not accept evidence from GPs.

I cannot plan anything, as I never know when I will be so ill that I will be confined to the house again. Most people I speak to have never heard of ME/CFS. If we weren’t so ill, those of us with this awful disease would be shouting it from the rooftops. Eleanor DentCardiff

George Monbiot is right to draw attention to the “shocking social crisis playing out behind closed doors” for people living with ME. Not only is ME a devastating condition, but too often those affected are failed by the very systems meant to care for them.

The level of political attention the issue has received is nowhere close to the scale of the problem. The government’s strategy on ME, published over a year ago, lacked both substantive funding and outcome targets. Its key action for those affected by the most severe form of ME – “exploring” whether a specialised service could be commissioned – is now delayed until April 2027. We hope that, as a first step, the health and social care select committee will take up this critical issue as a matter of urgency. Karen Hargrave and Emma Gore-LloydCo-founders, ThereForME charity

How poor public transport policy is putting the brake on cities

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:38:51 GMT

David Andrews suggests a tram network could be the answer to London’s clogged streets, while V Narayanan says unused cycle lanes are a waste of valuable road space

Your analysis of slowing buses in global cities sets out the mechanism exactly, and the remedy follows from it (London buses in decline? Why public transport in global cities is slowing to a crawl – visualised, 23 September).

Transport for London’s own calculation that a 10% fall in speed costs 6% of demand and Imperial College London’s finding of the same decline across 15 cities show what happens to buses as the traffic thickens around them. Retiming the lights will not reverse it, and London is already trying. The phrase to notice in the article is one used by TfL: signals will give more buses priority “where possible”.

There lies the difficulty. On a route running a bus every two minutes, the signals are asked to intervene 30 times an hour in each direction, and the junction cannot recover between calls before the next bus arrives.

Bristol city council’s engineers found precisely this when they reviewed their bus priority: in the most congested parts of the city, priority delivered no journey-time saving at all.

This is a bigger brake on the economy than it looks. What holds a city back is the plain difficulty of getting across it to work, to customers, to the shops. A firm can recruit from a smaller area, a worker can reach fewer jobs, and a high street can be reached by fewer people. Much of the decline of the high street is a decline in how easily people can get to it.

The cure is to carry the same people in fewer vehicles. One tram carries as many people as three or four buses, so it can be given priority junction after junction, and the crossing traffic still gets its turn.

About 30 French cities have put trams through their centres since Nantes started in 1985, and they rebuilt those centres around them. Their central streets are visibly busier for it. Sheffield’s trams share a shopping street with cars and vans, and run to the same timetable in the peak as at midday. David AndrewsChair, Light Rail Transit Association; lead author, Bristol Area Bus and Tram Business Case

Your article on London buses in decline highlights poor transport policy in London, which is guided by publicity rather than practicality.

Buses have slowed down as dedicated bus lanes have been largely replaced by a poor choice of cycle lanes. London is an old city with narrow lanes and, with individual cycle transport given priority over mass public transport, it’s no wonder that buses have slowed and become erratic in service.

One only needs to observe the utilisation of cycle lanes that are empty except during the peak hours of 7.30am-9am and 4pm-5pm on weekdays. That is a gross waste of valuable road space that could be used by buses.

Having a dedicated bus lane instead of a cycle lane would speed up buses and make them more reliable. The bus lane could be shared by cycles and during peak times be dedicated to them, while being free for buses rest of the day.

Sadly, politicians rarely look beyond elections, and fail to prioritise buses over bicycles. The authorities have wasted millions on cycle lanes while failing spectacularly to improve mass public transportation. V NarayananLondon

Disinformation is just one symptom of the authorities’ failure to regulate social media

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:38:43 GMT

Responding to an editorial on Russian threats, Aneet Morar says companies that profit from spreading harmful content need to face real consequences

Your editorial (The Guardian view on Russian disinformation: a foreign threat that relies on UK complicity, 23 September) is right that Andy Burnham’s warning about the Kremlin only tells half the story. I would go further: disinformation is one symptom of a wider failure to regulate the platforms that now function as critical national infrastructure.

The harms are evident across a wide spectrum. We know that engagement-driven feeds are damaging young people’s mental health. The same amplification mechanics that carry foreign propaganda also accelerate far-right radicalisation at home, as your analysis of the disorder in Belfast and Southampton showed. The new generation of wearable devices, such as Meta’s smart glasses, makes recording people without their knowledge or consent a routine part of life.

Yes, the government must step up its response to disinformation, but this alone is not enough. Platforms that profit from spreading harmful content need to face real consequences: enforceable duties of care, penalties proportionate to their scale, and transparency about how their algorithms decide what we see.

I have spent my career in the payments industry, where infrastructure operating at this scale would never be allowed to run without clear rules, independent oversight and liability when things go wrong. There is no good reason to hold these platforms that shape what millions of people believe to a lower standard.

Tackling the Kremlin’s bot armies matters, but until these platforms are held responsible for what they amplify, across every segment of society, we will keep treating the symptoms rather than the cause. Aneet MorarLondon

Terrible idea or major coup? Galliano’s Zara collection launches after Met controversy

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:05:56 GMT

Collaboration regarded as ‘really big thing’ for retailer in some quarters despite backlash around designer’s antisemitic remarks in 2011

A month after it was announced that a planned exhibition dedicated to fashion designer John Galliano at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art would not proceed, his debut collection for fast fashion company Zara has been released.

Called Re{form}, it was, according to a press release, “authored by the couturier John Galliano. Built from our memory. Made for now.”

Its launch in shops comes after controversy over plans to honour the former Dior designer, who was found guilty of a hate crime in 2011 after a series of racist and antisemitic rants, with an exhibition of his work at the Met and a corresponding Met gala – a juggernaut of popular culture viewed by billions globally online. The exhibition was cancelled but had it gone ahead, it would have been only the third time such an honour had been bestowed on a living designer. The only others being Yves Saint Laurent in 1983 and Rei Kawakubo of Comme des Garçons in 2017.

The backlash to the plans were vehement and widespread, with Met patrons, New York politicians and prominent Jewish leaders objecting. Writing in the New York Times, his biographer Dana Thomas labelled it a “terrible idea”, saying that “choosing this moment to glorify the life’s work of someone who was convicted of making antisemitic remarks … is downright bizarre”, and noting that “his infamous antisemitic rants were not an aberration”.

In other quarters in the fashion industry, not least in Anna Wintour’s corner, support for Galliano has been similarly full-throated. Many argue he has sufficiently atoned for his crimes. Others point out that it has been 15 years since Galliano, who was struggling with addiction at the time, committed them and that there ought to come a time for forgiveness.

Galliano said in his statement withdrawing from the exhibition: “I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry for it.”

Given this fraught atmosphere and renewed attention on Galliano’s past, why has Zara pushed ahead with its plans?

For Zara, says Orsola de Castro, designer and author, this is “the coup of their career, their life, their brand”. Fashion critic Philippe Pourhashemi agrees: “For Zara it’s still a major coup that they managed to get [Galliano] on board.

“That’s a really, really big thing because if we really look at it from a rational point of view, it doesn’t really make sense that someone like him would work with a platform like that.”

More tangibly, there are logistics. The collection, which was shot by acclaimed fashion photographer Steven Meisel, has been years – and a lot of money – in the making and for some, even in the immediate wake of the Met cancellation, Zara following suit was an unrealistic prospect. Online, and in the form of queues outside the Zara store on Bond Street on Thursday morning, there was huge excitement for the unveiling of the designs.

Galliano has been working elsewhere in the fashion industry for years. Sacked by Dior in 2011, by 2013 he had returned to work, doing a short residency with New York designer Oscar de la Renta. From 2014 onwards he spent a decade as creative director of Margiela, bowing out on a final show in 2024 that was widely celebrated in the industry as legendary and history-making. His designs have continued to appear even on the Met Gala red carpet: in 2024 Kim Kardashian wore a chainmail, corseted Galliano creation to walk the steps.

The venerable Met and the high street are different beasts. Zara, which is owned by Inditex, the largest fashion retailer in the world, is a fast fashion brand that has previously been criticised over allegations of unethical treatment of workers. “Zara has done a really good job at whitewashing its image, and Galliano is also a part of that,” says Pourhashemi.

In terms of grappling with Galliano’s past, according to fashion expert and historian Tony Glenville: “His antisemitism and problems are something that in discussions I suspect they just thought, ‘this is fashion and we want his name on some clothes,’ simply a business deal.” Fashion as an industry isn’t inherently known for its ethics.

Zara will be hoping that it bolsters its perceived fashion chops. The collection, prices for which run from £17.99 to £699, is being positioned as a dialogue between Galliano and the Zara archive – conceived from archival Zara garments, it will be produced in all new materials, rather than pre-existing stock.

The collection is also being seen as a pitch by Zara to be seen as the brand of affordable luxury. In the age of Shein, Temu, Primark and supermarket fashion, it is, according to Pourhashemi, “vital, from a business standpoint, for Zara to distance itself”. It will also be hoping to differentiate itself from its own cut-price brand, Lefties, which launched in Liverpool last month. For Glenville, “all this is Inditex leaving the bottom price line to Lefties to do the hard work – and elevating Zara”.

For Zara the move is likely more about reputation than actual sales. “It’s an absolute hook to draw us in,” says Glenville, noting that many garments from these designer collaborations never actually make it to the shop floor.

Galliano is known for his theatrical, storybook designs, not for clothes that are inherently wearable. The designs are inspired by characters from his notorious 1984 graduate collection titled Les Incroyables: “Les Incroyables and les Merveilleuses – the defiant dandies and divas of post-revolutionary France.” Speaking to Vogue, Galliano said he “had no intentions to dumb down” for a more mainstream market.

Galliano has signed a two-year contract, so the stakes are relatively low. “If he does a couple of collections a year in small quantities, they get the cachet without too much risk,” says Glenville. “If it’s phenomenally successful, they’ll extend his contract.”

Zara declined to comment.

Alleged flydubai attacker interrogated by Saudi security services as investigation into apparent crash attempt opens

The Omani co-pilot who stabbed his captain in an apparent attempt to crash an Israel-bound flight from Dubai had previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has claimed.

Israeli passengers intervened to stop the attack on Wednesday, restraining the co-pilot, while a reserve crew in the plane was able to stabilise the plummeting plane and ultimately land it safely in Saudi Arabia.

The plane had more than 170 people onboard and Israeli officials praised the bravery of those who intervened, announcing that four of the Israeli passengers would receive a “heroism” award for preventing a potential disaster.

Netanyahu told Fox News: “We know that he underwent Islamic radical indoctrination. That appears to be something we are gathering from his personal information.”

The co-pilot, whose identity is still not known, was being interrogated by Saudi security services, which arrested him on the plane’s arrival in Tabuk, in the north-west of the country.

Saudi investigators were cooperating with the United Arab Emirates, the US, Oman and Israel to try to determine the attacker’s motive, a regional official familiar with the investigation said. “All possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into. Nothing is ruled out for now,” they told the Associated Press.

Two Israeli security officials said that Israel’s initial assessment was that the co-pilot was probably acting alone, Reuters reported.

Netanyahu said that the co-pilot was probably suicidal, citing preliminary “indications”.

“It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane … The Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that are found in his background, I think that’s a pretty good clue,” he said, emphasising that final conclusions had yet to be made.

Netanyahu had previously said it was “too early to say” if there was any state backing – namely Iranian – of the attack. Two Israeli security sources told Reuters that they had not yet found Iranian involvement.

The attack came just days after Netanyahu warned of an unspecified security threat to Israel that could come during its October election. The Israeli military had said before the incident it had no specific intelligence of an imminent threat and the opposition leader Yair Lapid said that a security briefing on Tuesday night included no mention of a related threat.

Other Israeli officials, including the defence minister, Israel Katz, and the ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, suggested the incident was a “terror attack”, with the Israeli foreign ministry briefing its diplomats that the attack was against Israel and its relationship with the UAE.

Donald Trump suggested the co-pilot was “perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job”, and told reporters at the White House that he and Netanyahu had spoken at length.

Netanyahu also spoke to the president of the UAE, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who agreed to Israel’s involvement in the investigation.

Flydubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while the investigation took place and urged all parties “to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts”.

The UAE announced on Thursday that it would conduct its own investigation into the incident, which started about two and a half hours after takeoff from Dubai. It said its investigators had begun to look into the attacker’s motive and if he had any links to any “terrorist purpose”.

Passengers said they saw a knife-wielding man – apparently the Omani co-pilot – putting the captain of the plane on the floor, after which the plane began to plummet. The wounded pilot, Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, managed to send out an emergency signal and open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and stop the plane’s descent.

A video shared by the prime minister’s office showed one passenger, Yaniv Hayoun, a plumber, speaking to Netanyahu at length about how the events onboard had played out.

Hayoun told the prime minister he and other passengers heard screaming and felt the air pressure change as the plane dived before they forced their way into the cockpit and found the attacker at the instrument panel. “I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during the meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel.

Machchhar was widely praised for his bravery, with Netanyahu and the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, hailing him as a hero. India’s ambassador to the UAE met the wounded captain’s family and briefed them on his recovery, the Indian consulate in the UAE said.

Machchhar was being treated in a hospital in Tabuk, but was in good health and recovering well, according to the Indian embassy in the UAE, which said the ambassador had visited the pilot.

“Captain Smit Machchhar is a HERO,” Modi said, in a post on social media. “In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others.”

David Sullivan sues BBC for £150m over Panorama’s sexual misconduct claims

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:57:49 GMT

West Ham co-owner and former pornographer lodges high court claim over episode, in which several women accused him of abusing power

David Sullivan is suing the BBC for £150m over multiple claims of sexual misconduct made in a documentary.

Lawyers acting for Sullivan, who remains West Ham United’s co-owner, have lodged a high court claim against the corporation over its Panorama investigation Predator: The Billionaire Football Boss, which was broadcast in June.

It featured three women who alleged Sullivan had abused his power as the owner of the Sport newspapers to prey on them for sex when they were seeking work.

A further four women accused Sullivan of exploitative and predatory behaviour, including allegations he had tried to pressure them into sex during business meetings.

As part of a joint investigation, the BBC and the Times said their reporters had spoken to dozens of former models and industry insiders, with some sources alleging Sullivan was known for “casting couch” behaviour.

The former pornographer vowed to take legal action against the BBC even before the programme had aired. In a statement in which he also resigned as West Ham’s co-chair, he said the accusations were “factually incorrect and entirely false”.

“The false allegations levelled against me have been sensationalised by the media,” he said. “After a lifetime spent building businesses in the adult industry in which I have met thousands of women, it is sadly inevitable that a small number of improper conduct claims are being made against me. I categorically deny these claims.”

Sullivan’s high court claim, first seen by the Telegraph, accuses the BBC of “libel and malicious falsehood” in airing the documentary. It states the show caused Sullivan “grave, catastrophic, and irreparable harm” to his reputation and business interests.

It states that the programme’s claims opened the 77-year-old up to “profound public hatred, universal ridicule, and global opprobrium”, as well as “immediate and severe commercial alienation, banking disruption, and quantifiable financial destruction”.

The BBC declined to comment.

While Sullivan has resigned as West Ham’s co-chair, he remains the Championship club’s largest shareholder, owning 39% of its shares.

It has also emerged that Sullivan has faced restrictions on his contact with West Ham’s women’s and youth teams since 2023 because of a safeguarding investigation.

The Football Association began an inquiry three years ago after receiving a complaint, which the Guardian understands involves an allegation of sexual misconduct unrelated to football.

Sullivan said through lawyers that the restrictions were part of a “negotiated and temporary agreement” and that the safeguarding investigation related to a “single anonymous complaint” from an event in 1981. He said the alleged incident “never happened”.

After the BBC documentary, the presenter Tony Livesey stepped back from the broadcaster. Earlier in his career, Livesey had been the editor-in-chief of Sullivan’s Sport newspapers. The BBC investigation raised questions for the 62-year-old, with one alleged victim saying he had arranged a meeting between her and Sullivan.

Livesey has said he has “no recollection” of introducing the young woman to Sullivan and that it was “not part” of his job to do so. He said he had had “practically zero” contact with anyone appearing in the paper, such as female models.

Another high-profile legal case would be a blow for the BBC, which is already fighting a claim brought against it by Donald Trump. The US president has taken legal action over an episode of Panorama that spliced together two parts of a speech.

The BBC has apologised for the edit, but has always maintained the programme did not defame Trump.

Burnham’s reopening of Brexit debate is ‘biggest boost in my career’, says Farage

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:47:43 GMT

Reform UK leader tells supporters PM’s move has ‘opened up a huge flank to us’

UK politics live – latest updates

Nigel Farage has claimed that Andy Burnham has given him “the biggest boost in my career” by reviving the Brexit debate, which the Reform UK leader said had reopened a “huge flank” to his party.

The prime minister’s pledges to the Labour conference and admission on Wednesday that rejoining the EU was among options the government would look at had put “put me back into the debate”, he said.

Looking tanned and relaxed before his party’s first major rally since its conference last month, Farage indicated to reporters that he was relishing a return to the playbook that he and others deployed during the 2016 referendum.

Dismissing polls showing that as much as 59% of the public favoured rejoining the EU, Farage told the Guardian: “Of course they do, until you tell them it’ll cost 25bn quid a year, until you tell him it’ll mean joining Schengen [the area of Europe that has open borders], until he tells them it will mean actually having to recommit to joining the euro.

“Remember that the leavers haven’t made their arguments since 2016. The ‘remoaners’ have made their arguments every single week. I mean, do you know what? I actually think that Burnham has made a very big political mistake here.”

Farage was speaking before a rally in the South Yorkshire city of Doncaster, the first of a series Reform is holding around Britain on the theme of what the party would do in its first 100 days of government.

While the Reform UK leader said he believed Burnham had calculated that new language on the EU might help win back voters from the Greens in big cities, Farage added: “Here in Doncaster and across the ‘red wall’ in the north and Midlands, I think he’s opened up a huge flank to us.”

To cheers from hundreds of Reform supporters who gathered inside an event space at Doncaster racecourse, Farage said: “Today I’m back on the road and today is when our general election campaign starts.”

There were even bigger cheers when Farage said he would relish – “Bring it on, I say” – the prospect of fighting Burnham in red wall areas such as Doncaster on the issue of rejoining the EU.

“He might just have given me the biggest boost in my career I’ve ever had. Thank you, Andy, if you’re watching.”

The focus of the rally – “100 days to save Britain” – had been planned before Burnham’s announcement about UK-EU relations. However, Reform sources claim that the prime minister’s intervention has energised them and that specific donors are already discussing how they can fund a rerun of the 2016 campaign.

Meanwhile, Farage strongly hinted that Reform’s internal inquiry into the donations controversy that has overshadowed the party this year would absolve two key aides and that legal action would be launched against journalists involved.

Indicating that he had already seen the report and knew its conclusions, Farage said its release was “imminent”.

“It’s been done. It’ll be out in public very soon and I think some of your co-conspirators might find themselves with one or two legal challenges,” he told a Channel 4 journalist among reporters who questioned him.

Reform was rocked on the eve of its party conference after some of Farage’s team were filmed appearing to plot to avoid electoral laws on foreign donations in an undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News.

A group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party.

In Channel 4 News’s investigation, footage showed that the fake UK-based supporter also had conversations with Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, who talked about commissioning polling that would be paid for by the US-based father.

In footage of another meeting, a senior adviser to Farage, Dan Jukes, appeared to suggest to the fake UK-based supporter that his US-based father could make a substantial donation by channelling it through the son.

Jukes has denied “any wrongdoing” while Orr has said he would cooperate with the party’s internal investigation “fully”.

The Metropolitan police are carrying out a criminal investigation into Reform over allegations it broke foreign funding laws.

Sex, drugs and amoebic dysentery: the 20 best making-of documentaries – ranked!

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:31:13 GMT

From tropical disasters and doomed sci-fi epics to bribing Orson Welles and fending off a puma, we rate cinema’s most revealing glimpses behind the scenes

Behind-the-scenes footage from Dawn of the Dead is the highlight of this aficionados-only affair, which follows the 1979 satirical zombie horror all the way through to distribution. Director George A Romero, makeup maestro Tom Savini and the occasional zombie actor shoot the breeze in the deserted shopping mall that provides the movie with its incongruous central location.

Imagining what might have been if Tim Burton’s Superman Lives had got off the ground, documentary maker Jon Schnepp cosies up on screen with his interviewees and insinuates himself unforgivably into the story. The material is almost good enough to transcend his vanity: there is test footage of lead actor Nicolas Cage in his Man of Steel duds, plus interviews with Burton, original screenwriter Kevin Smith and producer Jon Peters, who was adamant that Superman should fight polar bears and a giant spider.

A group of actors with disabilities form the bulk of the cast of the short western Bulletproof, shot in the California desert courtesy of the inclusive arts project Zeno Mountain Farm. Crucially, Bulletproof itself isn’t about disability, but rather an attempt to highlight the lack of on-screen representation – and plug the gap. This affectionate documentary tracks the film from preproduction to premiere.

Orson Welles spent five years shooting what became his final film, The Other Side of the Wind, with three years elapsing before its star – director and sometime actor John Huston – even stepped in front of the camera. After all that, the footage ended up impounded by the Iranian revolutionary government. A version eventually premiered in 2018 and is now on Netflix, along with this scattershot documentary, presented by Alan Cumming, which strings together archive footage, new interviews and typically Wellesian stories of on-set bluffs, tomfoolery and procrastination.

A half-hour snapshot by Lucas of his new buddy Francis Ford Coppola, who is hard at work on his fourth film, The Rain People, and not too shy to argue with his lead actor, Shirley Knight. Contains one choice detail: in preparation for driving across the country shooting this road movie, all the men on the crew, Coppola included, shave off their beards to look more presentable for any hippy-hating officials they might encounter along the way.

In declining The Exorcist but taking on Exorcist II: The Heretic, John Boorman perhaps displayed a preference for poisoned chalices over champagne flutes. He is candid and good-humoured, if still a little shell-shocked, as he recounts the experience of filming the sequel once derided as “the stupidest major movie ever made”, and the despair that led him to contemplate self-immolation on Hollywood Boulevard. Sand-related illness, a sozzled Richard Burton, locusts and tap-dancing: this has it all.

Filmed in a rat-infested studio on sets recycled from the Jurassic Park rip-off Carnosaur, with special effects entrusted to a local outfit called Mr Film, this cheapo superhero adventure was made in a rush to prevent the rights to The Fantastic Four reverting from producer Bernd Eichinger to Marvel. (“That movie was never supposed to be shown to anybody,” said Stan Lee.) This heartening documentary, which shows the crestfallen cast refusing to let their film die, feels even more pertinent after Warner Bros recently shelved some movies as tax write-offs, including Batgirl and Coyote Vs Acme, the latter rescued only by the skin of its teeth.

In trying to adapt Frank Herbert’s Dune in the mid-1970s, cinematic shaman Alejandro Jodorowsky (Santa Sangre, El Topo) bit off more than he could chew, just as David Lynch would when his version came to painful fruition in 1984. But Frank Pavich’s documentary proves that Jodorowsky’s intention to make “a film that gives LSD hallucinations without taking LSD” was not too fanciful. Among those in his corner were the artist HR Giger, who went on to design the monsters in Alien, and a cast including Salvador Dalí, Mick Jagger and Orson Welles, with the latter being bribed to take part with the promise of having his favourite chef on set.

When the studio New Line tried to ditch South African director Richard Stanley from his own HG Wells adaptation, he asked a warlock called Skip to pull some cosmic strings. That did the trick for a while, helping Stanley to charm the film’s star, Marlon Brando. But black magic was no match for cast member Val Kilmer, who demanded a 40% reduction in his own shooting days, then spent his time on set playing power games. There was nature to contend with, too, in the form of wild animals (a puma pisses on Stanley’s tailored suit) and a hurricane that ravages the location in Cairns, Queensland. Finally replaced by curmudgeonly veteran John Frankenheimer, Stanley refuses to leave Australia, which is when things go from mad to worse.

Two behind-the-scenes Blue Velvet documentaries from one director. Peter Braatz was still a film student when David Lynch, with whom he had been corresponding for several years, invited him to Wilmington, North Carolina in 1985 to chart the making of what would become his twisted masterpiece. Braatz marshalled just under an hour of the resulting Super-8 material into his 1988 documentary, which straddled the line between orthodox and experimental. He then reshaped it into a full-on ambient head-trip for the 86-minute 2016 version, which mixes flickering footage and crisp black-and-white photographs with a woozy score and the voices of Lynch, Dennis Hopper and others to form an ethereal audiovisual collage.

Disney had high hopes for Kingdom of the Sun, a Prince and the Pauper-style animated musical drama set in the Inca empire. The studio sent Lion King co-director Roger Allers on a research trip to Peru and commissioned a suite of new songs by Sting. But it was back to the drawing board after a calamitous screening of an early rough cut; Allers and Sting were given the heave-ho, and the movie was retooled as the larky comedy The Emperor’s New Groove. Sting’s wife, Trudie Styler, charts every disastrous step in a documentary that Disney has done its darnedest to suppress.

A 10-a-penny title for an account of a once-in-a-lifetime film-making folly: Jerry Lewis’s abandoned, incomplete 1972 Holocaust drama The Day The Clown Cried. Directing himself as a former clown who entertains children in a concentration camp, Lewis made a misguided bid to be taken seriously. “It was bad work,” he admits here. It wasn’t only the dubious material that defeated the former Nutty Professor: unbeknown to him, the option on the script had expired, rendering the entire project illegal. It was his decision, though, to hire a repentant former concentration camp guard as part of the crew. “He was a human being!” Lewis protests.

Seventy-odd fans of horror exploitation studio Troma worked unpaid on Poultrygeist: Night of the Chicken Dead while living in a deserted church in a rundown corner of Buffalo, New York, with one cold shower between them. Meanwhile, the chicken-themed zombie flick was shot at a nearby abandoned McDonald’s. This documentary captures all the on-set horror, from the sexually disinhibited auditions to the hourly cast-and-crew bust-ups. Actors walk off, burst into tears and throw punches; a zombie extra accidentally sets himself on fire; and bilious co-director and Troma boss Lloyd Kaufman proves both lackadaisical and tyrannical.

When budding film-maker Sandi Tan met the enigmatic Georges Cardona, he cited Fitzcarraldo as his inspiration and claimed to know crew members from Apocalypse Now. Those pictures – famously troubled productions that spawned their own jaw-dropping documentaries – look like red flags considering what came next: Cardona directed Tan’s indie road movie Shirkers, swallowing up $10,000 of her savings when he ran out of money, then vanished with the resulting 70 reels of unprocessed film. She didn’t see the footage until decades later, when those reels were returned to her by Cardona’s widow. Tan’s sobering 2018 documentary attempts to make sense of the betrayal.

“Good film directors will notice many mistakes,” says prolific camcorder auteur and 67-year-old Santa Claus lookalike Daniel Burmeister. “But I like what I do: making hand-crafted films.” In exchange for a month’s food and accommodation, Burmeister sets up shop in a remote Argentinian village to bring the community together by shooting a movie from one of his own scripts. His budget may be nonexistent but his resourcefulness is boundless: in place of a dolly shot, for instance, he sits on a blanket, camera on his shoulder, while being dragged across the floor. This delightful, deeply humanistic portrait of grassroots DIY cinema has all the charm and idiosyncrasies of a Jared Hess comedy.

Terry Gilliam was happy to have documentary makers Keith Fulton and Louis Pepe on set for The Man Who Killed Don Quixote after being impressed by The Hamster Factor, their behind-the-scenes film on the making of his earlier 12 Monkeys. The anguished result shows exactly why Quixote was abandoned after six days’ shooting in Spain in September 2000. Takes were rendered unusable by the roar of F16s from a nearby Nato base; Jean Rochefort, co-lead opposite Johnny Depp, fell seriously ill; and the equipment was destroyed by a merciless storm. Gilliam’s on-set catchphrase sums it up: “We’re fucked!” (When Quixote was eventually made in 2018, Fulton and Pepe documented that shoot, too, in He Dreams of Giants.)

The subgenre of documentaries about unfinished films stretches back to the BBC’s 1965 The Epic That Never Was, which investigated Josef von Sternberg’s planned version of I, Claudius starring Charles Laughton and Merle Oberon. But it reached its apotheosis with Henri-Georges Clouzot’s Inferno, Ruxandra Medrea and Serge Bromberg’s ravishing reflection on an early-1960s Proustian psychological drama from the director of Les Diaboliques. Lavishly funded by Columbia, Clouzot’s vision was impossibly ambitious, with three crews and a trippy array of complicated in-camera special effects. The director, who could not be dissuaded from shooting time-consuming test footage, suffered a heart attack three weeks into the 18-week shoot. The fragments of his vision, cherrypicked here from 15 hours of unseen footage, are intoxicating: where else can you see Romy Schneider covered in glitter, cellophane and olive oil?

Deep in the rainforests of South America, Werner Herzog battles mud and misery, along with his leading man Klaus Kinski, to make Fitzcarraldo, about one man’s dream of building an opera house in the Amazon. Les Blank’s documentary, which is arguably more compelling than the movie it’s about, enables us to watch in disbelief as a film about a lunatic mission turns into one itself. Herzog’s initial footage has to be abandoned when the lead actor, Jason Robards, falls ill with amoebic dysentery and co-star Mick Jagger is needed on a world tour. Up and running again, the production is forced to relocate more than 1,000 miles away due to a border war, while Herzog’s plans to move a steamship up a hillside provide a textbook example of madness eclipsing method.

Mark Borchardt, a Milwaukee junkyard poet with a mullet and plateglass specs, may be best suited to factory work or serial killing, according to his brother, but he positively glows with a passion for cinema. Lacking the funds to finish his feature debut, he instead tries to complete a short horror film, Coven, undaunted by his inability to pronounce the title. More Wiseau than Welles, he has optimism and indefatigability to burn. Not to mention a crew of colourful collaborators, including his mother, whom he enlists as an extra despite her protestations that she needs to go shopping; his bleary, poodle-haired pal and former acid-head Mike; and the gnarled, trailer-dwelling Uncle Bill, who needs 30 takes to deliver four lines. Director Chris Smith (who later made the priceless Fyre festival documentary) rightly portrays Mark as one of cinema’s most inspiring heroes – even if he still hasn’t finished his first feature.

Megadoc, the forthcoming behind-the-scenes film about Francis Ford Coppola’s $120m passion project Megalopolis, is directed by Mike Figgis, though earlier Coppola-related documentaries tended to be family affairs. The director’s late wife, Eleanor, was responsible for Making Marie Antoinette, released later this month, about their daughter Sofia’s 2006 historical fantasia. And it was Eleanor, too, who co-directed the extraordinary Hearts of Darkness, which draws on her 60 hours of footage and 40 hours of audio recordings, as well as her own diaries, all from the turbulent 238-day shooting of Apocalypse Now. The film reveals her husband arguing on set with Dennis Hopper, frantically typing new scenes just moments before the cameras roll, and negotiating with Marlon Brando, who has piled on the pounds but neglected to learn his lines. “I’m thinking of shooting myself,” the director confides. “This is one crisis I can’t pull myself out of.”

Boorman and the Devil is in cinemas in the UK and Ireland now. Making Marie Antoinette is in cinemas in the UK, Ireland and US from 23 October and streaming on Mubi from 6 November

Cristiano Ronaldo’s Portugal walkout divides a nation as Jorge Jesus asserts control

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:04:11 GMT

Row sparked by head coach’s decision to leave the 41-year-old on the bench has left a great international career at risk of ending in acrimony

The drama surrounding Cristiano Ronaldo and the national team has naturally become the biggest story here in Portugal. It led Wednesday evening’s news broadcasts and made the front page of virtually every major newspaper. For some, Ronaldo was right to walk out on the squad days after spending half an hour warming up against Norway without being brought on in an apparent provocation by Jorge Jesus. For others, the forward’s behaviour was intolerable and his departure a matter of time, particularly once he found himself face to face with such a strong-minded head coach.

Ronaldo has promised to tell his side of the story soon, and Jesus will speak on Thursday night after the Nations League match in Denmark. A confrontation between these two huge personalities had been simmering in the background. Jesus was inevitably asked in his first press conference with the team in July how his relationship with Ronaldo would work. Jesus, who coached Ronaldo at Al-Nassr, answered categorically.

“Cris will never be a problem for the national team or for me,” he said, insisting he had Ronaldo’s temperament under control. The harmony between coach and player did not last long.

In Portugal, reaction has inevitably split into two camps. In many ways this is a repeat of the debate over Ronaldo’s automatic place in the starting XI at this summer’s World Cup, and Roberto Martínez’s decision to keep the captain on the pitch for the full 90 minutes in all but one of the five matches – despite there being no obvious tactical or physical explanation for it. Even when Ronaldo came off in the last 32 against Croatia, it was not until the 81st minute.

Ronaldo’s fans are firmly behind him, defending him fiercely on social media. Much of the general public, though, feels the player has turned his back on the national team. That was the message splashed in big letters across the front page of O Jogo, one of Portugal’s leading sports newspapers.

Across the Portuguese media, most newspapers and commentators have sided with the view that Ronaldo behaved selfishly. There are, however, some voices – particularly in newspapers and television outlets in which Ronaldo is a shareholder – who have turned their criticism towards Jesus, accusing him of ingratitude and of indefensibly going back on his word.

But what actually caused the controversy? According to Jesus, he and Ronaldo had a verbal agreement that the 41-year-old would not start against Norway last Sunday, three days after he played for 67 minutes against Wales in the coach’s first match, but would come on. During the game, which Portugal won 2-1, those plans changed: Ronaldo remained an unused substitute, Jesus making the decision for tactical reasons. Ronaldo reportedly viewed the incident as a humiliation.

The first signs of the breakdown came immediately after the final whistle when Ronaldo left the pitch and did not join his teammates as they saluted their supporters in Oslo. Ronaldo’s frustration with Jesus reportedly reached astronomical levels during the manager’s press conference on Wednesday.

Asked about keeping Ronaldo on the bench, Jesus asserted absolute control, in essence making clear that Ronaldo did not run the team and would not be able to change or influence the tactics. It was a transparent message to Ronaldo – and to the Portuguese football federation (FPF): the manager is in charge.

“I can promise whatever I want,” the 72-year-old said. “I’m the coach and I told the player that he wasn’t going to play. I told him I would take him to the bench and that, if I needed him for 30 minutes, he would play. But I saw the game differently, so he didn’t come on. It won’t be Cristiano, or any other player, who changes my ideas as a coach. Never. Neither him nor anyone else. Not even a president. Never. Zero.”

Jesus also stated his intention to start Gonçalo Ramos rather than Ronaldo in Monday’s game.

What happened next is what everyone has seen. Ronaldo abruptly left the team hotel, boarded a plane and posted on social media, promising to reveal the truth soon.

Some believe there has been a decline in Ronaldo’s communication since he split almost four years ago from the agent Jorge Mendes after giving an interview to Piers Morgan that triggered his departure from Manchester United. The Ronaldo-Mendes friendship and family connection reportedly remain intact, but the player is managed by a team he assembled himself. Some have questioned whether he is surrounded by too many yes-men, without enough people willing or able to tell him when something risks creating a negative image.

Once again, the narrative around Portugal’s national team is dominated by controversy surrounding Ronaldo. He is at risk of an FPF suspension of between one and six months, as well as a fine, for breaching its disciplinary code.

In the absence of both men’s accounts, rumours are spreading like wildfire. Some publications are claiming Ronaldo will never return to the national team. After 234 appearances over the past 23 years and 146 goals, is this how Ronaldo will say goodbye to his country?

Margot Robbie changing her name to her husband’s hurts my beautiful lesbian brain. Here’s why

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:00:56 GMT

I don’t flip a table every time this happens – but I actually do mind when it’s the default decision with no discussion

Being a lesbian in a heretofore heteronormative society means having to go along with lots of things that don’t make sense to your beautiful lesbian brain. One such thing for me is the ongoing expectation that women who marry men should change their surname to their husband’s.

Last week my tolerance was tested again when it was revealed that after a decade of marriage, Margot Robbie has changed her surname to that of her husband, Tom Ackerley.

Margot Ackerley – it simply rolls off the tongue. She will remain Margot Robbie in her public life, and we don’t know why she has done this, but it has nonetheless caused a stir. We got the usual discourse of blah blah tradition, blah blah patriarchy, blah blah women’s individual choice and so on.

We all know how it goes and Margot is not alone in doing this, of course. The statistics are hard to pin down (bearing in mind I dropped out of psychology at uni because of the statistics part) but I think it’s safe to say that in the overwhelming majority of straight marriages, the woman changes her name to the man’s. I see this in every part of my social life, from friends back home who married directly out of high school to my cabal of highly educated urban feminist friends. I play my part by putting all my married male friends in my phone under their wives’ surnames.

Of course I have no personal sense of the societal pressure and systems that inform such decisions, which is why I don’t flip a table every time it happens – but I actually do mind when it’s the default decision with no discussion.

There are plenty of reasons a woman might want to change her name. She might hate her dad. She might feel no attachment to her name. Her husband might have a meaningful attachment to his and so she might just think it’s a nice thing to do.

I’m not an unreasonable lesbian. My issue isn’t with women taking their man’s surname, the problem comes when there is no choosing. When it’s a foregone conclusion, when it hasn’t been actively decided. That’s your name!

If there is discussion, if there is equal respect for both people, if someone has a reason, then that’s fine with me. I once had a colleague whose future husband told her it was a dealbreaker if she didn’t take his name. That’s not a reason. That should have been the dealbreaker itself.

I don’t really care about the reasoning, I just care that there is a reason. That said, when it comes to which surname a baby gets, that’s when I really get irritated. If we really have stopped considering a man’s wife and children his property, why on earth is giving them his name still the default? Women carry and birth the babies. Women are still far more likely to do the lion’s share of childcare. Hello?? The lesbian mind boggles.

But never fear, because I have a solution. And you may be surprised that it doesn’t involve any gender politics whatsoever! My solution is that we throw tradition out the window and that if a couple wants to share a name, we make the decision based on … which surname is cooler. Which surname sounds better, which surname will offer more success – that’s the one you should both use.

In an ideal world, this would be done in a courtroom setting, where each couple comes in and sees me sitting high above them like Judge Judy, ready to bang my gavel. Congratulations, Mr Brown, you are now Mr Beaumont. Sorry, Mrs Jones, you’re now Mrs Wilder. Mr Cheeseman, I release you from your prison.

No longer would awesome surnames be swallowed by the crap oesophagus of patriarchy. No longer would it be considered weak or weird for a man to take his wife’s last name – instead it would be cool and wise. Even though my loyalty always lies with women, I am willing to maintain neutrality in the courtroom.

And sorry, Mr Ackerley, which sounds a bit like a cat throwing up – you’re now Mr Robbie.

Rebecca Shaw is a writer based in Sydney

Why is the UK-France ‘one in, one out’ migration deal being scrapped?

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 14:45:49 GMT

Agreement expected to end on Thursday after running for 423 days, during which it has been beset by problems

UK politics live – latest updates

The UK government’s “one in, one out” deal with France, which was supposed to help deter small boat arrivals, is expected to expire on Thursday, government sources have said.

The deal involved returning to France one asylum seeker who had arrived in the UK in a small boat, in exchange for another brought legally to the UK from France. It lasted 423 days – from 10 July 2025 until 1 October 2026.

The UK’s official explanation was that it had not been able to scale up the numbers of asylum seekers involved as much as it would have liked to. However, the scheme was beset with problems. Scores returned to the UK during the scheme because they felt unsafe in France. Some were returned to France a second time while others were allowed to remain in the UK to have their claims processed here. Many were believed to have vanished after being returned to France. Asylum seekers said they were threatened by smugglers because they owed them money and feared being sent back to their home countries or to another European country they had passed through on their journey.

Approximately 1,500 asylum seekers were returned to France, with a similar number brought legally from France to the UK. The numbers removed under the scheme were fewer than the total who arrived in small boats over seven days in the second half of last month. More than 40,000 have arrived in Britain in small boats during the period the deal has been in place.

It is understood France wanted to end the deal because it did not want to carry the weight of accepting small boat arrivals back from the UK alone and instead wanted the rest of Europe to also get involved. Other European countries have so far not agreed to join the scheme. “Why do we have to manage this border on our own?” the French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said at a parliamentary hearing this year. “We believe that France should not have to bear the burden alone, and that it would be better to incorporate it into an agreement between the European Union and the United Kingdom.”

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said at a recent session of the Commons home affairs committee that it was difficult to pinpoint exactly why there had been a reduction of more than 40% in the number of people crossing the Channel so far this year compared with the same period last year. Others say that lower levels of irregular migration into the UK from France in the first five months of this year compared with the same period last year are likely at least partially to be due to a drop in arrivals of irregular migrants to Europe overall. The Home Office said it would continue to remove as many small boat arrivals as possible. But it is not possible to forcibly remove people to unsafe countries such as Iran, Eritrea, Sudan and others, where many on small boats come from.

NGOs such as Medical Justice have condemned the trauma they have documented due to the detention of this group, many of whom are survivors of trafficking or torture. Force was used against one in 10 of 224 asylum seekers during their removal to France in the first three months of this year, according to Home Office freedom of information data. Both the NGO Médecins Sans Frontières and the French health organisation Samusocial, which provides treatment for returnees to France, documented physical and psychological injuries. At the home affairs committee the home secretary suggested these injuries may have been self-inflicted. The Labour MP and committee member Bell Ribeiro-Addy accused the home secretary of “victim blaming” and said there was independent evidence of injuries sustained as a result of use of force.

Successive prime ministers and home secretaries have vowed to stop small boats crossing the Channel. So far none have succeeded. For as long as people flee war and conflict a percentage of them are likely to turn up in the UK by one means or another. The use of return hubs in third countries is under discussion by some European countries although no details have been confirmed.

In a word, overjoyed. “Thank God. You gave me the best news,” said one asylum seeker forcibly returned to France, after hearing the news. He is now considering returning to the UK. Another who is also hoping to return said: “That’s good news. We just hope the UK doesn’t make a worse agreement with a new country.”

Warrington’s bid to make it fifth time lucky fuelled by 71 years of agony

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 14:16:42 GMT

Wakefield’s progress has brought romance to the Grand Final but Warrington ending their long title drought would be just as stirring

It is a tale of two potential fairytale endings on Saturday evening with a unique twist. An eye-catching statistic spread across social media since last weekend’s Super League playoff semi-finals, pointing out that the boroughs of Warrington and Wakefield are extreme rarities in Europe as they have populations of more than 200,000, but no professional football teams.

Those two settlements will be front and centre of the rugby league landscape, as Warrington Wolves and Wakefield Trinity go in pursuit of history at Old Trafford. Trinity were in the Championship only two years ago, and are hunting a first major trophy since 1968.

But to ignore Warrington’s own journey to this point would be doing everyone associated with the town a disservice. The longest-running joke in rugby league among supporters is Warrington’s long, long wait for a league title – you have to go back to 1955 to find their last. Unlike Wakefield, in their maiden Grand Final, Warrington have been here before: four times.

Whereas Wakefield are fuelled by romance and the prospect of “doing a Leicester” as it has been dubbed, Warrington are motivated, and perhaps even angered, by being the butt of the joke for just a little bit too long now.

“It pisses me off,” says the Warrington-born hooker Danny Walker. “It’s always been part and parcel of playing for Warrington and it’s up to us to shut people up and stop that song [the ironic ‘it’s always your year’] being sung.”

Walker has been in the stands on multiple occasions and seen Warrington lose Grand Finals, so what the Wolves possess is a deep-rooted understanding of how painful it is to lose at Old Trafford. That could be the difference.

“I still live locally and even this week we’ve had people stopping us, telling us what it would mean to them,’” says Walker. “There’s people that have been going for 70 years and never seen it. We know what it means. You don’t have to worry about that.

“I’ve been stood on the Wembley pitch as a loser, watching another team win the Challenge Cup and I’ve been in the stands enough times at Old Trafford watching us lose. I’ve been to three of the four, including in 2018 just after I’d signed for the club. It’s an exciting week but I know what it feels like to lose here.”

It is not just Warringtonians who possess that desire to bring the title to the town. George Williams won everything there was to win with Wigan and was ridiculed five years ago when he returned from the NRL and chose the Wolves. He insisted he could inspire the Super League title: in his final game for the Wolves before going back to Australia, he can make good on that promise.

“I’ve been there before and won it, but I’ve never wanted to win a game as much in my life,” he says. “I was bold enough to say it back then and I’ll stand on my word. The goal has never changed over the last five years. We’ve missed the mark at times but now we’ve got this opportunity.”

This time last year there was an internal review at Warrington into Sam Burgess’s future as head coach, after the Wolves limped to an eighth-placed finish. He survived that and deserves immense credit for turning the fortunes of the Wire and perhaps his own coaching career around.

The parallels with his greatest moment as a player, helping South Sydney Rabbitohs win a first Premiership in 43 years against all the odds, are too tantalising to ignore as he gears up for his first Grand Final as a head coach. “It was one of the most appetising things about the job,’ he says. “I’d be lying if I wasn’t very interested in breaking the drought when I took the job.”

Burgess has leaned on his mentor, the legendary Australian coach Wayne Bennett, in the run-up to the final, but all year he has insisted the pressure of the past does not weigh heavy on his side. On Saturday we will find out if that is true.

Jess Cartner-Morley’s October style essentials: glam jeans, an irresistible coat and my shoes of the year

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 14:00:54 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Ready to fall back in love with getting dressed? Our fashion expert’s favourites bring layers, colour and just the right amount of drama

The best women’s autumn wardrobe updates

October is when getting dressed starts to get interesting again. It is not yet cold enough for the full swaddling, but there is bandwidth for layers, texture, colour, a little drama. This month’s edit has all of the above. There is an irresistible coat, a tomato-red jumper to wake up everything you already own, and the bag I think may be the answer if you want something roomy that still feels neat. Also, stirrup leggings!

Elsewhere, I’ve finally located the right sheer shirt for anyone ready to dip a toe into transparency, some extremely glamorous Marks & Spencer jeans and a lovely ring that looks much more special than its price. And because October is also the month when staying in starts to sound as appealing as going out, there are candles for the kitchen table. A sensible autumn shopping list, but with a little soul.

Boden Camilla cotton crew sweater in crimson red

A classic tomato-red sweater will give your wardrobe a lift. Layer it over a stripe with the collar and cuffs showing, or tie it over the shoulders of your blazer for a flash of colour and a potential extra layer if it gets chilly later. This is a cotton blend, so it won’t swelter you, and it has slightly full sleeves so you can layer it over a shirt without the sleeves bunching.

M&S high-waisted embellished barrel jeans

I was in M&S stalking a brilliant skirt I saw at the press day that doesn’t seem to be in store yet (will let you know when I find it!) and found these jeans, which look so fancy, all embellished with black beads and gems, and would make a knockout but easy-to-wear party outfit with a camisole and a tuxedo jacket.

Rixo Micah embroidered jacket

I am not going to pretend this is the most practical coat in the world, and you’ll have to wait for it because it’s on preorder for delivery in December. But look at it! Absolutely delicious. You probably already know Rixo for its brilliant dresses – it has a capsule collaboration coming to John Lewis later this month; I have seen it, and I think you will love it – and the coats are great too. With vintage-style embroidery, kimono-width sleeves and deep faux fur trim, you can wear this over a party dress to make a dramatic entrance, but it will also look brilliant over a T-shirt and jeans.

Kurt Geiger Chelsea flap bag

Kurt Geiger has been London-based since the 1960s, when it opened a store on Bond Street. Lots of rainbow stripes, which I fully endorse as a brand-values symbol of kindness and inclusivity but don’t necessarily want to wear on a handbag. But the quality is great – details like adjustable shoulder straps, which really matter – and there are always classic colours as well as the rainbow. This shape is perfect if you want a large bag that still feels neat.

L’Agence Arleen kitten heel mules

When I got these shoes I thought they were a classic I would wear occasionally, but I’ve worn them more than any other non-flat shoe for months now. I hate shoes that slow me down, so I generally ignore mules, but these are comfortable and secure, so you can walk at a normal speed. They are the perfect travel shoe because they take up so little room, weigh almost nothing, and make every outfit look better. They also come in leather, which would arguably be more practical, but the suede is so soft, and you can’t be sensible all the time.

Vuori stirrup leggings

I saw another fashion editor at Heathrow during the recent month of catwalk shows, wearing stirrup leggings and ballet pumps and a crew-neck sweater, and I believe I have finally found my version of what the youngsters call an Airport Fit. Yes, stirrup leggings are kind of silly, but that’s sort of the point – they turn leggings (boring) into a look. And they tie the leggings to your shoe, visually, I mean, so the silhouette is more elegant. This won’t be for everyone, but, you know, putting it out there. These are mine: I am a big fan of Vuori; the fabrics are so comfortable yet hold their shape.

Arket silk organza shirt

Sheer clothes aren’t just for red-carpet exhibitionists any more. Sheer layers are happening in real life. I think they work right now because they stop oversized, untucked outfits from drowning you. A sheer shirt is a good place to start: you can wear it over a tank top during the day, but it will also look dead chic and modern for evening over a lace bra if you are feeling slightly racy. Found this organza one in Arket, and I love the deep grey shade.

Carrie Elizabeth vintage crest ring

Carrie Elizabeth jewellery has been around for a decade and is gaining traction – it is in Liberty for the first time this season – because in a market that often feels divided into cheap trend-led baubles and eye-wateringly expensive fine jewellery, it offers affordable pieces that feel personal and special. This 14-carat gold vermeil ring is beautifully detailed – it makes you want to look closer, which I love – with an elegant, slim band.

Nobody’s Child herringbone pleated skirt

This perfect, kicky little skirt has a matching herringbone blazer. The suit has a cute Cher-in-Clueless energy to it, but I’d wear this with a rugby shirt, black tights and biker boots.

Søstrene Grene bi-colour candles, set of two

Scented candles get all the love these days, but I love an old-fashioned taper candle as a cheap and cheering way to brighten up the kitchen table. The shell pink and electric blue colour combination is giving Roksanda energy.

School gate to checkmate: British chess prodigy, 11, is youngest ever woman grandmaster

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 14:00:52 GMT

Bodhana Sivanandan’s father taught her to play age five and soon she was beating ex-champions. Now she is lighting up the Chess Olympiad

Over the weekend, 11-year-old Bodhana Sivanandan became the youngest ever holder of the title of woman grandmaster at the Chess Olympiad in Uzbekistan – while playing on a car booster seat so she could reach the board. By Tuesday morning she was back at school in north London for a design and technology lesson.

Bodhana has to juggle the competing pressures of being an international chess sensation with the more ordinary challenges of childhood and her first term at secondary school.

She takes it all in her stride. “I’m used to going to tournaments and then coming back to school the next day,” she told the Guardian in her first interview since returning to the family home in Harrow. “Now that I’m in secondary school there might be more homework, but I should be able to manage.”

She has won three smartphones at various tournaments but she is still too young to be allowed to use them. “One day I’d like a phone, but I’m fine without,” she said. Sitting beside her, her father, Sivanandan Velayutham, who works in IT, added: “I don’t think it is the right time for her to have a phone.”

Bodhana’s meteoric rise up the chess rankings suggests she is thriving without the distraction of social media, even if it means missing congratulatory posts from her growing fanbase including Rachel Reeves, Rishi Sunak and the children’s commissioner, Rachel de Souza.

Competing in Uzbekistan meant the family had to secure an authorised absence from her new school and she will have to catch up on a fortnight of missed classes. But Bodhana is a fast learner; her father taught her to play chess when she was five, and within a year, and with the help of YouTube videos, she was beating him.

When she was seven, Bodhana won 5-1 playing simultaneously against six members of her local Harrow chess club. At eight she managed to beat the former British champion Peter Lee. In July she became the youngest girl to beat a grandmaster with a rating of over 2,600, and she was the youngest person ever to be selected for an England team in any sport.

Bodhana’s latest victories in Samarkand give her a rating of 2,382, surpassing the required 2,300 points to become a woman grandmaster. She is just a few points away from the 2,400 required for international master status and needs 2,500 points to be an outright grandmaster. If she achieves that in the next 11 months, she will become the world’s youngest ever grandmaster.

Bodhana is not aware of that deadline. “I want to become a grandmaster as soon as possible, but I’m doing it because I like it, not to just chase records,” she said.

Her ambition is simply to be the best player in the world.

Nigel Short, one of Britain’s best ever chess players, was roundly criticised in 2015 for claiming men’s brains were hardwired to be better at chess than women. Bodhana has other ideas. She said: “By rating, yes men are better than women, but a woman could also achieve the same thing if they work hard enough, so I don’t agree fully.”

She took on the current world No 1, Magnus Carlsen, in a game of speed chess earlier this year. “It was a blitz game, and I lasted about 10 minutes. No one likes losing, but losing is kind of necessary to learn.”

Bodhana has a fearless approach to chess. “I don’t get nervous, but even when I do, I just try to focus on the game and forget about everything else,” she said.

Jonathan Eckert, 67, a keen tournament player, could only manage to draw against Bodhana when she was six. “I was fairly confident of winning, but she played the endgame extremely well, which is the sign of a classical player. A lot of these youngsters are incredibly good at tactics, because they’re playing against computers all the time. I was quite surprised she was battling with me on strategy.”

Bodhana is used to being praised on her classical play and positional sense. “Lots of people say that about me. It means you don’t play very sharp tactics, but I can also do that if I need to.”

The booster seat can help unnerve opponents. “Sometimes it distracts them, but I don’t know if it freaks them out,” she said.

Her favourite player is José Raúl Capablanca, a Cuban world champion from the 1920s whose books and games she has studied. “I like the way he plays in his endgames,” she said.

Away from chess, Bodhana enjoys playing the piano and violin, and reading. She does not watch television because she does not have time; she has eight hours of chess tuition a week paid for by English Chess Federation and the Chess Trust.

Her father is keen to add that the family is also grateful for sponsorship from the Turkish investor Evren Üçok, Tangram Therapeutics and the John Robinson Youth Chess Trust.

Bodhana’s next nine-day tournament could be the London Chess Classic at the end of November, but only if it fits in with school and the schedules of her parents and younger twin sisters. “If good tournaments come up we try to work it around,” said her father.

“We’re not pushy, we just work on our goals and keep going. Opportunities are scarce in this world. You have to understand your kids and know what they like and allow them to shine.”

Burnham is right that ‘hope comes from honesty’. That’s why Labour must make the case for rejoining the EU

The Guardian Thu, 01 Oct 2026 13:04:31 GMT

Brexit was a disastrous act of national self-harm. Britain needs EU membership to bring growth and security in an increasingly volatile world

Hope again. That was the prime minister’s message to the country this week. A national social care system, greater public control of water and energy, help for first-time buyers and a crackdown on rogue landlords and empty homes. With clarity and conviction, Andy Burnham set out a bold plan to put Britain on a new path, steeped in Labour values.

It felt like a conference speech that would be remembered for years to come, marking a decisive break with a broken political model that has let British people down for decades. And perhaps most encouraging of all was the prime minister’s promise to rethink Britain’s relationship with the EU.

Burnham’s words were simple but stark: “Brexit has done more harm than good.” He is right – and the reality of the vote’s impact on the UK is sobering. Research commissioned by City Hall in 2024 showed that London’s economy was £30bn smaller than it would have been without Brexit and that there were nearly 2m fewer jobs overall in the UK as a result of us leaving. Earlier this year, we set out new analysis showing that our country has grown more slowly than our comparable European counterparts since 2016. If that trend continues, our economy could be £250bn smaller than similar EU countries’ by 2030.

Ten years after the referendum, the sunlit uplands promised by the Brexiters have proven to be a total fiction. Instead, Britain finds itself battling an economic and geopolitical storm.

Earlier this year, I warned that Donald Trump’s bombing of Iran could have catastrophic consequences for Londoners, and it gives me no pleasure to be proved right. The folly of this reckless war of choice is now clear for all to see. The conflict is sending shock waves through the global economy, hiking up mortgage costs and pushing up fuel prices. The price of diesel has hit an all-time high at nearly £2 per litre, while energy bills are forecast to rise 25% this winter, piling unbearable pressure on many households across the UK already grappling with a cost-of-living crisis.

At the same time, Trump’s fondness for unilateralism has shaken the foundations of the transatlantic alliance on which our national security depends. As Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, persists with his illegal and unconscionable full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Trump’s unpredictable actions and unsettling ambivalence towards European security can no longer be ignored.

In this geopolitical storm, Europe offers us not just a safe harbour, but a huge opportunity for growth. The EU is our biggest trading partner and our most reliable ally. That’s why, at the UK-EU summit in November, I will call on the government to lay the groundwork for Britain’s swift return to both the customs union and the single market – a move that should happen within this parliament.

Rejoining the customs union and the single market would deliver an immediate boost to economic growth, improving living standards for communities across the country and helping to grant Londoners some respite from the most acute cost of living pressures. In the long term, however, we must raise our ambitions higher still. Our party must immediately start making the case for rejoining the EU, so we can fight and win a general election with EU membership effectively on the ballot paper in 2029.

The brutal truth is that leaving the EU was the biggest act of economic and geopolitical self-harm in our country’s history. Rejoining is the only viable path to long-term prosperity and security. Anything less will fail to undo the severe damage that’s been done.

For far too long, the Labour party’s debate about Europe has been constrained by “red lines” that make rebuilding our relationship with the EU impossible. But Burnham has now recognised that these lines were drawn up for a different world.

In Canada, Mark Carney has set out his plan to partner much more closely with the EU on defence, critical minerals and energy security, with the country now on the path to becoming the bloc’s first associate member. In this multipolar world, middle powers such as Canada, the UK and our European neighbours must come together, both to safeguard our own security and economies and to stand up for free trade and our liberal democratic values.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Deeper integration can – and will – unlock a new age of growth and productivity, but it will also provide us with a louder voice on the world stage. From bolstering our military defences to safely developing AI and combating the climate crisis, if we are to make ourselves heard, we must speak as one. And in a world whose superpowers appear ever more comfortable with throwing their weight around, the EU is the only organisation with the economic and geopolitical heft to hold its own.

For me, the most memorable line in Burnham’s speech came a couple of minutes in: “Hope comes from honesty.” They were the words of a leader unafraid to change the terms of Britain’s dysfunctional political debate by taking on the seemingly intractable problems that too many would be inclined to avoid.

Today, Brexit is foremost among those problems. If we are to bring back hope, we must be honest about the disastrous costs of our decision to leave the EU. And we must be honest about the fact that reversing it is the best chance we have to get Britain back on track – and get the country firing on all cylinders again.
