Anthropic Says It Discovered a Crispr-Like System. Now What?

Wired September 29, 2026

Tech executives have long touted the potential for their AI models to accelerate the pace of biology discoveries. Last week, they announced one. In a September 23 announcement, Anthropic claimed that its large language model Claude had identified an enzyme system with properties “reminiscent of Crispr,” the Nobel Prize-winning gene-editing tool.

According to Anthropic, about 950 Claude agents running simultaneously found the interesting genetic sequences in 21.5 hours. “I sincerely compliment Anthropic for telling the world about their discovery,” says Fyodor Urnov, a gene-editing expert at the University of California, Berkeley and director for therapeutic R&D at its Innovative Genomics Institute. (IGI is collaborating with Anthropic, but was not involved with the new discovery.)

Other scientists are less enthusiastic about the finding, which is the first to come out of a research group formed by Anthropic earlier this year. “The experiments are still in the queue. The PR is already live,” says Le Cong, a professor at Stanford University focused on integrating AI into genome engineering research.

Anthropic, which has set up a wet lab for drug discovery, has been clear that the finding isn’t the end of its work. (“We don’t yet understand what this system does,” the company said in an X post, “but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA.”) One physical experiment was included in a technical report, which has not been peer-reviewed. However, a lot more needs to be done to determine the significance of this discovery. It remains unknown whether this enzyme system can be used as a gene-editing tool and, if so, whether it’s a useful gene-editing tool.

“Let's say we are on Santa Monica Beach and trying to scan through all the sand to find a diamond,” Cong says. “AI found this thing that looks very shiny, and then you have to go back to the lab to know—is it glass? Is it a diamond?”

Claude found this shiny object after researchers at Anthropic prompted it to search through huge genomic databases for “interesting new examples” of reverse transcriptases, proteins that copy RNA into DNA. This is the opposite of the normal process in our cells, in which DNA is transcribed into RNA, but is used by other organisms in a variety of biological functions, including inserting segments of DNA.

Claude agents initially identified more than 200,000 possible reverse transcriptases, according to Anthropic, and, after picking out several thousand that appeared to be new, narrowed the scope even further, eventually finding an “unusual” reverse transcriptase family containing a long region of repeat DNA sequences that resemble Crispr. Anthropic is calling this system ART, short for array-associated reverse transcriptases. The system is found in jumbo phages, large viruses that infect bacteria.

“I can see by eye a tandem repeat array … that's a Crispr-like … repeat array?!” an AI agent wrote. The agent also acknowledged that this system could be a retron, as noted in the technical report. Crispr and retrons are both bacterial immune systems, and while retrons have some utility in gene editing, they’re not the same multi-tool Crispr is. It’s therefore not too surprising Anthropic’s blog post played up the Crispr comparison.

Seth Shipman, associate investigator at the Gladstone Institutes, doesn’t think what Anthropic found is a new Crispr system, but says the discovery is still interesting. “The novel thing is how they found it, not what it is,” he says. His lab has used retrons to make gene-editing systems, so it is possible to use retrons in this way.

Identifying new reverse transcriptases can take months of mining genome databases manually, so Shipman says the fact that Anthropic was able to do this in a day is impressive. But he cautions against attributing the discovery entirely to an AI model. “I think we have to be careful about saying that Claude autonomously discovered something, because there are scientists involved in the study,” he says.

In fact, this same reverse transcriptase was previously identified by Jason Gill, a microbiologist at Texas A&M University, and his colleagues in a 2021 paper on jumbo phages. What’s perhaps new is that Claude identified repeats around it that hinted the enzyme might be part of a Crispr-like system.

“These models are good at finding patterns, better than a person staring at it with their eyeballs can,” Gill says. “A person could do all this but you have to already have a hypothesis in mind.” He adds that ART appears to have no “obvious relationship” to any known Crispr system, and it’s on Anthropic to prove that it actually has gene-editing activity.

Cong credits the scientists for finding the perfect kind of problem for Claude to tackle, given its pattern-seeking abilities. It’s possible the model could be used for similar large-data projects, but that doesn’t mean Claude will suddenly be accelerating all sorts of discoveries in the life sciences.

What kinds of information this model was trained on is also not something the scientific community can evaluate, which makes these findings unusually opaque in an era where major journals require scientists to freely publish their code in the name of reproducibility. This has also led a researcher who had been studying these exact enzymes to become suspicious that the model was trained on his work, since he’d shared yet unpublished findings with the public version of Claude. (“Claude was,” Anthropic told the New York Times, “not trained on any user transcripts, and our molecular biology team has no such access, either.”)

Even if Claude did identify the next big thing in gene editing, it would still take human scientists testing out that hypothesis in the lab to prove it. In a post on X about the discovery, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei mused, “Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment.” Even if this does prove possible, it will be in a fairly distant future. (The idea, of course, raises many questions about safety and oversight, and Amodei quickly followed up this thought by mentioning that Anthropic’s labs are at the lowest biosafety levels, and thus don’t contain anything greatly harmful to humans.)

Answers in this area don’t come quickly. It took 25 years from the initial discovery of Crispr sequences in bacteria in 1987 until Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier demonstrated it could be a programmable tool to cut DNA in 2012. And while Crispr is now ubiquitous in labs and is being tested in dozens of clinical trials to treat cardiovascular conditions, cancers, autoimmune diseases, and rare disorders, there is only one drug on the market so far that uses the technology, approved in late 2023. It’s a testament to the long arc of scientific progress—and the difficulties of translating promising basic science findings into medicines.

The limits of Anthropic’s finding also point to a more fundamental issue. What made Crispr revolutionary was that scientists identified a biological system that was previously unknown. It remains to be seen whether any AI model is capable of finding something useful without knowing exactly what it’s looking for.

“If you have an AI that only trained on knowledge from before people ever discovered Crispr, and then that AI actually discovered Crispr, that seems to be a better setup to test an AI scientist,” Cong says.

OpenAI’s Dots Are Always-On AI Agents—and Its Answer to Meta’s Muse

Wired September 29, 2026

Dots are OpenAI’s new always-on AI agents, announced at the company’s DevDay 2026 event on Tuesday in San Francisco. These agents complete tasks on a user’s behalf and are depicted as cute blobs you can personalize and assign multistep projects to complete.

OpenAI’s Dots are powered by the startup’s GPT-6 Astra model. A core selling point is their “always-on” design—unlike a single-turn chatbot experience, these agents constantly crawl the web and attempt to complete whatever task you assign to them. Dots also pull context from connected apps and learn more about your preferences over time.

In one demo example shared by OpenAI, a user’s Dot helps plan dinner. The Dot proactively saw that the user’s calendar showed they were working through dinner and messaged with two GrubHub food delivery options with pricing for each. The user followed up with their food pick and when they wanted it ordered. In another example, a user collaborated with the agent to launch a new website.

Users can message Dots through ChatGPT, Slack, and Microsoft Teams, with the user’s context shared with Dots across modes. In addition, Pro users can join a waitlist to text with their Dots in iMessage or RCS messaging on Android.

The Dots rollout starts today for subscribers to ChatGPT’s Pro tier that costs $100 a month. OpenAI often launches new features first for this higher subscription tier and then rolls them out to a larger subset of users over time. Users can start by controlling one Dot, but the company is expected to eventually roll out the ability to control multiple agents at the same time.

The Dots launch is also part of OpenAI doubling down on its efforts to attract more enterprise clients. On stage at DevDay, CEO Sam Altman announced “specialist Dots” for enterprise customers tuned for specific tasks, like accounting, email marketing, and legal analysis. It adds to the trend of AI agent coworkers being integrated into more professional workflows.

Dots are designed to get explicit approval before taking more sensitive actions on a user's behalf, like installing software or changing a password. Users can enable a Custom Rules tool to set explicit boundaries that they don't want agents to cross, as well as tasks that need more direct permission to complete.

As users connect their data and use agents, it's worth keeping potential security and privacy risks top of mind. OpenAI built safety guardrails into these Dots, but even so, asking agents to automate aspects of your life involves trusting the tools won’t accidentally share information you didn’t intend or get tricked by an online adversary into taking actions you didn’t want. Exercise caution when interacting with this nascent software and connecting data from your pre-existing apps. Also, if your OpenAI account is set to allow model training on your data, this setting carries over to your interactions with the agents.

Personal agents are currently having a breakthrough moment. While this year started with early adopters in Silicon Valley latching onto tools like OpenClaw, the recent release of Meta’s Muse agent reached a larger user base that is now experimenting with personalized agents. Muse rocketed to the top of smartphone app download charts, but Dots has come for Meta's lunch.

How to Beat Surveillance Pricing Before It Bleeds You Dry

Wired September 29, 2026

I always feel like I’m overpaying whenever I buy something these days. I never seem to have access to the best coupons, and apps with algorithmically adjusted prices don’t exactly lower the cost of what's in my cart. It feels like prices are constantly creeping up and my budget is being stretched thin.

These core frustrations were what drew me to Gouged: The End of a Fair Price and What That Means for Your Wallet. Author Lindsay Owens knows what it's like to advocate for consumers' economic interests. She’s the CEO of Groundwork Collaborative, a DC think tank and corporate watchdog, and previously worked as an economic policy adviser in Senator Elizabeth Warren’s office.

Before the launch of her book, available now, we spoke about how software has been instrumental in changing how goods are priced, and how generative AI could make existing issues worse. Owens also shared a couple of tips for readers who want to claw back a fair price.

The following conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

WIRED: The era of fixed prices for goods and services already feels like it's in the rearview mirror. How did we get to this current cultural moment where costs are so variable?

Lindsay Owens: It turns out we all got a little too comfortable with the fixed price. We'd had it for 150 years, since John Wanamaker stuck a price tag on the items in his department store in Philadelphia in the late 1800s. Maybe we just assumed it was a law, but it was actually a norm.

If you buy something using links in our stories, we may earn a commission. This helps support our journalism. Learn more.

It is under attack, if not gone. I think the biggest contributor to the end of a fair price is new technology. There was, of course, always an impetus to overcharge, but new technologies have supercharged that impulse. Big tech reinvented the rip-off. They supercharged these age-old impulses, and they made it possible to squeeze more out of Americans in almost every transaction. New technologies are the cornerstone of this shift.

An eye-opening moment for me earlier this year was when I requested all the data McDonald's keeps based on my app interactions. I got a 515-page dossier that estimated a zero percent chance I'd ever stop being a customer. How can loyalty apps negatively impact what people pay?

Loyalty programs are sophisticated data harvesting. Most of us kind of know that. We enter knowing it's a bit of a devil's bargain. We are giving up a lot of data, but we do it in exchange for the promise of deals and discounts tied to our loyalty. It turns out they're not holding up their end of the bargain.

In 2004, a Duke economist named Curtis Taylor put out a piece asking what would happen once companies could buy and sell records of what shoppers purchased. He said that once loyalty programs go high-tech, firms will use those records to identify their most eager customers and charge them more. The effect was that consumers would pay a price for their loyalty. I think his warning rings true today.

Could you explain what you mean by surveillance pricing?

Surveillance pricing is a technique that's at the intersection of two things Americans hate: getting preyed on and being ripped off. It’s a colloquialism for something you might have learned about in economics class called personalized pricing. This is the idea of changing prices not based on market conditions, not based on demographic groups. In first-degree price discrimination, the company uses information about me personally to decide and estimate my willingness to pay.

Importantly, willingness to pay isn't the same thing as ability to pay. Maybe you need something urgently—you're a mom in the middle of the night with a sick kid, and you need Tylenol on your doorstep in the morning. There are all sorts of reasons why you might be desperate.

You mentioned earlier that software innovations are a major driver of these changes. Do you see generative AI as exacerbating existing issues?

Absolutely. Agentic commerce is not ubiquitous quite yet. We're in the early stages, but the early warning signs are flashing. Walmart says Sparky cart totals are 35 percent higher than non-Sparky cart totals. These new technologies are supercharging age-old impulses to upsell you, to get you to purchase an add-on, to make sure you leave with the item instead of coming back tomorrow.

AI agents are often marketed as tools that can help automate your online shopping decisions. How else could this kind of outsourcing of decisionmaking backfire for consumers?

We're at an inflection point. We can quickly move to regulate this and require agents to work in consumers' interests, as other agents in our economy work in consumers' interests.

Your realtor has to work on your behalf. Your lawyer has a best-interest standard or a fiduciary standard even in some cases.

The cost of living and affordability crisis is making life hard for Americans. These new technologies are making consuming and shopping exhausting. Once you imagine layering in fighting off a snake oil salesman, then you realize consuming is about to be completely different.

In the US, do you see laws banning surveillance pricing happening primarily on the state level, or will federal decisionmakers get more involved?

It's a little of both, right now. I worked for Senator Warren as a staffer, and I just testified on behalf of [Senator] Josh Hawley on this issue. So, I think this issue is a nonpartisan one.

Obviously, federal momentum takes a long time; there's been more movement at the state level. We've seen dozens of pieces of legislation to crack down on surveillance and algorithmic pricing this year. Some of it has passed and been signed into law in states like Connecticut, New Jersey, and Maryland.

How can I beat surveillance pricing? What strategies can I try, even if it's a Sisyphean effort?

From the bottom of my heart, I do not believe it is every consumer's job to duck and dodge and bob and weave and beat the machine. There are some ways to fight back, like calling members of Congress. Look, I think raising your voice is important.

In addition, there are a handful of ways to try to get a better deal. The first is to change the way you comparison shop. You can't just comparison shop across brands; you have to compare within brands: logged in versus logged out, in the app versus on the website versus in the brick-and-mortar store. Maybe you also change geographies using a VPN? These are all ways to comparison shop the same item from the same company but in different modalities.

The second thing is they figure out how much they can overcharge us by experimenting on us. My organization exposed Instacart's massive experiment treating millions of Americans as guinea pigs without their knowledge in A/B tests. You can turn the experiment back on them. Call your friend. Ask them to fire up their app. See who gets a better deal. You can even have them purchase it, and Venmo each other. Sit next to your spouse, and both look at plane tickets.

These are useful tools, but when you use these suggestions, you lose something that is also valuable: your time. These are time-intensive efforts, and our time is valuable. The fact that corporate America is also sucking that dry is pretty frustrating.

Amazon Prime Day deals are back, baby. The second sale of the year is officially dubbed Prime Big Deal Days and will arrive on October 6 and 7. Don't miss our list of Prime Day tips put together by yours truly, plus our guide to Amazon Prime benefits you might be forgetting to use. Our guide to shopping safe on Amazon might be useful as well.

Trump’s ‘Morally Binding’ AI ‘Accord,’ the Rise of AI Agents, and Extremists on the Ballot

Wired October 01, 2026

This week on Uncanny Valley, Brian Barrett, Zoë Schiffer, and Leah Feiger discuss the “morally binding” AI accord tech executives signed following a meeting with Donald Trump. They’ve agreed that AI labs will regulate themselves—should work out great. Plus, the team digs into OpenAI’s Developer Day, where CEO Sam Altman introduced AI agents for normies, otherwise known as Dots; how AI agents are coming to workplaces near you; and a quick rundown of the most extremist candidates running for office.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer, and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger. Write to us at uncannyvalley@wired. com.

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Give us a rating, tell us what you think. Five stars is nice, but we'll take the feedback too. It really helps more people find the show. Also, if you're in the Bay Area, we will be doing a live audience recording of the podcast on Thursday, October 8, at 7 pm at The Commons, headquarters of our KQED friends in San Francisco. You can buy tickets on kqed. org or check out the show notes for the link. You won't want to miss it. OK, onto the show.

Zoë Schiffer: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor.

Brian Barrett: I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Brian Barrett: This week we've got a new proclamation or rather a "morally binding" AI accord from the White House. After a meeting between tech executives and Donald Trump, it basically says the AI labs are going to regulate themselves. Should work out great. Plus we'll talk about OpenAI's Developer Day, where CEO Sam Altman announced the company's new always-on AI agents for regular folks. More AI agents again, should work out great. Everything's working out great today.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. And as AI agents become way more popular in Silicon Valley and beyond, employers are pushing to have these agents harmoniously work alongside human employees. We'll get into how that process is actually going and what the chances are that we're all going to have to welcome some bot colleagues very soon.

Leah Feiger: And with the midterm elections closing in, we're going to be talking about some of the extreme candidates running for office. It's not just political candidates who feel emboldened to say whatever they want. It's also people who are currently or have been recently working for the government, including a retired army colonel turned Pentagon influencer who WIRED reported this week, posted plenty of praise for dictators and has a plan to strip the vote from anyone without kids.

Brian Barrett: Let's start though with a nice luncheon that happened on Tuesday. President Trump invited all his favorite AI executives over to the White House. It felt like a little bit of a motley crew in some ways, but that's neither here nor there. They came out with a signed document called the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. Super intelligence, of course, how the government is now referring to AI, artificial intelligence. That includes internal evaluations, letting an outside audit firm come in and make sure everything's OK, and having the company's own board review those audits. And it's all voluntary.

Leah Feiger: That remains the keyword here. When it ever comes to any sort of proposed regulation at all that we've seen thus far in the AI space when it comes to the White House, voluntary is the word. I don't know, is it so silly of me to be so hung up on this that none of this is real? This is all fake.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I don't think we were expecting the Trump administration to come out with real regulations for AI companies. Their big thing is—

Leah Feiger: For sure.

Zoë Schiffer: AI growth. But yeah, I mean when they came out, Trump came out in front of the White House with all of the CEOs, their kind of takeaway message was like, "We got this. We take it seriously. Don't worry about it." And I think it was actually stated by someone there like, "We'll regulate each other. We're looking out for each other."

Leah Feiger: I mean, we have to talk about this one particular moment. So here's what he said.

Here are the richest, most powerful men in the country lined up telling you we're going to regulate it. It's all good. We're aware this is not doing well with polls right now, but we've got this." It just feels like a grab bag. Which perhaps is most emphasized by the fact that the words US were quite literally misspelled in the accords document. It reads President of the Unites States under Trump's signature, which is, I don't know, I'm not saying they quickly rushed this together, slap dash, signed it on, flew people out, but I'm not saying it doesn't look like they didn't do that either.

Brian Barrett: Can I say one thing that is weird about this to me? Zoë Schiffer: I personally think Republicans are going to do great in the midterms, but you can cut that because I am not reporting on politics and that's just my vibe check.

Right now, I think that with gas prices the way that they are and certain polls coming back the way that they are, it will be really surprising to me if the Democrats manage to lose this. Not Republicans win this, this would require the Democrats messing up, which again, all possible.

Zoë Schiffer: Going back to the AI summit and luncheon, Brian, were you or were you not surprised to see not a hint of an Apple representative?

Brian Barrett: A little bit. Apple has been, they were the ones who memorably Tim Cook presented Donald Trump with a golden trinket.

Brian Barrett: No big enough. Not a big enough trinket. Do you read it, Zoë and Leah, as Apple just not being relevant enough in AI still today?

Zoë Schiffer: 100%.

Brian Barrett: I think they would be there in a heartbeat if they were invited.

Zoë Schiffer: It's not that they were bad at diplomacy.

Leah Feiger: But is Mark Zuckerberg that relevant?

Brian Barrett: Yes. 100%.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah.

Leah Feiger: You think? OK. All right, I'm wrong.

Brian Barrett: Meta has the most popular consumer AI agent today.

Zoë Schiffer: Not because the AI agent ... They just have distribution and so Meta's AI can be so popular so fast because they can shove it down everyone's throats and that's exactly what they're doing. And they're basically promoting a free AI agent that they're subsidizing pretty heavily at the moment. And so yeah, but I think Apple is just frankly not in the game. Not in the game.

Brian Barrett: Talking of AI agents and Muse is what we're talking about. Meta's Muse AI agent has taken the app store by storm, but that's because it hasn't had much competition until on Tuesday, as we said, OpenAI had its Dev Day. And in his big keynote speech, Sam Altman walked on stage and devoted most of his time to Dots, which is OpenAI's answer to Muse. It's their always-on agents. You can interact with them through ChatGPT or Slack. The features are pretty established at this point. You can basically tell your agent to go do whatever task online for you and they will get it done. Zoë, I know, has been playing around with her own agents. You're much deeper into that than Leah and I are. Two things here. One, how much does OpenAI need Dots to connect in order to maintain its position in the AI race? And two, how'd they do in terms of adorability? They're really going for adorability, they're trying to make them adorable, I don't think they quite connected. I think Muse is cuter. There, I said. It doesn't mean you should use either of them.

Zoë Schiffer: This is a conversation?

Brian Barrett: It is though. So I'm talking over you because—

Zoë Schiffer: No, no, do it.

Brian Barrett: I'm joking, but the whole point of I think the fact that they're making these so cutesy and fluffy and adorable is obviously intentional. It is what is going to win over the average consumer and make you forget that you are giving away all of your privacy and all of the information and all of your accounts to this adorable fuzzy-wuzzy little thing instead of a data center.

Leah Feiger: Is that part of internet safety conversations now, Brian? When you sit around with your kids and you're like, you're going to have access to this, don't be fooled by the fuzzy avatar. They just want your bank details.

Leah Feiger: Brian's rules for the road folks. You've heard it here.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. Well, I was just going to say, I was at the Developer Day yesterday, and I had a few observations. On one hand, OpenAI does seem really focused right now. They saw Instinct and Muse, these other kind of OpenClaw for normie-type agents and were like, "OK, we have to play this game." And they got it together really, really fast. I think it's interesting because a lot of these capabilities have actually existed for a minute now, but when you talk to people in the industry, they'll talk about form factor a lot. Dots gets access to your email, your calendar, sometimes your financial information, and then it can do things on your behalf. The kind of gateway drug, if you talk to people who use these, and I'm one of them, is restaurant reservations. You can say, "Hey, I'm going to New York at this time. I was actually, I have to say, Noah Shinn, who's the CEO of Instinct, he's 23 years old. I repeat, this man is 23 years old. His company, less than two years old, valued at $10 billion now. He gave his first longform interview since his app completely blew up, and he talked about restaurant reservations. I was really waiting to be like, "This man has thought deeply about what happens to the internet when agents are doing all of your browsing and booking." No, sir. No. Mm-mm. He was like, "It's going to be great because previously restaurant reservations were first come first serve, and now your agent can say if it's your birthday or an anniversary and then the restaurant can prioritize you." I was like, "You only have to think about this for two seconds to realize that then everyone will just say it's their anniversary or birthday. What do you mean?" Anyway.

Leah Feiger: Oh, my God, I'm so depressed.

Brian Barrett: It's funny, that reminds me of, we're getting a little bit off topic, but another in that same vein, there was a warning this week from one of the banks, I believe, or just sort of an observation that as everyone gets these agents, they're always going to be optimizing and they're always going to be looking for the best result for their user. And we're not set up in a world where everybody's optimizing all the time. The example they gave was banking. If everyone takes all of their money from low to no interest rate savings accounts and puts them all into money market accounts where they're making 3% to 6%, whatever, on that account, the US financial system could collapse basically. It's like a run on the bank, because we are built for, that system is built on assuming that people are going to have very low to no interest rates because that's how banks can make their own interest on it. So yeah, when we have this world where everybody has their own AI agent looking out for their best interests, negotiating with other AI agents to figure out who gets the best result, I think we're going to run into some really interesting unintended consequences.

Zoë Schiffer: For sure. And the other thing that I was really struck by yesterday, going back to Leah's point, is it just felt like there were a lot of different messages being said about what an agent like Dot can do. It's like this cute, fuzzy agent, except they kind of brushed away the restaurant reservation thing. It was like, of course they can book tables for you, but it can also do all of this hardcore engineering bug bashing stuff. And mentioned security and privacy, I do think this is something they're thinking about, but it just feels like the messaging around them is really confused. Ben Thompson talked about this recently on TBPN, and he was like, "Most people don't want to be more productive. They want other things. You shop because shopping's entertaining." This idea that we're all builders and we all want to optimize every area of our life, do more work, I don't think speaks to a lot of people.

Leah Feiger: I think that's the thing that I keep coming back to. Even with the restaurant reservation world, and look, this isn't for everyone, but you say to an agent, "I want to go to three of the best restaurants in New York City that will be priced under 150 a person." That's a very specific liminal space. Obviously, I get it. If you don't have a lot of time, you have a work trip, you have whatever. There's a lot of people who really enjoy reading the New York Times best restaurant reviews and combing through the blogs and this is where this person I really trust has told me that I should go. So the idea of optimizing everything also feels like then we lose so much, right?

Zoë Schiffer: Totally.

Leah Feiger: And again, I get that it's not for everyone. No everyone has the same interest here, but there is this very weird missing piece, missing cultural piece that all of a sudden goes.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. The other thing that Noah Shinn, again, the CEO of Instinct, talked about on that podcast when the interviewer, who again is setting up a pretty slam dunk interview, these questions were not super hard-hitting, but he's like, "What are you excited about?" He named the restaurant reservation thing. And then he's like, "Also, people are taking photos of every item in their closet and then Instinct is suggesting outfits for their week." And I was like, obviously, I'm not the core demographic here, but you think an agent built by a 23-year-old engineer is going to give you sartorial advice that you actually want to follow?

Leah Feiger: Again, it's the what culture are we losing people? I find a new argument every week for something making me mad, and that might be it today.

Brian Barrett: Well, I'll say not only that, not only is there the question of how many people really want these? And to be clear, maybe everyone wants these. Maybe these could be huge, a lot of people are enjoying their Muse.

Leah Feiger: I mean, not everyone is against this. Zoë, not to call you out, you want this life. You want the robot command center.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. I mean, I'm using the agents, and this is what is interesting to me, is I do think that they are useful and valuable. Last night, Andrew asked me when a babysitter was coming next week, and I had the agent put together a shared calendar, a child care calendar with the dates that the girls don't have school, the dates we have coverage, the dates we need coverage, share it with everyone relevant. That would've taken me an hour and it happens in less than a minute. It is really nice. Of course, to make that happen, you have to have an agent have calendar access, access to your email, be able to share a calendar with other people in your email. Again, these are all risks. But what's interesting to me is when you hear the AI executives talk about the technology and the possibility of the technology, to me, it feels like they don't even get what they're building. I don't know a lot of people, and certainly I don't want this, that want an AI agent to give them fashion advice. The stuff that they want, that I want is really basic and mundane.

Leah Feiger: You want an assistant.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, because the agents can do so much more, they're like, "Well, yeah, of course it can do that, but here are all these other things." But people actually just want the basic things done and done reliably and well and without putting all their information at risk, and we need to nail that in order for this to really go mainstream.

Leah Feiger: Do you have fears? OK. Yeah, I'm just so curious because in so many ways me not doing this is not because I decry the usefulness. Honestly, like you describing a shared family calendar, I'm like, "I need that. I need that yesterday and I just haven't gotten around to it," but I haven't done it because I'm scared, full stop. I'm just actively scared. How do you manage that?

Zoë Schiffer: I mean, I am scared. I talked about this in the article I wrote about Instinct last week. I live in fear of my personal information getting out, getting beyond my control, all of that stuff. And I think I'm more scared now with agents than I was before, for sure. At the same time, the agents can be useful for, the other week, a friend sent out a paperless post for a barbecue. My dad clicked on it. I was instantly warned by my agent that it was a phishing scam, and so I didn't. And so my kind of read was, I'm really busy. I could make a mistake just myself going around my life because I'm trying to multitask and pick the girls up from school while I'm working and all of this stuff. And so it's helpful having another set of eyes. The fact that set of eyes could then be its own security risk sucks. Tim Heidecker Is Bringing His Joe Rogan Parody Show to The Onion

Wired October 01, 2026

As satirical news outlet The Onion continued to wage a legal battle to acquire the assets of Infowars out of bankruptcy this summer, it launched a streaming program that spoofed the brand and its bellowing conspiracist ringleader, Alex Jones.

Comedian Tim Heidecker took the reins of the operation, adopting Jones’ guttural and paranoid bluster as he investigated, among other unconfirmed reports, whether Jones himself had exploded in his car after eating too much Whataburger.

But Heidecker wasn’t about to stop there in his quest to transform the Infowars brand into a gonzo comedy network along the lines of Adult Swim. Now he’s taking aim at another high-profile target: Joe Rogan, the bro podcaster whose rambling, misinformed conversations with everyone from Vice President JD Vance to [checks notes] Yakov Smirnoff have somehow kept his long-running series, The Joe Rogan Experience, at the top of the charts for years. Heidecker’s companion show, The Tim Heidecker Podcast, premieres at 8 pm ET on Thursday night, and WIRED can exclusively reveal that the debut episode includes lots of complaining about pronouns, wildly dumb speculation around AI, and plugs for a supplement called “Crab Salts” that makes your “head hurt” and causes you to shout.

A representative for Rogan did not immediately return a request for comment.

Heidecker first lampooned Rogan’s discursive and disorganized interviews in 2021, with a viral 12-hour podcast (in reality, one hour of footage looped a dozen times) covering topics including psychedelics, cancel culture, and whether Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson would run for president. His guests for that show, comedy duo and Onion contributors Rajat Suresh and Jeremy Levick, return for the new episode, offering their “expert” takes on hot-button topics. (The pair have essentially perfected the art of fake celebrity web content and once even got Justin Theroux in on the joke for a mock Hollywood Reporter-style actors roundtable.)

“What is essentially happening is, in place of Christianity, we have the 10 commandments of woke,” Levick says during a discussion of DEI policies on the first episode of The Tim Heidecker Podcast. The chat veers into concerns that bearded men are dressing as princesses to visit Disneyland. Heidecker then abruptly informs the boys that he’s planned a weekend trip to Glasgow “for Scotch wrestling.”

In 2026, it’s more difficult than ever to exaggerate the absurdities of the right-wing media ecosystem, with its fact-free moral panics and bizarre alternative medicines. Though if anyone is up to the task, it’s the endlessly inventive Heidecker—who will have no shortage of grifters and lunatics to go after once he’s done with his run as a Rogan type. Luckily for him, few of those potential impressions are as rough on the voice as Alex Jones.

Amazon Alexa Devices Are Already on Sale, but the Deals Aren’t All as Good as They Look

Wired October 01, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Amazon's Prime Day has returned for its fall edition, and the Amazon Alexa-powered devices are already on sale. But are the sales actually any good?

There's already the question of whether you want Alexa in your house, and now it's a question of whether the sales are more of a mind game than a real discount. That's thanks to Amazon raising prices across its device categories at the end of August, leaving us with the same product lineup but a worse case to recommend it. Some devices are already on sale right now ahead of Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days for $40 off, but went up in price by $20 just a few weeks ago, cutting that discount into something that feels barely worth the spend.

If you're interested in Amazon's device sales but want the real picture of what the discount is and which devices are worth it, I've got you covered. I've been testing Amazon Alexa speakers since they launched in 2012, and I am also WIRED's resident Kindle tester, which gives me almost too much insight into the price games Amazon plays with these devices. Here's my full breakdown.

Right now, Amazon's Alexa-powered Echo speakers and Fire TV sticks are currently on sale ahead of Amazon Prime Big Deal Days next week (October 6-7). These devices saw price hikes at the end of August, so some of the deals aren't as good as in the past. They do seem to be permanent price changes, though, so if you're certain you want one of these models, this is the best time to buy.

So far, most Kindles aren't on sale yet, but all three Kindle Kids models (the Kindle Kids, the Kindle Paperwhite Kids, and Kindle Colorsoft Kids) are already on sale. (Amazon also announced new versions of these Kindles today, along with the rest of its lineup, so it's up to you whether you want the current on-sale model or to preorder the new one!) If you're looking for a Paperwhite and Scribe, they aren't on sale yet as of this writing. Neither are Eero routers.

But I expect most of those models will be discounted once the event begins. Both Kindle and Eero products also saw price hikes at the end of August, so I recommend buying them only on sale (even if the sales aren't as good as they used to be, since they're similar discounts but on higher prices).

Not all deals are great, especially given the recent price increases. If you're set on getting a new Amazon Alexa-powered speaker, though, here are the discounts (and devices themselves!) that are still worth it.

Amazon

Amazon

Best Buy

The best deal in Amazon's early device deals is easily the second-gen Echo Spot, revived in 2024. It's 50 percent off its new price, and it's still a solid discount off its original price of $80. I really like this fun little smart speaker. It works great as a bedside alarm, shows when your next alarm is set, and can display the weather or your calendar details when you ask Alexa. Best of all, you get the fun benefits of a screen without a camera to worry about.

Amazon

Amazon

The only new Amazon Alexa speaker that didn't get hit with a price change is the second-gen Echo Studio. It still sits at $220, which is not only its original price, but also the original price of the first-gen model. It's a nice thing to see. Its discount isn't huge for Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days, but it's $40 for powerful, room-filling sound that could extend across great rooms without getting muddy.

Amazon

Amazon (65-inch)

Amazon (55-inch)

The Amazon Ember Artline TV is another rare device from Amazon that didn't see a price hike at the end of August, maintaining the $1,099 price it had at launch (and now has a $300 discount off that). It's a well-priced art television that is more accessible than its more expensive competitors, and comes with handy features like built-in Alexa+. I'm usually not a fan of the Fire TV devices, but this one keeps catching my eye and is already on sale for Amazon Prime Big Deal Days.

Amazon

Amazon

Out of Amazon's new smart displays, the Echo Show 11 is my favorite. It's a little larger than the Echo Show 8, but not so much that you can't comfortably fit it onto a kitchen counter. It also has better sound than the newer Echo Show 8. The price rose by $30 at the end of August, but $100 is still a good discount, even if it is off the new price.

Amazon

Amazon

If you're looking to get an Echo for as cheap as possible, this is the one to get, and this is the best time to buy it. The fifth-generation Echo Dot packs good sound for its size, but is best on sale since I don't think it's worth the new $80 price tag it got in August. But $40 is fine, and the cheapest you'll get for a current model. (Still more than I think it needs to be, though.)

If you're shopping for a Kindle, this is the best time to buy since most were hit with price increases. You won't get as good a deal anymore, but it's much better to buy it at a discount on the new price than the full, higher price for the same product. There's also new Kindles that were just announced, so it's up to you if you want to grab an older on-sale model (which all work great!) or wait for the new one.

As of this writing, only Kindle Kids models are on sale ahead of Amazon Prime Big Deal Days, but only one is a good deal after taking the price changes into account.

Amazon

Amazon

Best Buy

I think kids and kids' books have a much better chance of taking advantage of the color screen than adults, which is why I love the Kindle Colorsoft Kids if you're shopping for a young reader. It also comes with a full year of Kids+ content—more than any other Kids model—and the color covers are beautiful. It has a good discount, even though the price did increase by $30 at the end of August.

Looking for a different device during Amazon's sale event? We've tested several other Amazon Echo and Fire TV devices that are also on sale right now. Here's what else you can consider, and what the discount looks like.

Amazon raised prices across several of its device categories at the end of August. It's not a shocking move, but it hit many affordable products and makes for a worse sale season since we're getting discounts on a higher price tag for no other improvements. Here's a quick breakdown of most of the price changes to help you navigate what sales are good and which are really just bringing you back to the old price.

Either way, I'd only buy an Amazon device on sale now, but it is unfortunate the sales just won't be as good anymore on these existing devices. I expect most, if not all, of these devices to go on sale at some point during Amazon Prime Big Deal Days.

Amazon’s New Kindle Lineup Is Lighter, Thinner, and More Metal

Wired October 01, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The Kindle will turn 20 in 2027. Amazon says it plans to celebrate the milestone throughout the year, but to kick things off, it's starting with an entirely refreshed Kindle lineup.

On Thursday, the company introduced a handful of new Kindle models: a new 6-inch base Kindle, a 7-inch Kindle Paperwhite, and a 7-inch Kindle Colorsoft. You can buy Signature Editions of the latter two and Kids versions of the entire range, which include artist-designed kids cases, a year of Amazon's worry-free guarantee for damage, and a year of Kids+, the company's subscription service that offers unlimited access to ad-free, child-appropriate books.

The highlight is Amazon's use of aluminum for the Kindle's construction rather than traditional plastic. The starting tier is plastic, but you can upgrade to an all-aluminum model (Amazon uses 80 percent recycled aluminum) if you prefer that Kindle model and you just want something more robust.

It can get a little confusing with all the different SKUs, so here's a quick rundown:

The base Kindle, the aluminum version, and the Kids Kindle are on sale starting today. The Paperwhite and Colorsoft are available for preorder on a rolling basis and will launch at the end of October.

The Kindle's screen offers 30 percent faster book opening than its predecessor, Amazon says. The build is a whole millimeter thinner at 6.8 mm, and Amazon cut the weight by around 18 grams to 140 grams. The Kindle Paperwhite and Colorsoft are both similarly lighter (204 grams) and thinner (6.8 mm), retain the waterproof design, and feature adjustable warm reading lights. Like before, the screen has a higher pixel density that makes text appear sharper.

Amazon says the new Kindles are also compliant with the European Union’s new battery regulations, meaning the batteries should be easier to remove and replace.

Upgrading to the Signature Edition for the Colorsoft and Paperwhite nets you the aluminum build, an ambient light sensor that adjusts brightness automatically, and an accelerometer that lets you turn the screen to landscape orientation and have the pages adjust accordingly. The upgrade also adds the ability to use a double-tap gesture to turn pages.

Uniquely, the Signature Editions feature pogo pins that let you charge via Amazon's new $60 dock, which props the device up as it charges. There's also a new Page-Turn Cover ($80)—a case with physical page-turn buttons that magnetically attaches to the back of the devices and pairs via the pogo pins, which Amazon says offers page-turn buttons to the vocal minority that still loves them (around 5 percent of Kindle users) without adding unnecessary bulk to the device.

Don't worry, you don't need the case, the Signature Edition, or even a new Kindle if you just want page-turn buttons. Amazon is debuting its own Kindle Click, a $35 page-turn accessory that pairs over Bluetooth for the non-Signature (and older) Kindle models.

The Kindle business is booming. Amazon's Kevin Keith, vice president of devices, says Kindles have seen double-digit growth over the last three years, with 2025 being the highest sales year in more than a decade. He says 60 to 65 percent of people buying new devices have never had a Kindle before, with Gen Z, millennials, and even Gen Alpha driving the lion's share. This past January saw the highest single-month Kindle reading volume in history.

At the same time, Kindles are more expensive than ever. “Memory pricing is a little bit crazy,” Keith says, referring to the memory shortage behind the general price bump on all electronics. Amazon upped prices of existing Kindles earlier this year; the new devices match those prices.

Part of the redesign aims to lower overall manufacturing costs and standardize the hardware. Take the refreshed display on the base Kindle—Keith says many of the improvements trickle down from the development of the Kindle Scribe. For the first time, the base Kindle has a display that sits flush with the body, just like its pricier counterparts. (It previously had a raised plastic bezel around the screen.) That whole front panel is also available in a new color: Ube (purple).

While Amazon has made Kindles with colorful fronts (like the matcha green Kindle from 2024), it hasn't done this with flush displays. That's because simply coloring the front would make the Ube color, for example, scatter around the screen as the frontlight reflects it, casting a purple hue on the display. To counter this, Keith says Amazon developed a new “edge-to-edge” color technology that prints two different colors under the cover lens: the Ube color backed by a layer of black. The black absorbs the light, which solves the problem. Amazon says it perfected this tech in the Scribe and ported it down here.

Color is important. Keith says alternative colors typically make up just 15 to 20 percent of sales—the rest being classic options like black or white—but the matcha green model captured a surprising 55 percent. Amazon also chose that color because, at the time, it noticed a general increase in the popularity of matcha in drinks and sweets (it also noted that folks on #BookTok are reading in coffee shops). Hence the new ube color, which is based on the popular purple yam of the same name.

“We've been tracking food trends, and two years ago, ube just exploded—ube was growing 200 percent year over year,” says Chris Green, Amazon's vice president of design. “We expect it to do far better than the matcha.”

For the aluminum housing, instead of milling the device's frame from a block of aluminum and using a lot of water in the process, Amazon stamps a flat sheet, which then goes into a forge that presses down to create the backplate and sides. The process supposedly takes seconds compared to the hours it can take to machine a single aluminum device frame (like an iPhone or MacBook), saving material and energy. It helps lower the Kindle's carbon footprint, which is now equivalent to 11 hardcover books.

Green says these improvements bring down the device's density. The density of the average human body is around 1 gram per cubic centimeter; an iPhone is around 2.2 grams per cubic centimeter. The new Kindles are around 1.2 grams. Lowering that number can help make the hardware “disappear” during prolonged use.

“I truly want people to never think about the Kindle,” Green says. “I just want them to think about the magical world that the author has created inside of this device.”

For Green, who has designed nearly all of Amazon's hardware in his 19-year tenure at the company (and yes, he says he's embarrassed by the Fire Phone), chasing that 1.2-grams-per-cubic-centimeter target is all about getting the gadget out of the way so the Kindle can mimic the analog calm of physical print.

“More people are reading on paper, more people are reading on Kindles,” Green says. “Is it a backlash to AI? Probably. People are trying to find things more authentic—we're in a crisis of authenticity.” Surveys have shown that overall leisure reading is down across the US, but the people who are reading are buying more than ever.

As for the 20th anniversary of the Kindle in 2027, Keith says the company may roll out a significant refresh to the Kindle's user interface, though he didn't share more. Expect special anniversary editions of some Kindles. When I asked whether we could expect the return of the Kindle Oasis—an asymmetrical e-reader with physical page-turn buttons—Green chuckles.

“The first Oasis was one of my passion projects,” he says. “I loved that. I really, really loved that product. But I was a vocal minority on that—most of the people wanted slabs.”

So, probably not.

Correction on October 1, 2026 at 2:30 pm: We've updated this story to correct an incorrect statement about page-turn speed that Amazon initially provided (along with Kevin Keith's title).

I Found the Best Kindles to Take Your Library Anywhere

Wired October 01, 2026

Amazon

Amazon (16 GB)

Amazon (Colorsoft)

Amazon

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

There’s a lot to love about a Kindle if you’re a reader. If you’re looking for the best Kindle, you really can’t go wrong with any of the models. These Amazon-powered ebook readers let you bring thousands of books anywhere and typically give a month of battery life per charge. You can subscribe to get unlimited books from Amazon or get free books from your local library. Our guide will help you decode the differences to find which Kindle is right for you.

I've owned all kinds of Kindles, from the newest Kindle Scribes to hand-me-down base Kindles without a front light. The latter came from a friend who noticed I had spent my entire postpartum summer glued to library books on my phone, and I still have it to this day. But after trying all of the latest Kindles, I can say it's easy to spot the best one.

Read on to find out my favorite overall Kindle and my favorite Kindles for specific uses and younger readers. You can also check out my other buying guides made for readers like me, including the Best Kindle Accessories, Best E-Readers, Best Digital Notebooks, and Best Gifts for Book Lovers.

Updated October 2026: I've added details about the new Kindles announced today.

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon (Signature)

You came here to find out one thing: What is the best Kindle? The Kindle Paperwhite is Amazon's most popular Kindle and our favorite after testing every model, thanks to its great range of features. You'll get a large display with high resolution and warm lighting, and the technology inside has fast and smooth performance. Amazon launched the 12th-generation Paperwhite in late 2024, and it's been our new favorite ever since. Whether you want to read more or are tired of carrying physical books, all the extra features are worth the price. The basic Kindle may seem enticing, especially with the fun new colors it offers, but the Paperwhite will serve you better in the long run, especially if you're a nighttime reader like I am. The warm lighting is a great option on the eyes before bed.

If you already have a Paperwhite, the update isn't so major that you need to upgrade to the newest model, but it's the best to choose if you're shopping for a brand-new Kindle. You'll get a slightly larger screen and the highest contrast ratio on any Kindle, not just of the Paperwhites. The battery life also increased from two months to three months, and it has the thinnest form factor yet. The 12th-gen Paperwhite has two versions: the standard and the Signature Edition. The latter comes with auto-adjust brightness, wireless charging, and double the storage at 32 gigabytes. The regular Paperwhite is more than enough and easily one of the best Kindles to buy, but if you plan on buying the model without lock-screen ads, you may as well pay the extra $30 for the Signature Edition.

Speaking of price differences, both the Kindle Paperwhite and the Paperwhite Signature Edition recently became more expensive after Amazon increased some of its prices. The base Paperwhite went up $40 to hit $200, while the Signature Edition went from $200 to $250. I'm curious how much cheaper they'll be during fall sale season; we might now see the old base price as the new sale price. I'd wait for Prime Day or Black Friday to purchase either version of the Paperwhite.

Amazon

Amazon (16 GB)

Best Buy (16 GB)

Students who want something digital to take notes on but who also love to read will love a Kindle Scribe. While there's a new version of the Scribe out that's also great, the best one is still the second-generation Kindle Scribe from 2024.

This model has the same 10.2-inch (300 ppi) paperlike display as the first iteration, but it has a white border for a more notebook-style look, and the new Premium Pen is not only included but also has a soft-tipped eraser at the end. Personally, this is my most-used Kindle because I love to scribble notes and ideas all day long. It's easily my most-used Kindle and digital notebook because of the long battery life (12 weeks!) and the convenience of grabbing it for both my reading and note-taking needs. While I don't have as many options and layouts as I would on a true digital notebook, the Kindle Scribe still offers a handful of options to help me free up most of the ideas jumbling around in my brain, and solid options for students.

The second-gen Scribe also packs new software capabilities, even if it's the slightly older model. Active Canvas lets you write directly in the book you're reading, though it won't work like true annotation—instead, the notes will appear in a small square on the screen like a Post-It note. That means it'll always be there if you resize the screen, but it didn't feel as natural as our testers would've liked. There are now Expandable Margins as well that let you write notes in the side panel of books, which feels a little more intuitive, but still isn't the full annotation experience you might want.

There are also a couple of generative artificial intelligence features. The Refined Writing tool transforms your notes into a script font, while Summarization will quickly summarize pages of notes into bullets with a script font that you can then share from the notebook tab. Both features work well, but I never find myself reaching for them. These new software features can be downloaded onto first-generation Kindle Scribes if you already have one, or you can wait for an over-the-air update to hit your device. There are now three new Kindle Scribe models, which I detail below, but I still prefer this model. It also didn't see a price increase like other Kindle devices did, but that's true across the Kindle Scribe category.

Amazon

Amazon (Colorsoft)

Amazon (Colorsoft Signature Edition)

Amazon now has two versions of its colorful Kindle. There's the Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, which came out last year and was Amazon's first-ever model with a color screen, and now there's a basic Kindle Colorsoft. It competes with colorful models we’ve already seen from Kobo and Boox, so while it’s new for Amazon, it’s not new in the world of e-readers. Both models have a 7-inch display with an oxide backplane for speedy performance and higher contrast for both color and black-and-white content. The front light has also been changed to include nitride LEDs, which enhance color and increase brightness.

The Colorsoft Signature has a few extra features, but it also comes with a higher price tag. You'll get twice the amount of storage—32 GB to the base Colorsoft's 16 GB—wireless charging, and an auto-adjusting front light. It's a nice set of add-ons to get for just $20 more if you know you'll use the wireless charging and want an auto-adjusting light, but unless you already have a wireless charger you love, you'll probably be just as happy spending $20 less. It's already a hefty increase for the color screen and no other new features. The good news, at least, is Amazon did launch Dark Mode for Colorsoft, which it previously didn't have.

Amazon also raised prices of the Kindle Colorsoft and Colorsoft Signature Edition, bringing both up $40 to $290 and $320, respectively. I'm curious to see what sale prices both of these get come Prime Day and Black Friday—I'd hold off buying anything until then.

Amazon

Amazon

Best Buy

I’m a parent of a young kid, and the books in our house are very, very colorful. We're still getting started on reading, but pulling up a book on the colorful Colosoft Kids is a much more fun experience than a black-and-white option. The color makes everything more engaging: The bookshelf of your books! The options to choose from on Kids+! The pages in the illustrated books themselves! Having a colorful option is something a lot of users want, but I think kids of all ages have the best chance of really getting the most use out of it. They can enjoy everything from picture books to graphic novels with full-page color, and add colorful highlights to books they want to annotate or study. It's not quite as vibrant as a digital screen or color on paper since it's an E Ink screen, but it's still a fun feature that adds to the reading experience.

You can technically turn on Kids mode on any Kindle, so you don't necessarily need a Kids-branded model (there's both a basic Kids ($180) and a Paperwhite Kids ($230) model) to have your kiddos read books separated from adult ones. But the real benefit is that Kids models, whether it's the Colorsoft or a black-and-white model, come with free access to Kids+ for six months to a year. Kids+ is Amazon's subscription service that features tons of age-appropriate books. The Colorsoft Kids gets the longest access, a full year, while the other models will only receive six months. That extra six months, plus colorful pages, really make going for a kid-specific model worth it. The Colorsoft Kids is also waterproof and comes with a colorful cover (you get to choose between two fun designs).

It's no surprise that the Colorsoft Kids also went up in price like the regular Colorsoft models, as did the rest of the Kindle Kids line. This one went up $30 to hit $300, while the Kindle Kids is now $180 (up $50) and the Kids Paperwhite is now $230 (also up $50). My recommendations may change soon based on how expensive the color version has become.

Amazon

Amazon

If you're looking for something lightweight and affordable, Amazon's 11th-generation Kindle is your best bet. It was updated in 2024 and builds upon the 2022 update that added more storage, a higher-resolution screen, and USB-C charging. The 2024 model has a few nice updates, including a higher-contrast-ratio screen, a brighter front light, and a faster page-turning rate.

You still won't get a warm lighting feature, so if you want that, you'll have to upgrade to the Paperwhite or Colorsoft. But otherwise, you'll still get dark mode on this device (unlike the Colorsoft) and a snappy overall performance and nice screen brightness for the price point. Former WIRED reviewer Brenda Stolyar said the performance was a big improvement over the 2019 Kindle model she was previously using. If you have room to spend a little more, we still prefer the Paperwhite, since you'll also get a longer battery life and a waterproof build, along with the warm lighting, but this is a good Kindle for the price.

But not as great as it used to be since Amazon raised its prices, including this Kindle model. The 11th-gen Kindle used to retail for $110 and was often on sale for under $100, but now its starting price is $150. I'm curious how good the sales will be this fall, but I fear we won't see it fall under $100 anymore.

Amazon announced today that there's a whole new generation of Kindles coming, with every model getting a new version. Here are the details; I'll be updating this guide soon with thoughts as we review each model.

That's not all Kindle has coming out. There will also be a handful of new accessories, including the Kindle Click ($35) Bluetooth remote that will work with Kindle models as early as 2024, a Page-Turn Cover ($80), a Charging Dock ($60) designed to work with the pogo pins on the Signature Editions, and new Kindle covers in a variety of colors and textures. I'm most excited about the remote; I will update this guide and our Best Kindle Accessories guide with my notes as I test.

Amazon raised its prices across its product categories, including Kindle devices. The price increases hit several current Kindle models, leaving only the recent Kindle Scribe models with the original price tag. Amazon declined to comment to WIRED, but a spokesperson told CNET the price hikes were due to rising costs in memory and storage components. It's interesting that none of the more powerful Scribe models needed a price update, but it's also a relief since all three of those models are significantly more expensive than a regular Kindle.

Here are all the increases, including Signature versions:

If you have your eyes on one of these Kindles, I'd wait until Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday to shop when they're on sale. It's likely the sale prices will only bring the Kindle down to the price it was before, but better than paying more.

Amazon

Amazon (Kindle Scribe Colorsoft, 32GB)

Amazon (Kindle Scribe, 3rd Gen, 32GB)

Amazon (Kindle Scribe Without Front Light, 16GB)

Kindle has three new Kindle Scribes that launched between late 2025 and June 2026. There are now the Kindle Scribe ($500), Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($630), and the Kindle Scribe Without Front Light ($430). All three have a similar design and software experience, though the Scribe Colorsoft has a color screen and a shorter battery life—only eight weeks of reading time, compared to 12 weeks on the $500 Scribe and an impressive 16 weeks on the Scribe Without Front Light. Like the second-generation model, they're a great choice for note-takers and students, especially with the long battery life, but I still prefer the second-generation's price point.

All three models have a new, taller design with an 11-inch screen, a slightly slimmer form factor, and an updated stylus. They both also have a quad-core chip, a new homepage, and will support a variety of AI features, including AI search (along with some AI tools for summarizing books you're reading without giving spoilers, though those won't arrive until next year). Users can connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive to mark up documents, which the older model can't do.

Overall, I'd say they're good devices, but as long as the cheaper second-generation Kindle Scribe is available, I think it's the better buy. It has some AI capabilities but no AI search, and has a different homepage design that matches a classic Kindle rather than the notebook-forward design the new ones have. Amazon said it'll get the same homepage this year, but I haven't seen it so far. I'm disappointed these new devices are so much more expensive; at that price, you might as well shop reMarkable's line of digital notebooks and get better features and accessories.

If you've ever had a long reading session that gives you hand cramps, these accessories might help. You can check out more options in our Best Kindle Accessories guide.

This pillow stand holder can sit freely on your lap, bed, or any nearby surface while holding up your Kindle. There are two receptacles built into it, one of which is big enough for my larger mugs. I usually drop a snack or my phone into the other one.

If you're looking for something to hold up your Kindle that clamps onto something nearby, like your bed frame or a table, this gooseneck tablet holder does a great job. It's 3 feet tall and has plenty of length to work in all kinds of spots.

The PopSockets PopGrips are handy to add to Kindles so you can easily grip your device, but you will need to use an adhesive, add a MagSafe adapter, or grab a MagSafe Kindle case so you can attach it. There are a ton of fun designs, and you can even customize your own, like my custom WIRED PopGrip.

Amazon Kindles are, thankfully, not as fragile as a pricey smartphone, but you may still want to add a cover to protect the screen if you're frequently toting it around in a bag. These aren't padded for serious drops, but they are some of the best Kindle cases I've found for daily protection from scratches and scuffs. Also, don't forget that the Kids' editions come with cases, so if you're buying one of those, you won't need a case.

PopSockets came out with its own line of Kindle cases that have a built-in MagSafe adapter, so you can more easily add your PopSocket grip of choice to it. There are matching sets of cases and grips you can shop for, or mix and match as you please.

Amazon doesn't release new Kindles often—the company usually takes a few years between models. Whenever a new one arrives, its predecessor's stock starts to dwindle. It's not that we don't recommend these per se, but I only suggest these if you can find them on sale for the right price. And don't buy too old a model, since Amazon has started pulling support for older Kindles.

Before making your purchase, cross-check the price against the latest model to make sure you're paying a fair amount less for the older device.

Kindle (2022, 11th Generation): This is the smallest of the lot at 6.2 inches tall and 4.3 inches wide, with a 6-inch screen. If you find tablets too cumbersome to hold with one hand, consider this one. With this model, Amazon doubled the storage to 16 gigabytes and upgraded the display to 300 pixels per inch (PPI) resolution (up from 167 PPI). It's tough to find, and I usually don't see it for less than $75 these days.

Kindle Paperwhite (2021, 11th Generation): This is the next step up from the basic model. It has a bright 6.8-inch screen with adjustable warm lighting, a fast page-turn rate, a USB-C port, and 16 gigs of storage. It's waterproof too. We like the Signature Edition, which also includes auto-adjust brightness and 32 gigabytes of storage. Don't recommend spending more than $100 if you can find them.

Kindle Scribe (1st Generation): The original Scribe is a great option for note-takers. It has a giant 10.2-inch screen for taking notes, marking up PDFs, or drawing, and numerous paper formats you can choose, like college-ruled or dotted. It also comes with the Basic Pen, which feels natural to write with and attaches to the side of the Scribe magnetically. It's only worth it for $230 or less, and I often see it for under $200 on eBay.

Kindle Kids (2022): This is an older kid-friendly model. It comes with a cover, a year’s subscription to Amazon Kids+, parental controls, and a two-year warranty, but the fact that it's only available secondhand means you'll likely miss out on the subscription window and may or may not still have a cover. Ideally, don't spend more than $70 on this one.

Kindle Paperwhite Kids (2021): This older Paperwhite version is a step up from the previous basic Kids models. It has a high-resolution 300-ppi display with an adjustable warm screen and is also waterproof. You shouldn't spend more than $110 on this one.

Which Kindle Models Lost Amazon Support and Kindle Store Access?

As of May 20, 2026, Amazon stopped supporting Kindles released in 2012 or earlier. That means these models will not be able to get new books through Amazon's services or be registered to an Amazon account. You will be able to read books already on the device, though, and can manually download documents and books via USB cable and via software like Calibre.

The following Kindle devices are impacted:

What’s the Best Way to Buy or Sell an Older Kindle?

Have an old Kindle lying around? Are you looking at a used one for sale? If you're trying to figure out what model it is, this Amazon page includes photos, specs, and release years for the entire lineup. Once you know which one you have, you may be able to trade it in for credit toward a newer model.

Most old Kindles probably still work, just with fewer bells and whistles. It's best to avoid Kindles with keyboards or any other physical buttons other than page-turn buttons. Some older models lost the ability to browse, purchase, or borrow new books directly from the device. However, you'll still be able to do this via Amazon on your computer or phone and have it sent to your Kindle, which is a better experience anyway. These models include the Kindle 2nd Generation (International), Kindle DX International, Kindle DX Graphite, Kindle Keyboard, Kindle 4th Generation, and Kindle 5th Generation.

How Do You Get Free Ebooks on a Kindle?

If you buy every single book you want to read on a Kindle, it can add up! But there are ways to save some money while reading as much as your heart desires. You may want to subscribe to Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month. You can only choose from the Unlimited catalog, but there are millions of titles there, including audiobooks and magazines. Start out with the 30-day free trial.

If you already pay for a Prime account, you're eligible for some free ebooks through Prime Reading. There are not as many options as with Kindle Unlimited, and in a lot of cases, you'll see both Unlimited and Prime options lumped together; you'll have to look closely to find the free ebooks. It's still something, and there are even a few magazines.

If you don't want another monthly subscription and don't want to continue giving your money to Amazon, take advantage of the ebooks available with your library card. Browsing a digital catalog is not as magical as spending an afternoon looking over every shelf in a library, but such is the ebook life (no one says you can't read both!). We have a detailed how-to on this that you should check out, but here are some of the takeaways:

If you know someone else with a Kindle, you can lend books between your libraries, just as you would with a physical copy. Follow these instructions from Amazon if you want to share an ebook, but keep in mind that not all books can be loaned.

What Else Can a Kindle Do?

Kindles have helpful features you may want to take advantage of. Long-press a word or phrase to see its definition, highlight it, or take notes. You can also search the entire book for that particular word or phrase or translate it to or from other languages.

Word Wise shows short definitions in small text within the lines. Unfortunately, it's not available for all books, but when it is, you can turn it on or off and choose more and fewer hints. Clicking the short definition opens a longer one from Word Wise and the New Oxford American Dictionary or Oxford Dictionary of English (you can switch between the two), plus translations and a Wikipedia page, if applicable.

While reading, tap the top of the screen and click “Aa” to change font size or type—there's even a font called OpenDyslexic that helps make reading easier for people with dyslexia. You can control margin sizes and line spacing from that menu too.

When a Kindle is connected to a Bluetooth speaker or headphones, VoiceView Screen Reader (accessed through Settings > Accessibility) allows you to use gestures to navigate your device and reads aloud what you've pressed. It will also read a book aloud, though it doesn't sound nearly as nice as an audiobook.

Amazon owns Goodreads, so it syncs seamlessly to Kindles (press the three-dot menu > Goodreads). If you have a Goodreads account, you can review the Kindle books you've read or browse your bookshelf and recommendations. Long-pressing a word or phrase, in addition to what is mentioned above, opens up an option to share quotes directly to Goodreads.

There's a web browser too if you're connected to the internet (three-dot menu > Web Browser). It's not the best, so I'd reserve it for emergency searches.

How Do You Update a Kindle?

When Amazon releases a new software update, it will download and install to your Kindle automatically when it's connected to Wi-Fi. You can check if you're on the latest software by going to Settings > Device Options > Advanced Options > Update Your Kindle. If it's not on the latest software version, you'll see an update available and the Kindle will then prompt you to download and install it.

What Do I Do If My Kindle Colorsoft Has a Yellow Bar?

Following customer complaints in 2024 of a yellow bar at the bottom of the Colorsoft Signature’s screen and discoloration along the edges, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to WIRED that "customers who notice this can reach out to our customer service team for a replacement or refund.” The company also said it’s “making the appropriate adjustments to ensure that new devices will not experience this issue moving forward.” However, there are still customer complaints about this issue, even with the new model out. We have not run into this issue while testing the Colorsoft, Colorsoft Signature, or Scribe Colorsoft.

Is This a Good Time to Buy a Kindle?

The best time to buy a Kindle is during a major sale event like Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday, because Amazon often has steep discounts. Amazon has always had sales on some (if not all) of its Kindles on past Amazon Prime Day and similar events, like Amazon Big Deal Days.

You can also wait for other sale events if you're not ready to shop yet. Kindles are often on sale for Black Friday and Cyber Monday, which will occur in late November. Other sales often happen from time to time, but these sale events have consistent Kindle deals, so they're a good time to wait for if you want a better price.

Are Kindles Good for Students?

Kindles are great for students, though the model they'll like best will vary on how they use it. If they want to pair it with a stylus for highlighting and be able to take notes, get a Kindle Scribe model. These models also have long battery life, making them great for students to use for weeks on end without worrying about charging. You can get some textbooks on a Kindle too, and send library books to them. For students who love to read but don't want to take a ton of notes, a regular Kindle or Kindle Paperwhite will be best for them.
